topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Nature of partnership
topics.h: Two college friends in Pune start a cloud-kitchen and split the profit 50:50. Without signing anything formal, they may already be partners in the eyes of the law!
p: Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.
Essential features: two or more persons, an agreement (oral or written), a lawful business, sharing of profits, and mutual agency (each partner is both an agent and a principal).
Liability of partners is unlimited: if the firm's assets fall short, partners' private assets can be used to pay the firm's debts. Partners are jointly and severally liable.
Minimum 2 partners; the maximum is 50 under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014.
Accounts special to partnership: partners' capital (and current) accounts, the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account, and adjustments when the firm is reconstituted.

ex.q: Meera and Kabir jointly inherit a flat in Jaipur and share the rent they get from it. Are they partners?
st: Check each feature: two persons – yes; sharing of returns – yes.
But there is no agreement to carry on a business; they merely co-own property.
Sharing income from jointly owned property does not by itself create a partnership.
ex.a: No. Co-owners sharing rent are not partners, because there is no agreement to carry on a business together.

topics.rl: Many Indian CA firms, law chambers and family-run kirana wholesalers in Chandni Chowk work as partnership firms because partnership is quick to form and needs no heavy legal process.

rv.summary: Partnership (Section 4) is the relation between persons who agree to share profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. It needs 2 to 50 persons, an agreement, a business, profit sharing and mutual agency, with unlimited liability.
focus: The Section 4 definition and the five essential features
remember: Section 4, Indian Partnership Act, 1932
Minimum 2, maximum 50 partners (Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014)
Mutual agency: each partner is agent and principal
traps: Registration is not an essential feature
Co-owners sharing rent are not partners
Partners' liability is unlimited, not limited to capital

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Partnership deed and rules when there is no deed
topics.h: Friends fall out over money more often than over cricket. A partnership deed is the rulebook that prevents the fight before it begins.
p: A partnership deed is the written agreement among partners, ideally stamped as per the Indian Stamp Act. It usually states the firm's name, capital of each partner, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salary/commission, rules for admission, retirement and dissolution, and how accounts are kept.
If there is no deed (or the deed is silent), the Act applies: profits and losses are shared equally.
No deed: no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, and no salary or commission to any partner.
No deed: a partner's loan to the firm earns interest at 6% p.a. (Section 13).
Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Account, so it is allowed even if the firm makes a loss. It is not an appropriation.

ex.q: Asha and Vikram have no deed. Asha's capital is ₹5,00,000 and Vikram's ₹3,00,000. Vikram also lent the firm ₹1,00,000 on 1 April 2025. Profit for 2025-26 before any interest is ₹86,000. Divide the profit.
st: No deed → no interest on capital; partners share equally.
Vikram's loan gets 6% p.a.: ₹1,00,000 × 6% = ₹6,000, charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
ex.a: Interest on loan to Vikram ₹6,000; profit share ₹40,000 each.

topics.rl: Many CA firms, clinics and family businesses in Bengaluru run as partnership firms, and the partners' first legal document is the deed that spells out who gets what.

rv.summary: A partnership deed records the terms of partnership. If there is no deed, profits are shared equally, there is no interest on capital or drawings, no salary or commission, and interest on a partner's loan is 6% p.a., charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
focus: The rules that apply when there is no deed
Treating interest on a partner's loan as a charge
remember: No deed: equal sharing; no interest on capital or drawings; no salary or commission
Interest on partner's loan: 6% p.a. (Section 13), debited to P&L A/c
traps: Don't give interest on capital or salary when there is no deed
Interest on a partner's loan is a charge, not an appropriation
Don't share profits in capital ratio when the deed is absent

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Fixed and fluctuating capital accounts
topics.h: Two accounts or one? The choice decides whether a partner's capital looks rock-steady like Mount Abu or bobs up and down like a boat on the Ganga.
p: Fixed capital method: each partner has a Capital Account and a Current Account. The capital account changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn.
Under the fixed method, interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit, drawings and interest on drawings go to the Current Account.
Fluctuating capital method: only one Capital Account per partner; all these adjustments are recorded in it, so its balance keeps changing.
A fixed capital account always shows a credit balance; a current account (or a fluctuating capital account) can show a debit balance.
If the question does not say which method to use, prepare fluctuating capital accounts.

ex.q: Under fixed capitals, Nisha's capital is ₹5,00,000 and her current account opens with ₹20,000 Cr. During the year: interest on capital ₹50,000, salary ₹30,000, profit share ₹60,000, drawings ₹40,000, interest on drawings ₹2,000. Find her closing balances.

topics.rl: Big Indian partnership firms like audit firms often fix each partner's capital and run a current account, so the stake stays clear while yearly earnings flow separately.

rv.summary: Under the fixed capital method each partner has a capital account (changed only by permanent additions or withdrawals) and a current account for interest, salary, profit and drawings. Under the fluctuating method, all items go to one capital account.
focus: Which items go to the capital account and which to the current account
Showing a debit current account in the balance sheet
remember: Fixed method: capital account + current account
Fluctuating method: one capital account for all items
Method not stated → fluctuating capital accounts
Debit current balance → assets side
traps: Don't record drawings or profit share in a fixed capital account
A fixed capital account always has a credit balance
A debit current account is an asset, not a liability

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
topics.h: The firm has made its profit. Now comes the IPL-auction moment – who gets what, in which order?
p: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is an extension of the Profit and Loss Account. It starts with net profit and shows how it is distributed among partners.
Debit side: interest on capital, salary/commission to partners, transfer to reserve, and finally each partner's share of profit. Credit side: net profit (b/d) and interest on drawings.
Commission as a % of net profit before charging it = NP × rate/100. After charging it = NP × rate/(100 + rate).
Transfer to reserve is an appropriation; the remaining profit is then divided in the profit-sharing ratio.
Entry for appropriation items: Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c, Cr Partners' Capital (or Current) A/cs; for interest on drawings: Dr Partners' Capital/Current A/cs, Cr P&L Appropriation A/c.

ex.q: Net profit ₹4,00,000. Interest on capital: A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000. Salary to B ₹50,000. Interest on drawings: A ₹4,000, B ₹6,000. Transfer to reserve ₹40,000. A and B share 3:2. Find each share of profit.

topics.rl: A family-run sweets firm in Kolkata may pay the partner who runs the shop floor a salary first, put some profit aside as reserve before Durga Puja, and share the rest.

rv.summary: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account starts with net profit, adds interest on drawings, and deducts interest on capital, partners' salary or commission and transfer to reserve. The balance is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
focus: Items on each side of the appropriation account
Commission before vs after charging it
Journal entries for appropriation items and interest on drawings
remember: Debit: interest on capital, salary, commission, transfer to reserve, profit shares
Credit: net profit, interest on drawings
Commission before charging = NP × rate/100; after charging = NP × rate/(100 + rate)
traps: Salary to a partner is debited, not credited
Interest on a partner's loan belongs in the P&L Account, not the appropriation account
Use rate/(100 + rate) only when commission is on profit after charging it

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Interest on capital
topics.h: Money parked in a fixed deposit earns interest. Money parked in your firm deserves a reward too – if the deed says so.
p: Interest on capital is allowed only if the deed provides it. It is calculated on the opening capital for the year.
Additional capital introduced during the year earns interest from the date of introduction; capital withdrawn stops earning interest from the date of withdrawal.
Unless the deed treats it as a charge, interest on capital is an appropriation, so it is allowed only out of profits. If the firm makes a loss, no interest on capital is allowed.
If the profit is less than the total interest on capital, the available profit is divided in the ratio of interest on capital of each partner.
Working back: Opening capital = Closing capital − profit share credited − additional capital + drawings + losses debited (before interest on capital).

ex.q: Anil's capital on 1 April 2025 is ₹4,00,000. He adds ₹1,00,000 on 1 October 2025. Interest on capital is 10% p.a. Find interest for the year ending 31 March 2026.

topics.rl: An RBI repo-rate change ripples into FD rates, and firms often link the interest-on-capital rate in their deed to such market rates.

rv.summary: Interest on capital is allowed only if the deed provides it, on opening capital adjusted for additions and withdrawals by time. As an appropriation it needs profit: none in a loss, and profit shared in the ratio of interest if profit is insufficient.
focus: Calculating interest on opening and additional capital for the right months
No interest on capital in a loss
Sharing insufficient profit in the ratio of interest
remember: Interest on capital = capital × rate × months/12
Appropriation → allowed only out of profits
Profit < interest → share profit in ratio of interest due
traps: Don't calculate interest on closing capital
Don't allow interest on capital (as appropriation) when there is a loss
Additional capital earns interest only from the date it is introduced

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Interest on drawings
topics.h: Taking money out of the firm for your sister's wedding shopping? The firm may charge you interest – and the date you withdraw matters.
p: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed provides it. It is calculated for the time the money stays out of the business, up to the end of the year.
Different amounts on different dates: use the product method – multiply each amount by the months remaining, add the products, then interest = total products × rate/100 × 1/12.
Equal monthly drawings for a full year: average period 6.5 months (beginning of each month), 6 months (middle) and 5.5 months (end).
Equal quarterly drawings for a full year: average period 7.5 months (beginning of each quarter), 6 months (middle) and 4.5 months (end).
Dates not given: charge for 6 months on the total. If a flat rate is given (not 'per annum'), time is ignored.

ex.q: Partner Leela withdrew ₹10,000 on 1 July, ₹20,000 on 1 October and ₹15,000 on 1 January. The year ends on 31 March; interest is 6% p.a. Find interest on drawings.

topics.rl: Just as a bank charges interest from the day a credit-card amount is spent, a firm charges interest on drawings from the day money is withdrawn.

rv.summary: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed provides it, for the time money is out of the business. Use the product method for different dates, average periods for equal drawings, 6 months when dates are unknown, and ignore time for a flat rate.
focus: Average periods for monthly and quarterly drawings
Dates not given and flat-rate cases
remember: Monthly: beginning 6.5, middle 6, end 5.5 months
Quarterly: beginning 7.5, middle 6, end 4.5 months
Dates not given: 6 months
Product method: total products × rate/100 × 1/12
traps: Don't apply time when the rate is flat (not per annum)
End-of-quarter average is 4.5, not 7.5, months
Count months till the year end, not from the year start

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Guarantee of profit to a partner
topics.h: A star player joins a team only if promised a minimum fee. Firms do the same for a key partner – a guaranteed minimum profit.
p: A guarantee of profit assures a partner a minimum amount of profit. If his actual share is less, the shortfall (deficiency) is made good by the other partner(s).
Guarantee by the firm: the deficiency is borne by all the other partners in their profit-sharing ratio.
Guarantee by a particular partner: that partner alone bears the deficiency.
Guarantee by some partners in an agreed ratio: the deficiency is borne in that agreed ratio.
If the partner's actual share is equal to or more than the guaranteed amount, no adjustment is needed.

ex.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C is guaranteed ₹60,000 by the firm. Profit is ₹3,00,000. Distribute it.
st: A and B bear it 3:2: A ₹6,000, B ₹4,000.

topics.rl: Start-ups that bring in an experienced CFO as a partner often promise a minimum yearly profit share to attract them, just as franchises guarantee fees to star cricketers.

rv.summary: A guarantee of profit assures a partner a minimum share. Any deficiency is borne by other partners in their ratio (guarantee by the firm), by one partner alone, or in an agreed ratio. No adjustment is needed if the actual share is higher.
focus: Who bears it: firm, one partner or agreed ratio
remember: Deficiency = guaranteed amount − actual share
Guarantee by firm: other partners in their profit ratio
Entry: Dr guarantor's Capital A/c, Cr guaranteed partner's Capital A/c
traps: No adjustment if the actual share is more than the guarantee
The guaranteed partner does not bear his own deficiency
Debit the guarantor, not the guaranteed partner

topics.ch: Part I: Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts
topics.t: Past adjustments
topics.h: Accounts closed, profits shared – and then someone notices interest on capital was forgotten. Do we reopen everything? No – one smart entry fixes it.
p: Past adjustments are needed when items such as interest on capital, interest on drawings or salary were omitted or wrongly given after the accounts were closed, or profit was shared in a wrong ratio.
Prepare a statement: (1) credit what each partner should have got, (2) debit what should have been charged, (3) reverse the wrong profit share and redistribute it correctly, (4) find the net effect.
The net effects add up to zero, because the firm's total profit does not change.
Pass one adjusting entry: Dr the partner(s) with net excess received / Cr the partner(s) with net shortfall. With fixed capitals, use current accounts.
For a wrong ratio, the net effect is simply (correct share − share actually given) for each partner.

ex.q: A and B have capitals of ₹3,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. Profit of ₹80,000 was shared equally, but interest on capital at 10% p.a. was omitted. Pass the adjusting entry.
st: This ₹40,000 should have reduced profit shared equally: debit each ₹20,000.
ex.a: Dr B's Capital A/c ₹10,000 / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000

topics.rl: Just as Indian Railways issues a refund instead of re-running a train, accountants fix past errors with a single correcting entry instead of redoing the year's accounts.

rv.summary: Past adjustments correct omitted or wrong items after accounts are closed. A statement shows what each partner should have got, the net effect (totalling zero) is found, and one entry debits partners who got too much and credits those who got too little.
remember: Net effects of all partners total zero
Entry: Dr partner with net excess, Cr partner with net shortfall
Fixed capitals → use current accounts
traps: Don't redo the Profit and Loss Account; total profit does not change
Debit the partner who received too much
With fixed capitals, don't use capital accounts

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Reconstitution and admission of a partner
topics.h: A new bowler joins the team mid-season. The team continues, but the dressing-room agreement changes. That is reconstitution of a firm.
p: Reconstitution: any change in the existing agreement among partners while the firm continues – a change in profit-sharing ratio, admission of a partner, retirement or death of a partner, or amalgamation of two firms.
A new partner acquires two main rights: a share in the assets of the firm and a share in its future profits.
The new partner usually brings capital (for his share of assets) and a premium for goodwill (to compensate old partners for the profit share they give up).
Adjustments on admission: new profit-sharing ratio and sacrificing ratio, goodwill, revaluation of assets and liabilities, accumulated profits/reserves and losses, and partners' capitals.

ex.q: Neha and Sameer run a design studio. They admit Tara as a partner. List the accounting issues they must settle.
st: Decide Tara's share and work out the new ratio and the sacrificing ratio.
Value goodwill and record Tara's premium for goodwill.
Revalue assets and liabilities; distribute reserves and accumulated profits/losses to Neha and Sameer.
Record Tara's capital and adjust the capitals if required.
ex.a: New and sacrificing ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and accumulated profits/losses, and capital adjustment.

topics.rl: When a growing Indian start-up brings in a new co-founder, lawyers redraft the agreement and accountants revalue assets – the same steps as admitting a partner.

rv.summary: Reconstitution is any change in the partnership agreement while the firm continues. On admission, the new partner gets a share in assets and future profits, bringing capital and usually a premium for goodwill; ratios, goodwill, revaluation, reserves and capitals are adjusted.
focus: Why the new partner brings capital and premium
remember: Reconstitution: change in ratio, admission, retirement, death, amalgamation
New partner gets share in assets + share in future profits
Premium compensates old partners for their sacrifice
traps: A Realisation Account is for dissolution, not admission
Past profits do not go to the new partner
Capital and goodwill premium are separate payments

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: New profit-sharing ratio and sacrificing ratio
topics.h: Like slicing a pizza for a late-arriving friend: someone gives up a slice. The maths tells you exactly whose plate shrinks and by how much.
p: New share of an old partner = old share − share given up (sacrificed) to the new partner.
If nothing is said about sacrifice, old partners sacrifice in their old ratio; then the sacrificing ratio = old ratio.
If old partners surrender a fraction OF THEIR OWN share, sacrifice = old share × that fraction.
Sacrificing ratio = old share − new share, for each old partner. It is used to distribute the new partner's premium for goodwill.
Always check: the new shares of all partners must add up to 1.

ex.q: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, taken from A and B in their old ratio. Find the new ratio.
st: Remaining share for A and B = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5.

topics.rl: IPL franchises re-split ownership stakes when a new investor joins, exactly the way partners work out a new ratio.

rv.summary: On admission, each old partner's new share = old share − share given up. The sacrificing ratio (old share − new share) decides how the newcomer's goodwill premium is shared. If unspecified, old partners sacrifice in the old ratio.
focus: Calculating the new ratio in each case
Sacrifice when a partner surrenders a fraction of his own share
remember: New share = old share − sacrifice
Sacrificing ratio = old share − new share
Surrender of a fraction of own share: sacrifice = old share × fraction
New shares must total 1
traps: 1/3 of A's share is not 1/3 of the firm
A partner whose share is unchanged sacrifices nothing
When silent, sacrificing ratio = old ratio, not equal

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Goodwill: meaning, factors and need for valuation
topics.h: Why do people queue outside a famous chaat stall in Lucknow when a new one across the road is empty? That pull is goodwill.
p: Goodwill is the value of a firm's reputation that lets it earn more than normal profits. It is an intangible asset – it has value but no physical form – and is not a fictitious asset.

Factors raising goodwill: favourable location, efficient management, favourable market situation (monopoly or limited competition), nature of business (stable demand), special advantages such as licences, patents, trademarks and long-term contracts.
Goodwill must be valued when there is a change in profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement or death of a partner, dissolution involving sale of the business, or amalgamation of firms.
Goodwill cannot be sold separately; it goes with the business.

ex.q: A sweet shop opposite a busy railway station earns ₹2,00,000 a year while similar shops earn ₹1,40,000. What explains the gap?
st: Same product, same capital – the difference is the extra footfall from the location.
That ability to earn ₹60,000 more than normal is what goodwill represents.
ex.a: A favourable location gives the shop goodwill – the capacity to earn above-normal profit.

topics.rl: Brands like Amul built goodwill over decades through quality and trust; a new partner joining such a business pays for a slice of that pull.

rv.summary: Goodwill is an intangible asset: the value of a firm's reputation that lets it earn above-normal profits. It depends on location, management, market situation, nature of business and special advantages, and is valued whenever partners' profit rights change.
remember: Goodwill: intangible asset, ability to earn above-normal profit
Factors: location, management, market situation, nature of business, special advantages
Valued on change in ratio, admission, retirement, death, sale, amalgamation
traps: Goodwill is intangible, not fictitious
Goodwill cannot be sold separately from the business
A salary change does not require goodwill valuation

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Valuing goodwill: average and weighted average profit
topics.h: A firm earned ₹80k, ₹1 lakh and ₹1.2 lakh over three years. How much is its reputation worth today? Two quick methods give the answer.
p: Average profit method: Goodwill = Average profit × Number of years' purchase.
Average profit = total of (normal) past profits ÷ number of years. A loss year is subtracted, not added.
Weighted average method: multiply each year's profit by a weight (usually 1, 2, 3… with the latest year highest), add the products, divide by the total of weights. Use it when profits show a trend.

Normalise profits before averaging: deduct abnormal gains (e.g. profit on sale of a fixed asset), add back abnormal losses (e.g. loss by fire), and deduct any reasonable remuneration of a partner not charged.

ex.q: Profits for three years: ₹60,000, ₹90,000 and ₹1,20,000 (latest). Value goodwill at 2 years' purchase of weighted average profit with weights 1, 2, 3.

topics.rl: Analysts valuing an Indian listed company also clean up profits for one-time items, like a one-off land sale, before applying a multiple – just like normalising profits.

rv.summary: Goodwill by average profit = average normal profit × years' purchase. The weighted average method, used when profits show a trend, gives more weight to recent years. Past profits are normalised by removing abnormal gains, adding back abnormal losses and charging partners' remuneration.
focus: Simple average vs weighted average profit
Working back from goodwill to average profit
remember: Goodwill = average profit × number of years' purchase
Weighted average profit = Σ(profit × weight) ÷ Σ weights
Deduct abnormal gains; add back abnormal losses
traps: Subtract a loss year; don't add it
Don't include abnormal gains in normal profit
Charge a working partner's unpaid remuneration before averaging

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Super profit and capitalisation methods
topics.h: Every firm in the industry earns 10% on capital. Yours earns 16%. That extra 6% – the super profit – is the real engine of goodwill.
p: Normal profit = Capital employed × Normal rate of return ÷ 100. Capital employed = Total assets (excluding goodwill and fictitious assets) − Outside liabilities.
Super profit = Average profit − Normal profit. Goodwill = Super profit × Number of years' purchase.
Capitalisation of average profit: Capitalised value = Average profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate; Goodwill = Capitalised value − Actual capital employed.
Capitalisation of super profit: Goodwill = Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return.
Both capitalisation methods give the same goodwill for the same data.

ex.q: Capital employed ₹5,00,000; normal rate 10%; average profit ₹80,000. Find goodwill by (a) super profit at 3 years' purchase, (b) capitalisation of average profit.

topics.rl: When a large Indian company acquires a profitable start-up, it pays far more than the net assets – the excess is goodwill, often justified by super profits.

rv.summary: Normal profit = capital employed × normal rate. Super profit = average profit − normal profit; goodwill = super profit × years' purchase, or super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate. Capitalising average profit and deducting actual capital gives the same goodwill.
focus: Calculating capital employed and normal profit
remember: Normal profit = capital employed × normal rate ÷ 100
Super profit = average profit − normal profit
Goodwill = super profit × 100 ÷ normal rate
Goodwill = (average profit × 100 ÷ rate) − capital employed
traps: Super profit is not the highest past profit
Capital employed excludes goodwill and fictitious assets
Multiply super profit by 100 ÷ rate, not by the rate

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Premium for goodwill brought in cash or kind
topics.h: The newcomer pays for a seat at the table. Who pockets that payment – and why no 'Goodwill Account' shows up?
p: AS 26: goodwill is recorded only when purchased for consideration. So on admission no Goodwill Account is raised; the new partner's premium is used instead.
Premium brought in cash: Dr Cash/Bank A/c, Cr Premium for Goodwill A/c; then Dr Premium for Goodwill A/c, Cr Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs (in sacrificing ratio).
If old partners withdraw the premium: Dr their Capital A/cs, Cr Cash/Bank A/c. If retained, no further entry.
Premium in kind: Dr the asset brought (e.g. Machinery), Cr Premium for Goodwill A/c and the new partner's Capital A/c.
Premium partly brought: the unpaid part is debited to the new partner's Capital (or Current) A/c and credited to sacrificing partners.

ex.q: A and B share 3:2. C joins for 1/5 share. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000 and C brings his premium in cash. Pass the entries.
st: Sacrifice in old ratio 3:2: A ₹18,000, B ₹12,000.
Dr Bank 30,000 / Cr Premium for Goodwill 30,000.
Dr Premium for Goodwill 30,000 / Cr A's Capital 18,000, Cr B's Capital 12,000.

topics.rl: Think of the 'entry fee' a new partner pays in a big Mumbai CA firm: it goes straight to the partners whose profit share shrinks.

rv.summary: Under AS 26 no goodwill is raised on admission. The new partner's premium (in cash or kind) is credited to Premium for Goodwill A/c and then to sacrificing partners in the sacrificing ratio; any unpaid part is debited to the new partner's capital or current account.
focus: Entries for premium brought in cash
Withdrawal of premium by old partners
remember: Dr Cash, Cr Premium for Goodwill; then Dr Premium for Goodwill, Cr sacrificing partners
Unpaid premium: Dr new partner's Capital/Current, Cr sacrificing partners
AS 26: no Goodwill A/c on admission
traps: Share the premium in the sacrificing ratio, not the new ratio
Don't raise a Goodwill Account on admission
Withdrawal entry debits capitals and credits cash

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Goodwill not brought, existing goodwill and hidden goodwill
topics.h: Sometimes the newcomer cannot pay for goodwill, sometimes old goodwill sits in the books, and sometimes goodwill hides inside the capital he brings. Let's catch all three.
p: New partner unable to bring premium: Dr New Partner's Capital (or Current) A/c, Cr Sacrificing Partners' Capital A/cs (sacrificing ratio).
Goodwill already in the books: write it off among OLD partners in the OLD ratio – Dr Old Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr Goodwill A/c.
Hidden goodwill = Total capital of the new firm (implied by the new partner's capital and share) − (Old partners' adjusted capitals + New partner's capital).
Hidden goodwill is not shown in books; the new partner's share of it is treated as his premium for goodwill.

ex.q: A and B have adjusted capitals of ₹1,00,000 and ₹80,000. C brings ₹80,000 for 1/4 share. Find hidden goodwill and C's share of it.
st: C's share = 60,000 × 1/4 = ₹15,000, debited to C and credited to A and B in sacrificing ratio.

topics.rl: A rookie investor putting ₹80 lakh into a firm for a 1/4 stake when the books show much less is signalling the hidden goodwill the market sees.

rv.summary: If the new partner cannot bring premium, his capital or current account is debited and sacrificing partners credited. Existing goodwill is written off among old partners in the old ratio. Hidden goodwill = implied total capital − actual combined capital.
focus: Entry when premium is not brought
Calculating hidden goodwill and the new partner's share
remember: Premium not brought: Dr new partner's Capital/Current, Cr sacrificing partners
Existing goodwill: Dr old partners (old ratio), Cr Goodwill
Hidden goodwill = new partner's capital ÷ his share − total actual capitals
traps: Write off existing goodwill in the old ratio, not the new ratio
Hidden goodwill is not shown as an asset
With fixed capitals, use the current account

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Accumulated profits, losses and reserves on admission
topics.h: Before a new player joins, the old team splits the savings in the kitty. Reserves belong to the people who earned them.
p: General reserve, credit balance of Profit and Loss and similar accumulated profits: Dr Reserve/P&L A/c, Cr Old Partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio).
Accumulated losses and deferred revenue expenditure (debit balance of P&L, Advertisement Suspense): Dr Old Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr P&L/Advertisement Suspense A/c (old ratio).
Workmen Compensation Reserve: first meet the claim; any excess goes to old partners in old ratio. If the claim exceeds the reserve, the excess claim is debited to Revaluation A/c.

Investment Fluctuation Reserve (NCERT also calls it Investment Fluctuation Fund): first absorb the fall in market value of investments; the balance goes to old partners. If the fall exceeds the reserve, the extra is debited to Revaluation A/c.
Alternatively, reserves may be left undisturbed: the new partner's capital is debited with his share, and sacrificing partners are credited, by a single entry.

ex.q: Workmen Compensation Reserve is ₹30,000 and the claim is ₹20,000. A and B share 3:2. Show the treatment.
st: Cr Provision for Workmen Compensation Claim 20,000.
Cr A's Capital 6,000 and B's Capital 4,000 (excess 10,000 in 3:2).
ex.a: Claim ₹20,000 provided; excess ₹10,000 shared A ₹6,000, B ₹4,000.

topics.rl: Factories in Gujarat keep workmen compensation reserves for accident claims; when partners change, the unused part goes to those who built it up.

rv.summary: On admission, reserves and accumulated profits are credited, and accumulated losses and deferred revenue expenditure debited, to old partners in the old ratio. WCR and IFR first meet the claim or fall in value; any shortfall goes to the Revaluation Account.
focus: Workmen Compensation Reserve and Investment Fluctuation Reserve
remember: Reserves and P&L credit: Cr old partners (old ratio)
Losses, Advertisement Suspense: Dr old partners (old ratio)
Claim > WCR: excess debited to Revaluation A/c
traps: Don't give the new partner a share of past reserves
Credit only the excess of WCR over the claim
Undisturbed reserve: debit the new partner with his share

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities
topics.h: That office in Gurugram bought years ago is worth much more now. Before a new partner joins, the old partners should pocket that gain.
p: Revaluation Account (a nominal account) records changes in asset and liability values on reconstitution.
Credit: increase in assets, decrease in liabilities, unrecorded assets. Debit: decrease in assets, increase in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities.
Balance: profit (credit side larger) or loss, transferred to OLD partners' capital accounts in the OLD ratio.
Entry for increase in asset: Dr Asset A/c, Cr Revaluation A/c. Decrease: Dr Revaluation A/c, Cr Asset A/c. Profit: Dr Revaluation A/c, Cr Old Partners' Capital A/cs.
After revaluation, prepare partners' capital accounts and the new balance sheet with revised values.

ex.q: A and B (3:2) admit C. Building ₹2,00,000 is increased by 20%; stock ₹60,000 reduced by 10%; a 5% provision is made on debtors of ₹50,000; unrecorded investments ₹7,000; unrecorded outstanding salary ₹3,500; creditors reduced by ₹2,000. Find the revaluation result.

topics.rl: Land prices along new metro lines in Delhi, Bengaluru and Pune have jumped, so firms owning property there often show big revaluation gains when partners change.

rv.summary: The Revaluation Account records changes in values on reconstitution: credit for increases in assets, decreases in liabilities and unrecorded assets; debit for the opposite. Its profit or loss goes to old partners in the old ratio.
focus: What goes on each side of the Revaluation Account
remember: Credit: increase in assets, decrease in liabilities, unrecorded assets
Debit: decrease in assets, increase in liabilities, unrecorded liabilities
Profit or loss → old partners in old ratio
traps: The new partner does not share revaluation profit on admission
An unrecorded liability is a debit, not a credit
A revaluation loss is debited to capitals, not credited

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Adjustment of partners' capitals on admission
topics.h: After all adjustments, do the partners' capitals match their profit shares? If not, someone tops up and someone withdraws.
p: Case 1 – new partner's capital from old partners' capitals: Total capital of new firm = Combined adjusted capitals of old partners ÷ their combined new share; New partner's capital = Total × his share.
Case 2 – old partners' capitals from new partner's capital: Total capital = New partner's capital ÷ his share; each old partner's required capital = Total × his new share.
Adjusted capital = capital after goodwill, reserves, revaluation and similar adjustments.
Excess capital is withdrawn (Dr Capital, Cr Cash) or transferred to current account; deficiency is brought in cash (Dr Cash, Cr Capital) or debited to current account.

ex.q: C is admitted for 1/4 share and brings ₹60,000. New ratio A:B:C = 2:1:1. A's adjusted capital is ₹1,30,000 and B's ₹50,000. Adjust capitals.

topics.rl: Like co-founders topping up their stake before a funding round, partners align capital with their new profit shares.

rv.summary: After all admission adjustments, capitals may be made proportionate to the new ratio. Total capital is found from the old partners' adjusted capitals or from the new partner's capital; excess is withdrawn or sent to current account, and deficiency is brought in or debited to current account.
focus: Finding the new partner's capital from old partners' capitals
Finding old partners' required capitals from the new partner's capital
remember: Total capital = new partner's capital ÷ his share
Required capital = total capital × new share
Excess: Dr Capital, Cr Cash (or Current A/c); deficiency: Dr Cash, Cr Capital
traps: Use adjusted capitals, not opening capitals
Divide by the share (1/5 → multiply by 5)
With fixed capitals, use current accounts for surplus or deficiency

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Admission of a Partner
topics.t: Change in profit-sharing ratio among existing partners
topics.h: No one joins or leaves, yet the shares change – perhaps one partner now works harder. Whoever gains must pay the one who gives up.
p: On a change in ratio, some partners gain and some sacrifice: gain = new share − old share; sacrifice = old share − new share.
Goodwill: the gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner for his share of goodwill – Dr Gaining Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Sacrificing Partner's Capital A/c.
Reserves and accumulated profits/losses are distributed in the OLD ratio (or adjusted by a single entry between gaining and sacrificing partners).
Revaluation profit or loss on a change in ratio is shared in the OLD ratio.

ex.q: A and B share 3:2 and decide to share equally from now. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,00,000. Pass the goodwill entry.
st: Dr B's Capital A/c 10,000 / Cr A's Capital A/c 10,000.
ex.a: Dr B's Capital A/c ₹10,000 / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000

topics.rl: When a partner in a family business starts handling the new Surat branch and gets a bigger share, the other partners are compensated for goodwill they give up.

rv.summary: On a change in profit-sharing ratio, gaining partners compensate sacrificing partners for goodwill (Dr gainer, Cr sacrificer). Reserves, accumulated profits or losses and revaluation results are shared in the old ratio.
focus: Finding gain and sacrifice for each partner
Goodwill entry on a change in ratio
remember: Gain = new share − old share; sacrifice = old share − new share
Goodwill entry: Dr gaining partner, Cr sacrificing partner
Reserves and revaluation: old ratio
traps: Debit the gaining partner, not the sacrificing one
Don't distribute reserves in the new ratio
A partner with equal old and new shares neither gains nor sacrifices

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Amount due to a retiring or deceased partner
topics.h: A senior partner of a Chennai textile firm retires after 25 years. What exactly should his cheque say? Let's build the figure line by line.
p: Amount due = credit balance of capital (and current) account, plus his share of goodwill, reserves and accumulated profits, revaluation profit, profit up to the date of retirement/death, interest on capital and any salary/commission due.

Deduct: drawings, interest on drawings, his share of revaluation loss, accumulated losses (debit balance of P&L) and fictitious items (e.g. advertisement suspense), and any debit balance of his current account.
All these adjustments are posted to his capital account; its final balance is the amount payable.
The same rules apply on death; the amount is then payable to the deceased partner's executors.

ex.q: C retires. Capital ₹1,00,000; share of goodwill ₹30,000; share of reserve ₹12,000; revaluation profit share ₹6,000; profit till retirement ₹8,000; interest on capital ₹2,000; drawings ₹15,000; interest on drawings ₹500. Amount due?

topics.rl: Just as a retiring government employee receives a final settlement that adds gratuity and leave encashment and subtracts dues, a retiring partner's dues are added and subtracted item by item.

rv.summary: The amount due to a retiring or deceased partner is his capital (and current) balance plus his share of goodwill, reserves, revaluation profit, profit to date and interest on capital, less drawings, interest on drawings, and his share of losses and fictitious assets.
focus: Items added to and deducted from the retiring partner's capital
Treatment of a debit current account balance
remember: Add: goodwill share, reserves, revaluation profit, profit to date, interest on capital, salary
Less: drawings, interest on drawings, revaluation loss, accumulated losses, fictitious assets
Amount due = final capital balance
traps: Don't add drawings; deduct them
The retiring partner also bears his share of accumulated losses
A debit current balance reduces, not increases, his dues

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: New ratio and gaining ratio on retirement
topics.h: When a partner leaves, his slice of the cake is shared by those who stay. How much extra does each one get?
p: New share of a continuing partner = old share + share acquired from the retiring partner.
If nothing is stated, continuing partners take the retiring partner's share in their old ratio, so the new ratio equals their old mutual ratio.
Gaining ratio = new share − old share, for each continuing partner.
Gaining ratio is used on retirement/death; sacrificing ratio (old − new) is used on admission.
If the new ratio is given, compute gains directly; a partner may gain nothing.

ex.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires and A and B take his share equally. Find the new ratio and gaining ratio.

topics.rl: When a senior doctor retires from a private clinic partnership in Hyderabad, the remaining doctors split his share – exactly the gaining-ratio calculation.

rv.summary: On retirement, each continuing partner's new share = old share + share acquired. The gaining ratio (new − old) decides who compensates the retiring partner for goodwill. If unstated, continuing partners keep their old mutual ratio.
focus: Finding the new ratio after retirement
remember: New share = old share + share acquired
Gaining ratio = new share − old share
Silent case: new ratio = old mutual ratio of continuing partners
traps: Gaining ratio is not always equal
A partner whose share does not change gains nothing
Use gaining ratio on retirement, sacrificing ratio on admission

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Treatment of goodwill on retirement or death
topics.h: The retiring partner helped build the firm's name. When he leaves, the partners who keep enjoying that name must pay him for it.
p: Under AS 26, no Goodwill Account is raised. The retiring/deceased partner's share of goodwill is credited to his capital and debited to continuing partners in the GAINING ratio.
Entry: Dr Continuing Partners' Capital A/cs (gaining ratio), Cr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c.
Goodwill already in the books is first written off among ALL partners (including the retiring one) in the OLD ratio.
Hidden goodwill: if the amount agreed to be paid exceeds his dues (before goodwill), the excess is his share of goodwill – debited to continuing partners in gaining ratio.

ex.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Pass the entry.
st: Gaining ratio (nothing stated) = old ratio of A and B = 3:2.
Dr A's Capital 12,000; Dr B's Capital 8,000 / Cr C's Capital 20,000.

topics.rl: When a founding partner of a well-known Indian law firm retires, the remaining partners effectively buy his share of the firm's reputation.

rv.summary: Under AS 26, the retiring or deceased partner's share of goodwill is credited to his capital and debited to continuing partners in the gaining ratio. Existing goodwill is first written off among all partners in the old ratio; extra payment over dues is hidden goodwill.
remember: Entry: Dr continuing partners (gaining ratio), Cr retiring partner
Existing goodwill: written off by all partners in old ratio
Hidden goodwill = agreed payment − dues before goodwill
traps: Debit continuing partners in the gaining ratio, not the new ratio
The retiring partner also shares in writing off existing goodwill
Don't raise a Goodwill Account

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Revaluation and reserves on retirement or death
topics.h: The retiring partner should not lose out if the factory is now worth more, nor escape if the stock has lost value.
p: Assets and liabilities are revalued on retirement/death, and unrecorded assets and liabilities are brought into the books.
Revaluation profit or loss is shared by ALL partners, including the retiring/deceased partner, in the OLD ratio.
Reserves and accumulated profits (General Reserve, P&L credit balance) are credited to all partners in the old ratio.
Accumulated losses and fictitious assets (P&L debit balance, advertisement suspense) are debited to all partners in the old ratio.

ex.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires. Building is increased by ₹25,000; stock reduced by ₹5,000; an unrecorded liability of ₹5,000 is recorded. General reserve is ₹50,000. Find C's share of each.

topics.rl: A retiring partner of a Kochi spice-export firm benefits if the warehouse near the port has appreciated – revaluation captures that gain before he leaves.

rv.summary: On retirement or death, revaluation profit or loss, reserves and accumulated profits or losses are shared by all partners, including the retiring or deceased one, in the old ratio.
focus: Revaluation on retirement and who shares it
remember: Revaluation result, reserves, losses → all partners in old ratio
Unrecorded asset: Dr Asset, Cr Revaluation
Unrecorded liability: Dr Revaluation, Cr Liability
traps: The retiring partner does share revaluation profit and reserves
Don't use the gaining ratio for reserves
An unrecorded investment is credited to Revaluation, not to the partner directly

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Disposal of the amount due to a retiring partner
topics.h: Cash now, a loan to be repaid, or instalments with interest? The firm's bank balance decides how the retiring partner is paid.
p: Paid in full immediately: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Cash/Bank A/c.
Not paid immediately: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c. The loan appears on the liabilities side of the balance sheet.
Partly paid: cash for the part paid, loan for the balance.
Paid in instalments with interest: interest on the outstanding balance is credited to the loan account (Dr Interest A/c, Cr Loan A/c); each payment is debited to it (Dr Loan A/c, Cr Bank A/c).
Interest on the retiring partner's loan is an expense of the firm, charged to the Profit and Loss Account.

ex.q: C's loan of ₹1,20,000 is to be repaid in 3 equal annual instalments plus 10% p.a. interest on the outstanding balance. Find each year's payment.

topics.rl: Much like an EMI on a car loan from an Indian bank, a retiring partner's loan is paid down with interest on the reducing balance.

rv.summary: The amount due to a retiring partner may be paid at once (Dr Capital, Cr Bank), transferred to his loan account (Dr Capital, Cr Loan), or partly paid. Instalments carry interest on the outstanding balance, credited to the loan and charged to Profit and Loss.
focus: Entries for full, nil and partial payment
Instalments with interest on the outstanding balance
remember: Unpaid dues: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital, Cr Retiring Partner's Loan
Interest: Dr Interest, Cr Loan; payment: Dr Loan, Cr Bank
Loan → liabilities side
traps: Calculate interest on the outstanding balance, not the original loan
The retiring partner's loan is a liability, not an asset
Interest on his loan is a charge, not an appropriation

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Adjusting continuing partners' capitals
topics.h: One partner leaves with a big cheque. The rest may need to top up – or take some back – so their capitals match the new ratio.
p: After settling the retiring partner, continuing partners may agree to keep capitals in their new profit-sharing ratio.
If the total capital of the new firm is given, each partner's required capital = total × his new share.
If not given, the total of continuing partners' adjusted capitals (after all adjustments and payment to the retiring partner) is taken as the total capital.
Deficiency: partner brings cash (Dr Cash, Cr Capital). Surplus: partner withdraws (Dr Capital, Cr Cash) or it goes to current account.

ex.q: After C's retirement, A and B (new ratio 3:2) agree that the firm's total capital will be ₹3,00,000. Their adjusted capitals are A ₹1,50,000 and B ₹1,40,000. Adjust.

topics.rl: Partners of a Ludhiana hosiery firm often top up capital after a senior partner retires so the bank sees a well-funded, balanced firm.

rv.summary: After retirement, continuing partners' capitals may be set in the new ratio. Required capital = total capital × new share; a deficiency is brought in cash and a surplus withdrawn or transferred to the current account.
focus: Finding required capital from a given total
Taking total capital from adjusted capitals when not given
remember: Required capital = total capital × new share
Deficiency: Dr Cash, Cr Capital
Surplus: Dr Capital, Cr Cash (or transfer to current account)
traps: Use the new ratio, not the old one
Use adjusted capitals after all adjustments
A deficiency means bringing in, not withdrawing, cash

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Death of a partner: profit up to the date of death
topics.h: A partner passes away mid-year. His family is entitled to his share of profit up to that day – but the year's accounts are not ready. How do we estimate it?
p: On death, accounting is like retirement: new ratio, gaining ratio, goodwill, revaluation and reserves are dealt with, and the amount due is paid to the executors.
Time basis: deceased's share = Previous year's (or average) profit × months up to death ÷ 12 × his share.
Turnover (sales) basis: estimated profit = Sales up to death × (last year's profit ÷ last year's sales); deceased's share = that × his share.
Entry: Dr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c, Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c (the profit is not yet ascertained, so a suspense account is used).

ex.q: Accounts close on 31 March. D (share 1/4) dies on 30 June 2025. Last year's profit was ₹1,20,000. Find his share on time basis.
ex.a: ₹7,500, credited to D's capital by debiting Profit and Loss Suspense A/c.

topics.rl: Insurers and lawyers settling the estate of a partner in an Indian family firm rely on exactly these time- or sales-based estimates.

rv.summary: On death, accounting is like retirement, but the amount is paid to the executors. Profit up to death is estimated on time basis or turnover basis and recorded through the Profit and Loss Suspense Account.
focus: Calculating the deceased's share of profit
remember: Time basis: last year's profit × months/12 × share
Turnover basis: sales to date × (last profit ÷ last sales) × share
Entry: Dr P&L Suspense, Cr Deceased Partner's Capital
traps: Don't debit the deceased partner's capital for his profit share
Count months only up to the date of death
The payee on death is the executor, not the partner

topics.ch: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner
topics.t: Deceased partner's capital account and executor's account
topics.h: The family of a deceased partner deserves a clear, fair statement. Two accounts – his capital account and the executor's account – provide it.
p: Deceased partner's capital account is credited with his capital, share of reserves, goodwill, revaluation profit, profit till death, interest on capital; and debited with drawings, interest on drawings and share of losses.
Its balance is transferred to the Executor's Account: Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Deceased Partner's Executor's A/c.
Payment to executors: Dr Executor's A/c, Cr Bank A/c. Any unpaid balance stays in the executor's account (a liability), often paid in instalments with interest.
Interest on the unpaid balance: Dr Interest A/c, Cr Executor's A/c.

ex.q: D dies. Capital ₹1,50,000; share of reserve ₹20,000; goodwill ₹30,000; profit till death ₹10,000; revaluation profit ₹5,000; interest on capital ₹3,000; drawings ₹18,000. Find the amount transferred to his executors.

topics.rl: Banks in India ask for a succession certificate or a legal heir's documents before releasing such dues – the executor's account tracks what the firm owes the estate meanwhile.

rv.summary: The deceased partner's capital account collects all his credits and debits; its balance is transferred to the executor's account. Payments are debited to that account, and interest on the unpaid balance is credited to it. Any balance is a liability.
focus: Preparing the deceased partner's capital account
remember: Transfer: Dr Deceased Partner's Capital, Cr Executor's A/c
Payment: Dr Executor's A/c, Cr Bank
Interest: Dr Interest, Cr Executor's A/c
Unpaid balance → liabilities side
traps: Don't credit drawings to the deceased partner's capital
The executor's balance is a liability, not an asset
Interest on the unpaid balance is credited, not debited, to the executor's account

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm
topics.h: A partner retires and the shop stays open – or the shutters come down for good. Both are 'dissolution', but they are very different.
p: Dissolution of partnership: the existing agreement ends and a new one is formed (e.g. on admission, retirement, death or change in ratio); the firm continues.
Dissolution of firm: the partnership among ALL partners ends; business stops, assets are sold and liabilities paid, and the books are closed.
Dissolution of a firm always dissolves the partnership, but dissolution of partnership does not necessarily dissolve the firm.
Differences: continuation of business, court intervention (possible only for dissolution of firm), settlement of assets and liabilities, and closure of books.

ex.q: Ravi, Sana and Joseph run a café. Joseph retires; Ravi and Sana carry on. Later the café closes and everything is sold. Classify each event.
st: Joseph's retirement: agreement ends, business continues → dissolution of partnership.
Closing the café, selling assets and paying debts → dissolution of firm.
ex.a: Retirement = dissolution of partnership; closure = dissolution of firm.

topics.rl: Many small partnership firms during the COVID-19 lockdowns in India had to choose between reconstituting with fewer partners and dissolving the firm entirely.

rv.summary: Dissolution of partnership ends the old agreement while the firm may continue; dissolution of the firm ends the partnership among all partners, closes the business, realises assets, pays liabilities and closes the books.
focus: Dissolution of partnership vs dissolution of firm
Bases of difference: business, court, settlement, books
remember: Dissolution of firm always dissolves the partnership, not vice versa
Retirement, admission, death, change in ratio → dissolution of partnership
Firm dissolved → Realisation Account
traps: Retirement of one partner does not dissolve the firm if others continue
Court intervention applies to dissolution of firm
Revaluation is for reconstitution; realisation is for dissolution

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Modes of dissolution of a firm
topics.h: Firms can end by choice, by law, by circumstance, by a letter, or by a judge's order. Know all five doors out.
p: By agreement (Sec 40): with the consent of all partners, or as per a contract among them.
Compulsory dissolution (Sec 41): when all partners or all but one become insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful.
On certain contingencies (Sec 42), subject to contract: expiry of the fixed term, completion of the venture, death of a partner, or insolvency of a partner.
By notice (Sec 43): in a partnership at will, any partner may give written notice to all others of his intention to dissolve.

By court (Sec 44), on a partner's suit: unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct affecting the business, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of whole interest to a third party, business can be carried on only at a loss, or just and equitable grounds.

ex.q: Three partners formed a firm only to organise a trade fair in Pragati Maidan. The fair is over. What happens to the firm?
st: The firm was formed for a particular venture.
On completion of the venture, the firm is dissolved on the happening of a contingency (unless the partners agree otherwise).
ex.a: It is dissolved on completion of the venture (Section 42).

topics.rl: If a government ban makes a product illegal – as happened with some single-use plastics in India – a firm dealing only in it faces compulsory dissolution.

rv.summary: A firm may be dissolved by agreement (Sec 40), compulsorily (Sec 41), on contingencies like expiry of term, completion of venture, death or insolvency (Sec 42), by notice in a partnership at will (Sec 43) or by the court (Sec 44).
focus: The five modes and their sections
Matching a case to the mode
remember: Sec 40: agreement
Sec 41: compulsory – all or all but one insolvent, or business unlawful
Sec 42: contingencies; Sec 43: notice (partnership at will)
Sec 44: court
traps: Insolvency of all partners is compulsory dissolution, not dissolution by court
Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency (Sec 42)
A short absence is not a ground for court dissolution

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Settlement of accounts: Section 48
topics.h: When a firm closes, there's a strict queue for the money. Outsiders first, partners' loans next, capitals after that.
p: Losses, including deficiencies of capital, are paid first out of profits, then out of capital, and lastly by partners individually in their profit-sharing ratio.

Assets (including sums contributed by partners) are applied in this order: (i) debts of the firm to third parties; (ii) partners' loans/advances (as distinct from capital); (iii) partners' capitals; (iv) any surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Private assets and liabilities (Sec 49): firm's property goes first to firm's debts; a partner's private property goes first to his private debts, and any surplus may be used for the firm's debts.
This course excludes piecemeal distribution, sale of the firm to a company and insolvency of partners.

ex.q: On dissolution, a firm has ₹3,00,000 after selling assets. Creditors are owed ₹1,80,000 and partner A's loan is ₹40,000. Partners' capitals total ₹1,00,000. How is the cash used?
st: Capitals of ₹1,00,000 can be paid only ₹80,000; the ₹20,000 shortfall is a loss shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
ex.a: Creditors → A's loan → capitals; ₹20,000 loss shared by partners in profit-sharing ratio.

topics.rl: Like passengers stepping off an Indian Railways coach in order, claims are settled strictly: outside creditors, then partners' loans, then capitals.

rv.summary: Under Section 48, losses are met from profits, then capital, then partners in profit-sharing ratio. Assets go to outside debts, then partners' loans, then capitals, and any surplus in profit-sharing ratio. Section 49 keeps firm's and private assets for their own debts first.
focus: How losses and capital deficiency are borne
Section 49 on private and firm's assets
remember: Order: outside creditors → partners' loans → partners' capitals → surplus in profit-sharing ratio
Losses: profit-sharing ratio
Firm's property → firm's debts first; private property → private debts first
traps: Partners' loans are paid before capitals, after outsiders
Losses are shared in profit-sharing ratio, not capital ratio
Private property does not go first to the firm's debts

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Realisation Account: transfers and sales
topics.h: On dissolution, every asset is sold and every outside debt paid – all through one account that tells you if the firm sold at a profit or a loss.
p: Realisation Account is a nominal account prepared on dissolution to record the sale of assets and payment of liabilities and find the profit or loss on realisation.
Debit: all assets at book value EXCEPT cash/bank and fictitious assets (e.g. advertisement suspense, P&L debit balance). Entry: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Asset A/cs.

Credit: all outside liabilities and provisions against assets (e.g. provision for doubtful debts, accumulated depreciation). Partners' loans and capitals and reserves are NOT transferred. Entry: Dr Liability A/cs, Cr Realisation A/c.
Sale of assets: Dr Cash/Bank, Cr Realisation. Payment of liabilities: Dr Realisation, Cr Cash/Bank.
If no realisable value is given, assume tangible assets realise their book value and intangible assets (like goodwill) realise nothing.

ex.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Which items go to the Realisation Account at book value?
st: Debit side: Building 2,00,000; Machinery 1,00,000; Stock 50,000; Debtors 40,000 = ₹3,90,000.
Credit side: Provision 2,000; Creditors 60,000; Bills payable 20,000 = ₹82,000.
Cash stays in the Cash Account; A's loan, General reserve and capitals are not transferred.
ex.a: Assets ₹3,90,000 debited; liabilities and provision ₹82,000 credited.

topics.rl: When a well-known Delhi bookshop closed, its stock was sold off, landlord dues paid and the remaining money split – a real-life Realisation Account.

rv.summary: The Realisation Account is debited with all assets except cash and fictitious assets, and credited with outside liabilities and provisions. Partners' loans, capitals and reserves are not transferred. Sales are credited and payments debited to it.
focus: Which items are transferred to Realisation and which are not
Totals of assets and liabilities transferred
Assumptions when no value is given
remember: Debit: assets at book value except cash and fictitious assets
Credit: outside liabilities and provisions
Not transferred: cash, partners' loans, capitals, reserves, fictitious assets
traps: Don't transfer a partner's loan to Realisation
Debtors go at gross value; the provision is credited separately
Goodwill with no stated value realises nothing

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Assets and liabilities taken over; creditors accepting assets
topics.h: A partner wants to keep the delivery van; a supplier happily takes stock instead of cash. These twists change the entries, so watch carefully.
p: Asset taken over by a partner: Dr Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Realisation A/c (at the agreed value).
Liability taken over by a partner: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Partner's Capital A/c.
Creditor accepts an asset in full settlement: NO entry (both are already in the Realisation Account).
Creditor accepts an asset and some cash: record only the cash paid (Dr Realisation, Cr Cash). If an asset is accepted at a value in partial settlement, cash paid = liability − value of asset.
Unrecorded asset sold: Dr Cash, Cr Realisation; taken by a partner: Dr Partner's Capital, Cr Realisation. Unrecorded liability paid: Dr Realisation, Cr Cash.

ex.q: Creditors of ₹50,000 accept machinery (book value ₹40,000) plus ₹8,000 in cash in full settlement. What entries are needed?
st: Machinery and creditors are already in the Realisation Account.
The machinery handed over needs no entry.
Only the cash paid is recorded: Dr Realisation A/c ₹8,000 / Cr Cash A/c ₹8,000.

topics.rl: When small garment units in Tiruppur close, suppliers often accept leftover fabric instead of cash – a real 'creditor accepts asset' case.

rv.summary: On dissolution, an asset taken over by a partner is debited to his capital; a liability taken over is credited to it. A creditor accepting an asset needs no entry except for any cash paid. Unrecorded assets and liabilities are routed through Realisation.
focus: Asset or liability taken over by a partner
Creditor accepting an asset fully or partly
remember: Asset taken by partner: Dr Partner's Capital, Cr Realisation
Liability taken by partner: Dr Realisation, Cr Partner's Capital
Creditor takes asset in full: no entry
Asset + cash: record cash only
traps: Don't record the asset handed to a creditor
Cash paid in part settlement = liability − agreed asset value
Unrecorded assets sold still go through Realisation

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Realisation expenses and profit or loss on realisation
topics.h: Closing down costs money – brokers, lawyers, transport. Who pays, and who finally bears it? Five cases, five different entries.
p: Expenses paid by the firm: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Cash A/c.
Paid by a partner on behalf of the firm: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr that Partner's Capital A/c.
To be borne by a partner and paid by him: no entry. Borne by a partner but paid by the firm: Dr Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Cash A/c.
A partner is given a fixed remuneration for completing the dissolution and bears the expenses: Dr Realisation A/c, Cr Partner's Capital A/c (remuneration); no entry for the actual expenses.
Balance of Realisation: profit → Dr Realisation, Cr Partners' Capital A/cs; loss → Dr Partners' Capital A/cs, Cr Realisation; both in the profit-sharing ratio.

ex.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Assets realise: Building ₹2,40,000, Machinery ₹80,000, Stock ₹45,000, Debtors ₹36,000. Creditors and bills payable are paid in full. Expenses ₹3,000 are paid. Find profit on realisation.
st: Credit: provision 2,000 + liabilities 80,000 + cash from assets 4,01,000 = ₹4,83,000.

topics.rl: Just as a seller on an online marketplace nets the sale price minus fees, a firm's realisation profit is what's left after costs of winding up.

rv.summary: Realisation expenses are debited to Realisation when the firm bears them (paid by firm or by a partner). If a partner bears them, either no entry (he pays) or Dr his capital (firm pays). A fixed remuneration is credited to the partner. The balance is shared in profit-sharing ratio.
focus: Entries for each case of realisation expenses
remember: Firm pays: Dr Realisation, Cr Cash
Partner pays for firm: Dr Realisation, Cr Partner's Capital
Partner bears, firm pays: Dr Partner's Capital, Cr Cash
Partner bears and pays: no entry
traps: Don't record the actual expenses when a partner gets fixed remuneration and bears them
A loss is debited to capitals, not credited
Use profit-sharing ratio for realisation profit or loss

topics.ch: Part I: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
topics.t: Closing the books: capitals, loans and cash
topics.h: The final scene: every account must hit zero. If the cash account balances to the last rupee, you've done the dissolution right.
p: Accumulated profits and reserves are credited, and accumulated losses and fictitious assets debited, to partners' capitals in the profit-sharing ratio.
Partner's loan is paid after outside liabilities: Dr Partner's Loan A/c, Cr Cash A/c (it does not go through Realisation).
After the realisation profit/loss is transferred, each capital account is closed: credit balance paid (Dr Capital, Cr Cash); debit balance brought in by the partner (Dr Cash, Cr Capital).
The cash/bank account closes automatically when final payments are made – total receipts equal total payments.
Key journal entries: assets/liabilities to Realisation; sale and payments; reserve distribution; loss/profit transfer; partner's loan payment; final settlement of capitals.

ex.q: Balance sheet of A and B (1:1): Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 less provision ₹2,000; Cash ₹20,000. Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000; Capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Assets realise ₹4,01,000; liabilities ₹80,000 and expenses ₹3,000 are paid; profit on realisation ₹10,000. Settle the partners.
st: Total ₹3,08,000 = cash available. The cash account closes.

topics.rl: Like the final settlement of a closed bank account, every balance must be paid out and the books closed with nothing left over.

rv.summary: To close the books, reserves and losses go to capitals in profit-sharing ratio, partners' loans are paid after outsiders, realisation profit or loss is transferred, and capitals are settled in cash. The cash account closes with no balance.
focus: Why cash and capitals match exactly
remember: Partner's loan: Dr Loan, Cr Cash
Credit balance of capital: Dr Capital, Cr Cash
Debit balance: Dr Cash, Cr Capital
Cash left for partners = total final capital balances
traps: Partners' loans do not go through Realisation
A debit capital balance is brought in, not written off
Don't add the partner's loan to his final capital payment

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Features of a company
topics.h: Reliance, Infosys and Tata Steel outlive their founders and are owned by lakhs of shareholders who never meet. What makes such a creature possible?
p: A company is an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity distinct from its members – it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name.
Perpetual succession: members may come and go, but the company continues.
Limited liability: in a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on his shares.
Common seal: traditionally the company's official signature (now optional under the Companies Act, 2013). Shares of a public company are freely transferable.
Separation of ownership and management: shareholders own the company, but an elected Board of Directors manages it.

ex.q: Priya holds 100 shares of ₹10 each in a company, on which ₹7 per share has been paid. The company goes into heavy debt. What is the most she can be asked to pay?
st: Limited liability: only the unpaid amount on her shares can be claimed.
ex.a: ₹300 – her personal assets are otherwise safe.

topics.rl: Lakhs of Indians hold shares of companies through demat accounts; they own a slice of the company, while professional boards and managers run it.

rv.summary: A company is an artificial person created by law with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, transferable shares (in a public company), an optional common seal and separation of ownership and management.
focus: Separate legal entity and artificial person
Limited liability: maximum a shareholder can lose
remember: Limited liability = unpaid amount on shares
Common seal: optional under the Companies Act, 2013
Board of Directors manages; shareholders own
traps: Perpetual succession does not mean a company can never be wound up
Liability is limited to the unpaid amount, not the full face value already paid
Shareholders do not manage the company directly

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Kinds of companies
topics.h: Private, public, one-person, government, holding, subsidiary, associate – company labels can feel like a cricket team's batting order. Let's set the line-up.
p: By liability: company limited by shares (liability up to unpaid amount on shares), company limited by guarantee (liability up to the amount members undertake to contribute on winding up), unlimited company (no limit).

By membership: private company – minimum 2 and maximum 200 members (excluding employee/ex-employee members), restricts transfer of shares and cannot invite the public to subscribe; public company – minimum 7 members, no maximum; One Person Company – only one person as member.
Government company: at least 51% of paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government and/or State Government(s).
Holding and subsidiary: a holding company controls the composition of the subsidiary's Board of Directors or controls more than half of its total voting power.

Associate company: a company over which another has significant influence – control of at least 20% of total voting power or of business decisions under an agreement – but which is not its subsidiary.

ex.q: The Government of India holds 60% of the paid-up share capital of a company. Classify it.
st: The test for a government company is at least 51% of paid-up share capital held by government(s).

topics.rl: Companies like Coal India and ONGC are government companies, while a solo founder's start-up may begin life as a One Person Company.

rv.summary: Companies may be limited by shares, by guarantee or unlimited; private (2–200 members), public (7 or more) or One Person Companies; government companies (51% or more held by government); and holding, subsidiary or associate companies.
focus: Kinds of companies by liability and membership
remember: Private: 2–200 members, restricts transfer
Public: minimum 7, no maximum
Government company: at least 51% paid-up capital with government
Associate: at least 20% voting power, no control
traps: An associate is not a subsidiary: there is influence but not control
A private company cannot invite the public
50% government holding is not enough; it must be at least 51%

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Shares: preference and equity
topics.h: Two shareholders, same company: one gets a fixed 8% dividend first, the other gets whatever is left – and the vote. Which would you choose?
p: A share is a unit of a company's share capital. Shares are movable property, transferable as provided in the articles.
Preference shares carry two preferential rights: dividend at a fixed rate before equity holders, and repayment of capital before equity holders on winding up.

Types: cumulative (unpaid dividend accumulates) vs non-cumulative; participating (share surplus profits) vs non-participating; convertible vs non-convertible into equity; redeemable vs irredeemable. Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company cannot issue irredeemable preference shares.
Equity shares are those that are not preference shares. They carry residual rights to profit and capital, normal voting rights, and a dividend that varies with profits.

ex.q: A company has 10,000 8% cumulative preference shares of ₹100 each. It paid no dividend last year. This year it decides to pay preference dividend. How much is due?
st: Cumulative: last year's unpaid ₹80,000 is carried forward.
Total due = ₹1,60,000 before any equity dividend.

topics.rl: Many Indian banks raise funds through preference shares, while retail investors on NSE mostly buy equity shares for voting rights and growth.

rv.summary: Shares are units of share capital and movable property. Preference shares get a fixed dividend and capital repayment before equity; they may be cumulative, participating, convertible or redeemable. Equity shares carry residual rights and voting control.
remember: Cumulative: arrears carried forward; non-cumulative: arrears lapse
Irredeemable preference shares cannot be issued (Section 55)
Equity: residual rights, voting, variable dividend
traps: Don't carry forward arrears on non-cumulative shares
Preference shareholders do not get full voting rights
A share is movable, not immovable, property

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Categories of share capital
topics.h: A company may be allowed ₹5 lakh of capital, offer ₹4 lakh, get applications for ₹3.6 lakh and collect even less. Each layer has its own name.
p: Authorised (registered or nominal) capital: the maximum capital a company is allowed to raise, stated in its Memorandum.
Issued capital: the part of authorised capital offered for subscription (including shares issued to vendors). Unissued capital: the rest.
Subscribed capital: the part of issued capital actually taken up. It may be 'subscribed and fully paid up' or 'subscribed but not fully paid up'.
Called-up capital: the amount on subscribed shares that the company has asked shareholders to pay; uncalled capital is the rest. Paid-up capital = called-up capital − calls in arrears.
Reserve capital: a portion of uncalled capital that the company, by special resolution, decides to call only on winding up.

ex.q: Authorised: 50,000 shares of ₹10. Issued: 40,000. Subscribed: 36,000. ₹8 per share called; holders of 1,000 shares have not paid the last ₹2 call. Find each category.

topics.rl: When an Indian company comes out with an IPO, it usually issues only part of its authorised capital; the prospectus spells out these layers.

rv.summary: Share capital is classified as authorised, issued (and unissued), subscribed (fully or not fully paid up), called-up (and uncalled) and paid-up capital (called-up less calls in arrears). Reserve capital is uncalled capital kept for winding up.
focus: Defining each category of share capital
Calculating called-up, uncalled and paid-up capital
remember: Paid-up capital = called-up capital − calls in arrears
Uncalled = subscribed − called-up
Unissued = authorised − issued
traps: Reserve capital is not capital reserve
Calls in arrears reduce paid-up capital
Shares issued to vendors are part of issued capital

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Share capital in the balance sheet and notes
topics.h: Open any listed company's annual report: 'Share capital – Note 2'. Behind that one line sits a whole table. Let's read it like a pro.
p: Balance sheet (Schedule III): Equity and Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds → Share Capital, with details in Notes to Accounts.
Note on Share Capital shows: Authorised capital; Issued capital; Subscribed capital – (a) Subscribed and fully paid up, (b) Subscribed but not fully paid up (called-up less calls in arrears).
Amount in the balance sheet = subscribed and fully paid up + (subscribed but not fully paid up − calls in arrears) + share forfeiture account balance.
Calls in advance are not part of share capital; they are shown under Other Current Liabilities.
Securities premium is shown under Reserves and Surplus, not under Share Capital.

ex.q: A company issued 40,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called. All were subscribed. Calls in arrears are ₹5,000. Show share capital.

topics.rl: The Companies Act, 2013 requires every Indian company to present its balance sheet in the Schedule III format, so investors everywhere see the same layout.
