rv.summary: In the balance sheet, share capital appears under Shareholders' Funds, with details in the Notes to Accounts: authorised, issued and subscribed capital, less calls in arrears, plus any forfeiture balance. Calls in advance are a current liability; securities premium is a reserve.
focus: Where share capital appears in Schedule III
Placing calls in advance and securities premium
remember: Share capital → Shareholders' Funds; details in Notes to Accounts
Calls in arrears deducted; forfeiture balance added
Calls in advance → Other Current Liabilities; securities premium → Reserves and Surplus
traps: Don't add authorised capital to the balance sheet total
Calls in advance are not share capital
Securities premium is not shown under Share Capital

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Issue of shares at par: process and entries
topics.h: An IPO opens: you apply with some money, get an allotment message, then pay calls. Each step is a journal entry in the company's books.
p: Process: issue of prospectus → receipt of applications → allotment → calls. The company must receive minimum subscription of 90% of the issue before allotting shares.
Shares may be issued for cash in a lump sum or in instalments (application, allotment, first call, final call). Issue at par means at face value.

Entries: Bank Dr / Share Application Cr; Share Application Dr / Share Capital Cr; Share Allotment Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share Allotment Cr; Share First Call Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share First Call Cr.
Without separate call accounts, money received on allotment and calls can be credited directly to Share Capital (Bank Dr / Share Capital Cr).

ex.q: Mehta Ltd issues 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 at par: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on first and final call. All money is received. Find amounts at each stage.
st: Application: 10,000 × 3 = ₹30,000 (Bank Dr / Share Application Cr; then transferred to Share Capital).
Allotment: 10,000 × 4 = ₹40,000 (Share Allotment Dr / Share Capital Cr; Bank Dr / Share Allotment Cr).

topics.rl: During a popular IPO on NSE, ASBA blocks your application money in your own bank account until allotment – the company records it only when shares are allotted.

rv.summary: Shares are issued through prospectus, applications, allotment and calls, and need 90% minimum subscription before allotment. Each instalment is first debited to its account and credited to Share Capital, then cash received is credited to that account.
focus: Steps in issuing shares and minimum subscription
Journal entries for application, allotment and calls
remember: Minimum subscription: 90%
Application: Bank Dr, Share Application Cr; then Share Application Dr, Share Capital Cr
Allotment due: Share Allotment Dr, Share Capital Cr
traps: Application money is not credited straight to Share Capital on receipt
Below minimum subscription, refund the money; don't allot
'At par' means face value, not market price

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Issue of shares at a premium; discount rule
topics.h: Investors happily pay ₹12 for a ₹10 share of a strong company. That extra ₹2 can't be spent on anything you like – the law tells you where it may go.
p: Issue at premium: issue price above face value. The premium is credited to Securities Premium Account (Reserves and Surplus), usually collected with allotment.
Allotment with premium: Share Allotment A/c Dr (total) / Share Capital A/c Cr (capital part), Securities Premium A/c Cr (premium part).

Section 52 uses of securities premium: issuing fully paid bonus shares; writing off preliminary expenses; writing off expenses of, or commission paid or discount allowed on, any issue of shares or debentures; providing premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures; buy-back of own shares (Section 68).
Securities premium cannot be used to pay dividend.
Section 53: a company cannot issue shares at a discount; such issue is void. Exception: sweat equity shares (Section 54).

ex.q: 10,000 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12: ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including premium), ₹4 on first and final call. Show the allotment entry.
st: Share Allotment Dr 50,000 / Share Capital Cr 30,000, Securities Premium Cr 20,000.
ex.a: Dr Share Allotment ₹50,000 / Cr Share Capital ₹30,000, Cr Securities Premium ₹20,000

topics.rl: Hot IPOs on Dalal Street are priced well above the ₹10 or ₹1 face value; the difference sits in securities premium in the company's books.

rv.summary: Shares issued above face value carry a premium credited to Securities Premium (Reserves and Surplus), usually with allotment. Section 52 limits its uses, and it cannot pay dividend. Section 53 bans issue at a discount, except sweat equity.
focus: Splitting allotment money into capital and premium
remember: Allotment entry: Share Allotment Dr; Share Capital Cr, Securities Premium Cr
Section 52 uses: bonus shares, preliminary expenses, issue expenses and discounts, premium on redemption, buy-back
Section 53: no discount except sweat equity
traps: Securities premium cannot be used for dividend
Don't credit the premium to Share Capital
Issue at a discount is void, except sweat equity

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Calls in arrears and calls in advance
topics.h: Some shareholders pay late; a few eager ones pay early. The company tracks both in separate accounts.
p: Calls in arrears: amount called but not paid by some shareholders. Entry when receiving a call: Bank A/c Dr (amount received), Calls in Arrears A/c Dr (unpaid) / Share Call A/c Cr.
Calls in arrears are deducted from called-up capital in the Share Capital note.
Calls in advance: money received before a call is made. Entry: Bank A/c Dr / Calls in Advance A/c Cr.
When the call is later made: Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Share Call A/c Cr.
Calls in advance appear under Other Current Liabilities until adjusted. (Interest on these is outside this course.)

ex.q: First call of ₹3 on 10,000 shares is made. Holders of 1,000 shares fail to pay. Record the receipt.
st: Bank Dr 27,000; Calls in Arrears Dr 3,000 / Share First Call Cr 30,000.
ex.a: Bank ₹27,000 and Calls in Arrears ₹3,000 debited; Share First Call ₹30,000 credited.

topics.rl: Just as some flat-buyers in a Noida housing project pay instalments late and some prepay, shareholders can fall into arrears or pay in advance.

rv.summary: Calls in arrears are amounts called but unpaid (debited to Calls in Arrears and deducted from called-up capital). Calls in advance are amounts paid before a call is made (credited to Calls in Advance, a current liability, and adjusted when the call is made).
focus: Entries for calls in advance and their later adjustment
Presenting both in the balance sheet
remember: Calls in arrears: Bank Dr, Calls in Arrears Dr / Share Call Cr
Calls in advance: Bank Dr / Calls in Advance Cr; later Calls in Advance Dr / Share Call Cr
Paid-up = called-up − calls in arrears
traps: Calls in advance are not added to share capital
Calls in arrears are deducted, not added
Don't credit calls in advance to the call account when received

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Under-subscription, over-subscription and pro-rata allotment
topics.h: A hot IPO is subscribed 30 times; a dull one limps to 92%. Each needs different handling of application money.
p: Under-subscription: applications are fewer than shares offered. If at least the minimum subscription (90%) is received, shares are allotted to all applicants.
Over-subscription: applications exceed shares offered. The company may (a) reject some applications and refund money, (b) allot pro-rata, or (c) combine both.

Pro-rata allotment: shares allotted in proportion to shares applied. Excess application money of pro-rata applicants is adjusted towards allotment (and calls, if the articles allow); any balance is refunded.
Entries: Share Application Dr / Share Capital Cr (allotted), Share Allotment Cr (excess adjusted), Bank Cr (refund).

ex.q: A company offers 10,000 shares of ₹10: ₹3 on application, ₹4 on allotment, ₹3 on call. It receives applications for 15,000 shares and allots pro-rata. Find cash due on allotment.

topics.rl: Big IPOs on NSE often see institutional, HNI and retail portions oversubscribed many times, leading to lottery or pro-rata allotment.

rv.summary: If at least the 90% minimum subscription is received, an under-subscribed issue is allotted to all applicants. In over-subscription, some applications may be rejected and refunded and others allotted pro-rata, with excess application money adjusted towards allotment.
focus: Pro-rata allotment and adjusting excess money
remember: Pro-rata: shares in proportion to shares applied
Excess adjusted: Share Application Dr, Share Allotment Cr
Rejected: Share Application Dr, Bank Cr
traps: Only rejected applicants get refunds, not pro-rata ones (unless excess remains)
Excess money is adjusted to allotment before calls
Under-subscription above 90% still allows allotment

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Shares issued for consideration other than cash
topics.h: A company buys a factory but pays in shares instead of cash. How many shares does the seller get?
p: A company may issue shares to vendors for assets or a business purchased. Entry 1: Assets A/c Dr / Vendor A/c Cr (purchase consideration).
Entry 2: Vendor A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr (and Securities Premium A/c Cr if issued at a premium).
Number of shares = Purchase consideration ÷ Issue price per share.
When a business is bought: Assets Dr, Goodwill Dr (if consideration exceeds net assets) / Liabilities Cr, Vendor Cr, Capital Reserve Cr (if consideration is less than net assets).
Shares may also be issued to promoters for their services in forming the company; Share Capital is credited and the cost of their services is treated as part of formation (incorporation) costs.

ex.q: A company buys machinery for ₹4,40,000 and pays by issuing equity shares of ₹10 at a premium of 10%. Find the number of shares and the entry.
st: Vendor Dr 4,40,000 / Share Capital Cr 4,00,000, Securities Premium Cr 40,000.

topics.rl: Indian tech companies acquiring smaller start-ups often pay part of the price in their own shares – a share-swap that is issue for consideration other than cash.

rv.summary: Shares may be issued to vendors for assets or a business. The purchase is recorded first (Assets Dr / Vendor Cr), then shares discharge the vendor (Vendor Dr / Share Capital and Securities Premium Cr). Excess net assets go to Capital Reserve; shortfall is goodwill.
focus: Entries for issuing shares to vendors
Number of shares = consideration ÷ issue price
Goodwill vs capital reserve on purchase of business
remember: Number of shares = purchase consideration ÷ issue price
Consideration < net assets → Capital Reserve
Consideration > net assets → Goodwill
traps: Divide by the issue price, not the face value
Capital reserve is not securities premium
Record the vendor liability before issuing shares

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Private placement, ESOP and sweat equity
topics.h: Not every share issue is a public IPO. Some go to a chosen few investors, some reward employees, and some pay for brains instead of cash.
p: Private placement (Section 42): offer of securities to a select group of persons (not the public) through a private placement offer letter. Under the rules, an offer may be made to at most 200 persons in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP.

Employee Stock Option Plan, ESOP (Section 2(37)): an option given to directors, officers or employees of the company (or its holding/subsidiary) to buy or subscribe for shares at a future date at a predetermined price.
An option is a right, not an obligation; the employee decides whether to exercise it.

Sweat equity shares (Section 2(88)): shares issued by a company to its directors or employees at a discount or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how, intellectual property rights or value additions. This is the only case where shares may be issued at a discount (Sections 53 and 54).

ex.q: An employee holds ESOP options for 1,000 shares at an exercise price of ₹50 each. He exercises all of them. How much does the company receive?
st: He pays the predetermined price for each share.

topics.rl: Indian start-ups widely use ESOPs to attract talent – employees join on lower salaries hoping their options will be valuable after a funding round or IPO.

rv.summary: Private placement offers securities to a select group (at most 200 persons a year). ESOP gives employees the option to buy shares at a set future price. Sweat equity shares, issued for know-how or value additions, are the only shares allowed at a discount.
focus: Sweat equity and the discount exception
remember: Private placement: Section 42, at most 200 persons per year
ESOP: Section 2(37), right but not obligation
Sweat equity: Section 2(88), only allowed discount issue
traps: An ESOP is not free shares
Bonus shares and ESOP are not discount issues
Private placement is not a public issue

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Forfeiture of shares
topics.h: Miss your calls repeatedly and the company can take your shares away – keeping what you already paid. That's forfeiture.
p: Forfeiture: cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or calls, after due notice, as per the articles. Money already received is not refunded.
Shares at par: Share Capital Dr (called-up amount) / Unpaid Allotment or Calls Cr / Share Forfeiture Cr (amount received).
Shares at premium, premium RECEIVED: Securities Premium is not touched; debit Share Capital with called-up amount.
Shares at premium, premium NOT received: also debit Securities Premium with the unpaid premium.
Pro-rata cases: excess application money already adjusted counts as received; find unpaid amounts carefully. Share Forfeiture balance is added to paid-up capital in the Share Capital note.

ex.q: Raj holds 100 shares of ₹10 issued at par. He paid ₹3 on application and ₹4 on allotment but not the ₹3 final call. The shares are forfeited. Pass the entry.
st: Unpaid call: 100 × 3 = ₹300 → credit Share Final Call.
ex.a: Share Capital Dr ₹1,000 / Share Final Call Cr ₹300, Share Forfeiture Cr ₹700

topics.rl: Several listed Indian companies have forfeited partly-paid shares when holders ignored call notices after a rights issue.

rv.summary: Shares are forfeited for non-payment after notice. Share Capital is debited with called-up value, unpaid amounts credited to the call accounts, and money received credited to Share Forfeiture. Unpaid premium is also reversed; received premium is untouched.
focus: Forfeiture entries for shares issued at par
Treatment of premium received and not received
remember: Share Capital Dr (called-up) / unpaid calls Cr / Share Forfeiture Cr (amount received)
Premium not received: Securities Premium Dr
Forfeiture balance: added to paid-up capital
traps: Don't debit Securities Premium if the premium was received
Excess application money adjusted counts as received
Forfeited money is not refunded

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting for Share Capital
topics.t: Re-issue of forfeited shares
topics.h: Forfeited shares are back with the company. It can sell them again – even cheaply – but only so cheaply.
p: Forfeited shares may be re-issued at par, at a premium or at a discount. The discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on those shares.
Entry: Bank Dr (amount received), Share Forfeiture Dr (discount allowed) / Share Capital Cr (paid-up value credited); premium, if any, to Securities Premium Cr.
After re-issue, the remaining forfeited amount on re-issued shares is a capital profit: Share Forfeiture Dr / Capital Reserve Cr.
If only some forfeited shares are re-issued, transfer to capital reserve only the gain on those shares: (forfeited amount per share × shares re-issued) − discount allowed.
Balance sheet: capital reserve goes to Reserves and Surplus; any forfeiture balance on shares not re-issued stays in the Share Capital note.

ex.q: 100 forfeited shares (₹10 each; ₹700 forfeited) are re-issued at ₹8 per share fully paid. Pass entries.
st: Bank Dr 800; Share Forfeiture Dr 200 / Share Capital Cr 1,000.
Share Forfeiture Dr 500 / Capital Reserve Cr 500.

topics.rl: When a company re-issues forfeited shares cheaply, it is a bit like an airline reselling a cancelled seat – it already kept part of the first passenger's money.

rv.summary: Forfeited shares may be re-issued at par, premium or a discount not exceeding the amount forfeited. The discount is debited to Share Forfeiture, and the remaining gain on re-issued shares is transferred to Capital Reserve.
focus: Capital reserve when only some shares are re-issued
remember: Re-issue: Bank Dr, Share Forfeiture Dr (discount) / Share Capital Cr
Capital reserve = forfeited amount on re-issued shares − discount
Maximum discount = amount forfeited per share
traps: Transfer to capital reserve only the gain on shares actually re-issued
Don't credit an amount above face value to Capital Reserve: it is premium
Discount cannot exceed the forfeited amount

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Debentures: meaning and comparison with shares
topics.h: When NHAI or a big company raises money through bonds, investors become lenders, not owners. That loan certificate is a debenture.
p: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of a debt by a company under its common seal (where used), carrying a fixed rate of interest and repayable as per terms.
A debenture trust deed appoints trustees to protect debenture-holders' interests and records terms like interest, security and redemption.
Debentures and bonds are borrowed (debt) capital; debenture-holders are creditors of the company.

Shares vs debentures: shareholders are owners, get dividend (an appropriation, paid only from profits) and have voting rights; debenture-holders are creditors, get interest (a charge, payable even in a loss), have no voting rights, may be secured, and are repaid before shareholders on winding up.
Debentures may be issued at a discount; shares cannot (except sweat equity). Debentures may be convertible into shares.

ex.q: Neha buys 50 9% debentures of ₹100 each. The company makes a loss this year. Does she get interest? How much?
st: Interest on debentures is a charge, payable whether there is profit or loss.

topics.rl: Indian Railways' financing arm IRFC and many PSUs raise thousands of crores through bonds that work just like debentures.

rv.summary: A debenture is a written acknowledgement of debt with a fixed rate of interest. Debenture-holders are creditors: they get interest (a charge) even in a loss, have no voting rights, may be secured and are repaid before shareholders.
focus: Meaning of debenture and debenture trust deed
remember: Debenture-holders are creditors
Interest: a charge, payable even in a loss
Dividend: an appropriation, only from profits
Debentures can be issued at a discount; shares cannot (except sweat equity)
traps: Debenture-holders are not owners and cannot vote
Debenture interest is not paid only out of profits
Debentures are borrowed, not owned, capital

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Types of debentures
topics.h: Secured or naked, perpetual or redeemable, convertible or not, zero coupon or not, registered or bearer – debentures come in many flavours.
p: Security: secured debentures carry a charge on assets; unsecured (naked) debentures have no such charge.
Tenure: redeemable debentures are repaid after a fixed period; perpetual (irredeemable) debentures are not repayable during the life of the company.
Convertibility: fully convertible (wholly into shares), partly convertible, and non-convertible debentures (NCDs).
Coupon rate: specific coupon rate debentures carry a stated interest rate; zero coupon rate debentures carry no interest but are issued at a deep discount and redeemed at face value.
Registration: registered debentures – holders' names recorded and transfer needs a transfer deed; bearer debentures – transferable by mere delivery, interest paid to whoever holds the coupon.

ex.q: A company issues debentures of face value ₹1,000 at ₹750, with no interest, redeemable at ₹1,000 after 5 years. What type is it, and what does the investor earn?
st: No interest → zero coupon rate debenture.
ex.a: Zero coupon debenture; return ₹250 per debenture.

topics.rl: Indian investors buy NCDs from NBFCs for steady interest, while many PSU bonds are secured and redeemable after a fixed tenure.

rv.summary: Debentures are classified by security (secured, naked), tenure (redeemable, perpetual), convertibility (fully, partly, non-convertible), coupon rate (specific, zero coupon) and registration (registered, bearer).
focus: Each basis of classification and its types
Return on a zero coupon debenture
remember: Naked = unsecured
Perpetual = irredeemable during company's life
Zero coupon: no interest, issued at deep discount, redeemed at face value
Bearer: transfer by delivery
traps: Zero coupon debentures pay no interest; the gain is the discount
Naked debentures are unsecured, not convertible
Registered debentures need a transfer deed

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Issue of debentures for cash at par, premium or discount
topics.h: Like shares, debentures can be issued in one go or in instalments – and unlike shares, they may be issued at a discount.
p: Lump sum / instalments: Bank Dr / Debenture Application & Allotment Cr; then Debenture Application & Allotment Dr / Debentures Cr. Calls are recorded like share calls.
At premium: Debenture Application & Allotment Dr (issue price) / Debentures Cr (face value), Securities Premium Cr (premium).
At discount: Debenture Application & Allotment Dr (issue price), Discount on Issue of Debentures Dr (discount) / Debentures Cr (face value).
Securities premium on debentures can be used as per Section 52, e.g. to write off discount or loss on issue of debentures.
Over-subscription: excess application money is refunded (Debenture Application & Allotment Dr / Bank Cr) or adjusted towards allotment.

ex.q: A company issues 5,000 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 10%, payable fully on application. Pass the entries.
st: Cash received = 5,000 × 90 = ₹4,50,000: Bank Dr / Debenture Application & Allotment Cr.
Debenture Application & Allotment Dr 4,50,000, Discount on Issue of Debentures Dr 50,000 / 9% Debentures Cr 5,00,000.

topics.rl: Infrastructure companies in India often issue debentures at a premium when credit ratings are strong, and at a discount when markets are nervous.

rv.summary: Debentures issued for cash are credited at face value. A premium is credited to Securities Premium; a discount is debited to Discount on Issue of Debentures. Excess applications are refunded or adjusted.
focus: Entries for issue at par, premium and discount
remember: Debentures always credited at face value
Premium → Securities Premium Cr
Discount → Discount on Issue of Debentures Dr
traps: Don't credit debentures at issue price
Debentures can be issued at a discount; shares cannot
Securities premium cannot be used for dividends or interest

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Debentures issued for consideration other than cash
topics.h: A company buys a business and pays with debentures. The seller becomes a lender to the company.
p: First record the purchase: Sundry Assets Dr (and Goodwill Dr if needed) / Sundry Liabilities Cr, Vendor Cr (purchase consideration), Capital Reserve Cr (if consideration < net assets).
Then issue debentures: Vendor Dr / Debentures Cr (face value), Securities Premium Cr (if at premium); for discount, Discount on Issue Dr.
Number of debentures = Purchase consideration ÷ Issue price.
Goodwill = Purchase consideration − Net assets (if positive). Capital reserve = Net assets − Purchase consideration (if positive).

ex.q: Assets ₹5,50,000 and liabilities ₹50,000 are taken over for ₹4,80,000, paid by 10% debentures of ₹100 at a 20% premium. Find capital reserve and number of debentures.
st: Vendor Dr 4,80,000 / 10% Debentures Cr 4,00,000, Securities Premium Cr 80,000.

topics.rl: Acquisitions in Indian manufacturing sometimes pay sellers in debentures, giving them steady interest while the buyer conserves cash.

rv.summary: When debentures are issued for assets or a business, the purchase is recorded first (Assets Dr / Liabilities and Vendor Cr, with goodwill or capital reserve), then the vendor is paid by issuing debentures at par, premium or discount.
focus: Entries for purchase and for issuing debentures to the vendor
Number of debentures = consideration ÷ issue price
remember: Number of debentures = purchase consideration ÷ issue price
Goodwill = consideration − net assets
Capital reserve = net assets − consideration
traps: Divide by the issue price, not the face value
Paying more than net assets gives goodwill, not capital reserve
Record the purchase before the debenture issue

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Debentures as collateral security
topics.h: A bank lends ₹10 lakh but wants extra comfort. The company hands over its own debentures as a backup pledge – collateral security.
p: Collateral security is a subsidiary or additional security given besides the primary security for a loan. The lender can sell the debentures only if the borrower defaults.
No interest is paid on debentures issued as collateral (interest is paid only on the actual loan).
First method: no journal entry; the fact is shown in a note under the loan in Long-term Borrowings.
Second method: Debenture Suspense A/c Dr / Debentures A/c Cr (face value). In the balance sheet, debentures are shown under Long-term Borrowings and Debenture Suspense is deducted from them.
When the loan is repaid, the debentures are cancelled (reverse entry under the second method).

ex.q: A company takes a bank loan of ₹10,00,000 and issues 12,000 9% debentures of ₹100 each as collateral. Show the second method.
st: Debenture Suspense A/c Dr 12,00,000 / 9% Debentures A/c Cr 12,00,000.
Balance sheet note: 9% Debentures 12,00,000 less Debenture Suspense 12,00,000 = nil; Bank Loan 10,00,000 (secured by collateral debentures).

topics.rl: MSMEs borrowing from SBI often pledge extra security; companies can do the same with their own debentures.

rv.summary: Debentures may be issued as collateral (additional) security for a loan, carrying no interest. Either no entry is made with a note under the loan, or Debenture Suspense is debited and Debentures credited, with the suspense deducted in the balance sheet.
focus: Balance sheet presentation and cancellation on repayment
remember: No interest on collateral debentures
Second method: Debenture Suspense Dr / Debentures Cr (face value)
Debenture Suspense deducted from debentures under Long-term Borrowings
traps: Don't pay interest on collateral debentures
Don't show collateral debentures as an extra real liability
The first method needs no journal entry

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Terms of issue and redemption of debentures
topics.h: Issue at par, premium or discount; redeem at par or at a premium – six combinations, one rule: put any loss in a 'loss on issue' account up front.
p: Six cases: issued at par/premium/discount × redeemable at par/premium.
If redeemable at a premium, record the premium payable on redemption as a liability (Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c Cr) at the time of issue, and debit Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c.
Issue at discount, redeemable at premium: Loss on Issue = discount + premium on redemption.
Issue at premium, redeemable at premium: Securities Premium Cr (issue premium) and Premium on Redemption Cr; Loss on Issue Dr = redemption premium.
Actual redemption of debentures (methods, DRR, sinking fund) is outside the CBSE syllabus for this course.

ex.q: 1,000 debentures of ₹100 are issued at a 5% discount and redeemable at a 10% premium. Pass the issue entry (cash received in full).
st: Loss on Issue of Debentures Dr 15,000 (discount 5,000 + redemption premium 10,000).
Debentures Cr 1,00,000; Premium on Redemption of Debentures Cr 10,000.
ex.a: Bank ₹95,000 + Loss ₹15,000 = Debentures ₹1,00,000 + Premium on Redemption ₹10,000

topics.rl: Corporate bonds sold to Indian mutual funds often promise a redemption premium – the company records that future cost as a liability right at issue.

rv.summary: Debentures may be issued at par, premium or discount and redeemed at par or premium. A redemption premium is recorded at issue as a liability with a matching Loss on Issue; discount plus redemption premium both form the loss.
focus: The six terms of issue and redemption
Entries at the time of issue
remember: Redemption premium: credit Premium on Redemption, debit Loss on Issue
Discount + redemption premium = loss on issue
Issue premium → Securities Premium
traps: Issue premium does not reduce the loss on issue
Premium on Redemption is a liability, not an asset
DRR and actual redemption are outside this syllabus

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Interest on debentures
topics.h: Debenture interest is the rent a company pays for borrowed money – on the face value, at the coupon rate, often twice a year.
p: Interest is calculated on the FACE (nominal) value at the coupon rate, regardless of issue price.
Many companies pay interest half-yearly: half-yearly interest = face value × rate × 6/12.

Entries: Debenture Interest A/c Dr / Debentureholders' A/c Cr (interest due); Debentureholders' A/c Dr / Bank A/c Cr (payment); Statement of Profit and Loss Dr / Debenture Interest A/c Cr (transfer at year-end).
Debenture interest is a finance cost and a charge against profit. (TDS on debenture interest is excluded from this course.)
If debentures were issued during the year, interest is only for the months they were outstanding.

ex.q: A company has ₹5,00,000 10% debentures, interest payable half-yearly. Find each half-year's interest and the year's total.
st: Year's total = ₹50,000, transferred to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

topics.rl: PSU bonds bought by Indian pension funds pay coupons half-yearly – exactly how debenture interest is computed.

rv.summary: Debenture interest is calculated on face value at the coupon rate (half-yearly if so payable), only for months outstanding. It is credited to Debentureholders when due, paid through bank and charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss as a finance cost.
remember: Interest = face value × rate (× months/12)
Due: Debenture Interest Dr / Debentureholders Cr
Year-end: Statement of P&L Dr / Debenture Interest Cr
Finance Costs
traps: Don't calculate interest on issue price
Interest is a charge, not an appropriation
Charge interest only for months the debentures were outstanding

topics.ch: Part II: Issue and Redemption of Debentures
topics.t: Writing off discount or loss on issue of debentures
topics.h: A discount on issue is a cost of borrowing. Don't carry it around for years – write it off in the year of allotment.
p: Discount or loss on issue of debentures is written off in the year the debentures are allotted.
Order: first from Securities Premium (if any balance exists), then the balance from the Statement of Profit and Loss as a finance cost.
Entry: Securities Premium A/c Dr, Statement of Profit and Loss Dr / Discount (or Loss) on Issue of Debentures A/c Cr.
Using securities premium for this purpose is allowed by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013.

ex.q: Loss on issue of debentures is ₹60,000. Securities Premium has a balance of ₹40,000. Write off the loss.
st: Balance ₹20,000 from Statement of Profit and Loss.
Securities Premium Dr 40,000; Statement of P&L Dr 20,000 / Loss on Issue of Debentures Cr 60,000.
ex.a: ₹40,000 from premium, ₹20,000 from Statement of Profit and Loss

topics.rl: Indian companies clean up such issue costs quickly so their balance sheets don't carry 'fictitious' items that analysts frown upon.

rv.summary: Discount or loss on issue of debentures is written off in the year of allotment, first from Securities Premium (Section 52) and the balance from the Statement of Profit and Loss as a finance cost.
focus: Order of writing off discount or loss
remember: Write off in the year of allotment
First Securities Premium, then Statement of P&L
Entry: Securities Premium Dr, Statement of P&L Dr / Discount (or Loss) on Issue Cr
traps: Securities premium cannot be paid as dividend
Use securities premium before charging profit
Don't spread the write-off over the debentures' life under this method

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Financial statements: meaning, nature and objectives
topics.h: Every year, Infosys, Tata Motors and your neighbourhood listed company publish a thick annual report. Its heart is a few pages of financial statements.
p: Financial statements are the end products of the accounting process. For a company they include the Balance Sheet, the Statement of Profit and Loss, Notes to Accounts and the Cash Flow Statement (Section 2(40)).

Nature: they are based on recorded facts, accounting conventions (e.g. conservatism, consistency), postulates (e.g. going concern, money measurement) and personal judgements (e.g. depreciation method, inventory valuation).
Objectives: provide information about economic resources and obligations, about earning capacity (profitability), about cash flows, and to judge management's effectiveness (stewardship).
They are general-purpose statements used by many groups – investors, lenders, creditors, government and employees.

ex.q: A company values inventory at cost or market price, whichever is lower, and charges depreciation by the straight-line method. Which elements of 'nature' are at work?
st: Lower of cost or market reflects the convention of conservatism.
Choosing straight-line depreciation is a personal judgement.
Both rest on recorded facts (purchase cost of assets and stock).
ex.a: Accounting conventions and personal judgements applied to recorded facts.

topics.rl: SEBI requires listed companies to publish audited financial statements; analysts in Mumbai read them to rate shares and bonds.

rv.summary: Financial statements (balance sheet, statement of profit and loss, notes and cash flow statement) are the end products of accounting, based on recorded facts, conventions, postulates and personal judgements. They inform users about resources, earning capacity, cash flows and stewardship.
remember: Section 2(40): balance sheet, statement of P&L, cash flow statement, notes
Conservatism: lower of cost or NRV
Going concern: business continues in foreseeable future
traps: Personal tax returns of directors are not financial statements
The choice of depreciation method is a judgement, not a recorded fact
Going concern does not mean the business never makes losses

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Schedule III balance sheet and shareholders' funds
topics.h: One format for every company in India – from a small private company to Reliance. Learn it once, read every balance sheet.
p: Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires financial statements to give a true and fair view, comply with accounting standards and follow the form in Schedule III.

Balance sheet has two parts: Equity and Liabilities (Shareholders' Funds; Share Application Money Pending Allotment; Non-current Liabilities; Current Liabilities) and Assets (Non-current Assets; Current Assets).
Shareholders' Funds: (a) Share Capital, (b) Reserves and Surplus, (c) Money received against Share Warrants.
Reserves and Surplus include capital reserve, securities premium, general reserve and surplus (balance in Statement of Profit and Loss); a debit balance of P&L is shown as a negative figure here.
Share Application Money Pending Allotment is shown as a separate head between Shareholders' Funds and Non-current Liabilities.

ex.q: A company has share capital ₹10,00,000, securities premium ₹1,00,000, general reserve ₹2,00,000 and a debit balance of P&L of ₹50,000. Find shareholders' funds.

topics.rl: MCA's online filing (MCA21) expects every Indian company's balance sheet in this exact Schedule III layout.

rv.summary: Section 129 requires a true and fair view in the Schedule III format. The balance sheet has Equity and Liabilities (Shareholders' Funds, Share Application Money Pending Allotment, Non-current and Current Liabilities) and Assets (Non-current and Current).
focus: Main heads of the Schedule III balance sheet
Where the P&L debit balance and share application money go
remember: Shareholders' Funds: share capital, reserves and surplus, money against share warrants
P&L debit balance: negative under Reserves and Surplus
Share application money pending allotment: separate head
traps: A P&L debit balance is not shown as an asset
Securities premium is not part of Share Capital
Schedule III, not Schedule VI, applies under the 2013 Act

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Non-current and current liabilities
topics.h: A 10-year debenture and next week's supplier bill are both liabilities – but they sit in very different places on the balance sheet.
p: Non-current Liabilities: (a) Long-term Borrowings – debentures, bonds, term loans from banks, public deposits; (b) Deferred Tax Liabilities (net); (c) Other Long-term Liabilities; (d) Long-term Provisions – e.g. provision for employee benefits like gratuity.

Current Liabilities: (a) Short-term Borrowings – bank overdraft, cash credit, loans repayable on demand; (b) Trade Payables – creditors and bills payable; (c) Other Current Liabilities; (d) Short-term Provisions – e.g. provision for tax.
Other Current Liabilities include calls in advance, unpaid dividend, interest accrued on borrowings, income received in advance and outstanding expenses.
A liability is current if it is due within 12 months after the reporting date or within the operating cycle, or is held for trading.

ex.q: Classify: 9% Debentures; Bank overdraft; Bills payable; Provision for tax; Unpaid dividend; Provision for gratuity (long-term).
st: Provision for tax → Short-term Provisions; Unpaid dividend → Other Current Liabilities; Gratuity → Long-term Provisions.

topics.rl: Banks look closely at a company's short-term borrowings and trade payables before renewing a cash-credit limit.

rv.summary: Non-current liabilities are long-term borrowings, deferred tax liabilities, other long-term liabilities and long-term provisions. Current liabilities are short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities and short-term provisions.
focus: Classifying liabilities under the correct sub-head
remember: Long-term Borrowings: debentures, term loans, public deposits
Short-term Borrowings: overdraft, cash credit
Trade Payables: creditors, bills payable
Other Current Liabilities: calls in advance, unpaid dividend, accrued interest, outstanding expenses
traps: Bank overdraft is a short-term borrowing, not a trade payable
Accrued interest on debentures is not part of Long-term Borrowings
Provision for tax is short-term, not long-term

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Non-current and current assets
topics.h: Factories, patents and long-term investments versus stock, debtors and cash – the assets side tells you how the company uses its money.
p: Non-current Assets: (a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets – (i) Property, Plant and Equipment (tangible: land, building, plant, furniture, vehicles), (ii) Intangible Assets (goodwill, patents, trademarks, copyrights, software), (iii) Capital Work-in-Progress (e.g. building under construction), (iv) Intangible Assets under Development.
Also non-current: (b) Non-current Investments, (c) Deferred Tax Assets (net), (d) Long-term Loans and Advances (e.g. capital advances, security deposits), (e) Other Non-current Assets.

Current Assets: (a) Current Investments, (b) Inventories (raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, stock-in-trade, stores and spares, loose tools), (c) Trade Receivables (debtors and bills receivable), (d) Cash and Cash Equivalents (cash, bank balances, cheques and drafts on hand), (e) Short-term Loans and Advances, (f) Other Current Assets (e.g. accrued income).
Provision for doubtful debts is deducted from trade receivables, and accumulated depreciation from PPE.

ex.q: Classify: Patents; Loose tools; Bills receivable; Building under construction; Cheques in hand; Investments held for 5 years.
st: Building under construction → Capital Work-in-Progress; Cheques in hand → Cash and Cash Equivalents; long-held investments → Non-current Investments.

topics.rl: When ISRO's commercial arm builds a new facility, the half-finished building sits in capital work-in-progress until it is ready for use.

rv.summary: Non-current assets include PPE, intangible assets, capital work-in-progress, non-current investments, long-term loans and advances. Current assets include current investments, inventories, trade receivables, cash and cash equivalents, short-term loans and other current assets.
focus: Classifying assets under the correct sub-head
remember: Intangible Assets: goodwill, patents, trademarks, software
Inventories include loose tools and stores and spares
Cheques in hand: Cash and Cash Equivalents
Provision for doubtful debts: deducted from trade receivables
traps: Loose tools are inventories, not PPE
A building under construction is capital WIP, not PPE
Provision for doubtful debts is not a liability provision

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Operating cycle, notes to accounts and classifying items
topics.h: A bakery's cycle is a day; a shipyard's is years. The operating cycle decides what counts as 'current'.
p: Operating cycle: time between acquisition of assets for processing and their realisation in cash or cash equivalents. If it cannot be identified, it is assumed to be 12 months.

An asset is current if it is expected to be realised, sold or consumed in the normal operating cycle; is held mainly for trading; is expected to be realised within 12 months after the reporting date; or is cash/cash equivalent not restricted for more than 12 months. All others are non-current.
A liability is current if it is expected to be settled in the normal operating cycle, is held mainly for trading, or is due within 12 months after the reporting date.

Notes to Accounts give details behind each balance sheet and P&L line (e.g. breakup of share capital, reserves, PPE), accounting policies and contingent liabilities – keeping the main statements short.
Exercise type: classify a given item under the correct major head and sub-head of Schedule III.

ex.q: A rice mill ages its premium basmati rice for 2 years before selling it, as is normal in that trade. Is this stock current or non-current?
st: Its normal operating cycle includes the ageing period.
Items realised within the operating cycle are current, even if it exceeds 12 months.
ex.a: Current asset (inventory), because it is realised within the normal operating cycle.

topics.rl: A real-estate developer in Mumbai may have an operating cycle of 4–5 years, so flats under construction are still inventory.

rv.summary: An asset or liability is current if it is realised or settled within the normal operating cycle (assumed 12 months if unclear) or within 12 months after the reporting date, or held for trading. Notes to Accounts give details behind each line.
focus: The test for current vs non-current
Classifying items under head and sub-head
remember: Operating cycle: acquisition of assets for processing → realisation in cash
Default operating cycle: 12 months
Items realised within the operating cycle are current, even if longer than 12 months
traps: Don't call stock non-current just because the cycle is longer than 12 months
Calls in advance are a current liability, not share capital
Interest accrued on investments is an asset, not a liability

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Statement of Profit and Loss (Schedule III)
topics.h: Revenue in, expenses out, profit before tax, tax, profit for the period – the Statement of Profit and Loss tells the year's story in one column.
p: Revenue from operations (sale of products, sale of services, other operating revenues such as scrap sales) + Other income (interest, dividend, profit on sale of assets/investments) = Total income.

Expenses: cost of materials consumed; purchases of stock-in-trade; changes in inventories of finished goods, work-in-progress and stock-in-trade; employee benefits expense; finance costs; depreciation and amortisation expense; other expenses.
Changes in inventories = opening inventory − closing inventory (a negative figure when inventory has increased).
Profit before tax = Total income − Total expenses; Profit for the period = Profit before tax − Tax expense.
Exceptional items, extraordinary items and discontinued operations are outside this course.

ex.q: Revenue from operations ₹10,00,000; other income ₹50,000; purchases of stock-in-trade ₹6,00,000; opening inventory ₹1,00,000, closing ₹1,50,000; employee benefits ₹1,20,000; finance costs ₹30,000; depreciation ₹40,000; other expenses ₹60,000; tax 30%. Find profit for the period.
st: PBT = ₹2,50,000; tax = ₹75,000; profit for the period = ₹1,75,000.

topics.rl: Quarterly results of listed Indian companies in newspapers follow this exact layout – revenue, other income, expenses, PBT, tax, PAT.

rv.summary: The Schedule III Statement of Profit and Loss shows total income (revenue from operations + other income) less expenses (materials, purchases, changes in inventories, employee benefits, finance costs, depreciation, other expenses) to get profit before tax and profit for the period.
focus: Revenue from operations vs other income
Computing profit before tax and profit for the period
remember: Total income = revenue from operations + other income
Changes in inventories = opening − closing
Profit for the period = PBT − tax
traps: Don't put interest received under revenue from operations for a manufacturer
An increase in inventory gives a negative 'changes in inventories'
Scrap sales are operating revenue, not other income

topics.ch: Part II: Financial Statements of a Company
topics.t: Uses and limitations of financial statements
topics.h: Financial statements guide investors, banks and the government – but they are not crystal balls. Know their power and their blind spots.
p: Uses: report on stewardship of management; basis for fiscal policy and taxation; help in credit decisions by lenders; help in investment decisions; basis for labour contracts and wage negotiations; information to the public.

Limitations: not exact – figures use estimates (depreciation, provisions); historical in nature – based on past data; ignore price-level changes (inflation); ignore qualitative aspects (employee skill, brand, management quality); may be window-dressed; may carry bias from personal judgement.

ex.q: A company bought land in 1995 for ₹10 lakh. Its market value today is ₹5 crore, but the balance sheet still shows ₹10 lakh. Which limitation is this?
st: The figure is based on historical cost.
It ignores the rise in price levels since 1995.
ex.a: Historical nature and ignoring price-level changes.

topics.rl: The Government uses company accounts to frame tax policy, while unions in industries like steel use them during wage talks.

rv.summary: Financial statements help in judging stewardship, framing fiscal policy, credit and investment decisions and labour contracts. Limitations: they are not exact, are historical, ignore price-level changes and qualitative factors, and may be window-dressed or biased.
remember: Uses: stewardship, fiscal policy, credit decisions, investment decisions, labour contracts, public information
Limitations: estimates, historical, price-level changes ignored, qualitative factors ignored, window dressing, bias
traps: Stewardship reporting is a use, not a limitation
Historical cost ignores inflation
Window dressing is a limitation, not conservatism

topics.ch: Part II: Analysis of Financial Statements
topics.t: Analysis of financial statements: meaning, significance and objectives
topics.h: A balance sheet is a photo; analysis is the X-ray. It shows what the numbers really mean for profit and safety.
p: Analysis of financial statements is the systematic study of relationships among items in the financial statements to judge profitability and financial position.
Analysis breaks data into meaningful groups and relationships; interpretation explains what those results mean. Analysis comes first, interpretation follows.

Users: finance manager (planning), top management (efficiency), trade payables (short-term solvency), lenders (long-term solvency and interest-paying ability), investors (profitability and growth), labour unions (capacity to pay wages), and government/analysts.
Objectives: assess earning capacity, managerial efficiency, short-term and long-term solvency, make inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons, and help forecasting and budgeting.

ex.q: A supplier wants to sell goods on 60 days' credit to a company. What will the supplier mainly look for in its financial statements?
st: A trade payable cares about getting paid soon.
That depends on the company's short-term solvency (liquidity).
ex.a: Short-term solvency – its ability to pay current liabilities.

topics.rl: Credit-rating agencies such as CRISIL and ICRA analyse company statements before rating bonds that Indian investors buy.

rv.summary: Analysis of financial statements studies relationships among their items to judge profitability and financial position; interpretation explains the results. Different users seek different information, and objectives include judging earning capacity, efficiency, solvency and comparisons.
remember: Trade payables: short-term solvency
Lenders and debenture-holders: long-term solvency
Investors: profitability and growth
Intra-firm: same firm over years; inter-firm: different firms
traps: Interpretation comes after analysis, not before
Suppliers care about short-term, not long-term, solvency
Comparing a firm with itself is intra-firm, not inter-firm

topics.ch: Part II: Analysis of Financial Statements
topics.t: Tools of analysis and limitations
topics.h: A doctor has a stethoscope, BP cuff and blood test. An analyst has four tools too – and like all tools, they have limits.
p: Tools: comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis and cash flow analysis (trend analysis is also used).
Horizontal analysis compares figures across two or more periods (e.g. comparative statements); it is also called dynamic analysis.
Vertical analysis studies relationships among items of one period (e.g. common-size statements); it is also called static analysis.

Limitations: ignores price-level changes, ignores qualitative aspects, is based on historical data, can be affected by window dressing, is influenced by differing accounting policies, and may suffer from personal bias.

ex.q: An analyst expresses every item of this year's Statement of Profit and Loss as a percentage of revenue from operations. Which tool and type of analysis is this?
st: Expressing items as % of a common base is a common-size statement.
It uses one period only, so it is vertical analysis.

topics.rl: Equity research teams in Mumbai combine all four tools – comparing years, common-sizing, ratios and cash flows – before recommending a stock.

rv.summary: The tools of analysis are comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis and cash flow analysis. Horizontal (dynamic) analysis compares periods; vertical (static) analysis relates items of one period. Analysis has limitations like ignoring inflation and qualitative factors.
remember: Horizontal = dynamic, across periods (comparative statements)
Vertical = static, one period (common-size statements)
Limitations: price-level changes, qualitative aspects, historical data, window dressing, policy differences, bias
traps: A trial balance is not a tool of analysis
Common-size statements are vertical, not horizontal, analysis
Comparative statements are horizontal, not vertical, analysis

topics.ch: Part II: Analysis of Financial Statements
topics.t: Comparative statements
topics.h: Revenue grew from ₹10 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh. Good – but did expenses grow faster? Comparative statements answer in two columns: absolute change and % change.
p: A comparative statement shows figures for two (or more) years side by side, with absolute change and percentage change.
Absolute change = Current year − Previous year. Percentage change = Absolute change ÷ Previous year × 100.
Comparative balance sheet compares items of equity, liabilities and assets; comparative statement of profit and loss compares revenue, expenses and profit.
Interpretation: e.g. if revenue grows faster than expenses, profit margins improve; if current liabilities rise faster than current assets, liquidity weakens.

ex.q: Revenue from operations: 2024-25 ₹10,00,000; 2025-26 ₹12,50,000. Expenses: ₹6,00,000 and ₹7,20,000. Prepare the comparative figures.

topics.rl: Business newspapers in India report a company's quarterly revenue and profit 'YoY growth' – that's a comparative statement in a headline.

rv.summary: A comparative statement shows two or more years side by side with absolute change (current − previous) and percentage change (change ÷ previous × 100), and is used to judge trends in profitability and liquidity.
remember: Absolute change = current year − previous year
% change = absolute change ÷ previous year × 100
Base = previous year's figure of the same item
traps: Divide by the previous year, not the current year
A fall gives a negative % change
Don't use totals as the base in comparative statements; that is common-size

topics.ch: Part II: Analysis of Financial Statements
topics.t: Common-size statements
topics.h: Compare a ₹100-crore company with a ₹10-lakh one? Turn both into percentages and suddenly they speak the same language.
p: Common-size statement of profit and loss: each item as a % of revenue from operations (revenue = 100).
Common-size balance sheet: each item as a % of total assets (or total equity and liabilities) (total = 100).
They show the structure (composition) of the statements and allow comparison between firms of different sizes and across years.
They are a tool of vertical analysis.

ex.q: Revenue from operations ₹10,00,000; cost of materials consumed ₹6,00,000; employee benefits ₹1,00,000; other expenses ₹1,00,000. Prepare common-size percentages.

topics.rl: Comparing Zomato and a small local food-delivery start-up is easier when you see marketing cost as a % of revenue for both.

rv.summary: Common-size statements express each item as a percentage of a common base: revenue from operations for the Statement of Profit and Loss, and total assets for the balance sheet. They are vertical analysis and allow comparison across firms and years.
remember: Statement of P&L: % of revenue from operations
Balance sheet: % of total assets (or total equity and liabilities)
Common-size = vertical analysis
traps: Don't use the previous year's figure as base in a common-size statement
A rising % share means faster growth than the base, not an absolute fall
Balance sheet items are not expressed as % of revenue

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Accounting ratios: meaning, objectives, advantages and limitations
topics.h: ₹50 lakh profit – good or bad? It depends on whether sales were ₹1 crore or ₹100 crore. Ratios turn raw numbers into meaning.
p: An accounting ratio is an arithmetical relationship between two related accounting figures. It may be expressed as a pure ratio (2:1), a percentage (25%), times (6 times) or a fraction.
Objectives: know the operational efficiency, liquidity, solvency and profitability of the business, and make inter-firm and intra-firm comparisons.
Advantages: helps judge efficiency of decisions, simplifies complex figures, helps comparative analysis, identifies problem areas, helps in SWOT analysis, and aids planning and forecasting.

Limitations: depends on the limitations of accounting data; ignores price-level changes and qualitative factors; may be affected by window dressing; different accounting policies reduce comparability; there is no universally accepted standard ratio.

ex.q: A company has current assets ₹3,00,000 and current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Express their relationship in three forms.
st: Times: current assets are 2 times current liabilities.

topics.rl: Bank loan officers in India look at a handful of ratios – current ratio, debt-equity, interest coverage – before sanctioning a business loan.

rv.summary: An accounting ratio is an arithmetical relationship between two related figures, expressed as a pure ratio, percentage, times or fraction. Ratios judge efficiency, liquidity, solvency and profitability but share the limitations of accounting data.
focus: Forms in which ratios are expressed
Objectives and advantages of ratio analysis
remember: Forms: pure ratio (2 : 1), percentage, times, fraction
Limitations: data limits, price-level changes, qualitative factors ignored, window dressing, policy differences, no standard ratio
traps: Ratios do not remove the effect of inflation
There is no single standard ratio for all industries
Comparing with another firm is inter-firm, not intra-firm

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Types of ratios and liquidity ratios
topics.h: Can the company pay its bills next month? Two quick ratios answer that – the current ratio and the quick ratio.
p: Traditional classification: Statement of Profit and Loss ratios (e.g. gross profit ratio), Balance Sheet ratios (e.g. current ratio, debt-equity), and Composite ratios using both (e.g. trade receivables turnover, return on investment).
Functional classification: liquidity, solvency, activity (turnover) and profitability ratios.
Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities. A ratio of 2:1 is traditionally considered safe.
Quick (liquid) ratio = Quick assets ÷ Current liabilities, where Quick assets = Current assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses. 1:1 is considered ideal.
Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities. If CR = r and WC is known: CL = WC ÷ (r − 1), CA = CL × r.

ex.q: Inventories ₹1,00,000; trade receivables ₹1,20,000; cash ₹60,000; prepaid expenses ₹20,000; current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Find current and quick ratios.

topics.rl: Suppliers to large retailers like DMart check liquidity ratios before extending long credit periods.

rv.summary: Ratios are grouped traditionally (P&L, balance sheet, composite) or functionally (liquidity, solvency, activity, profitability). Liquidity ratios are the current ratio (ideal 2 : 1) and the quick ratio (ideal 1 : 1).
focus: Finding CA and CL from the ratio and working capital
remember: Current ratio = CA ÷ CL (2 : 1 safe)
Quick ratio = (CA − inventories − prepaid expenses) ÷ CL (1 : 1 ideal)
CL = WC ÷ (CR − 1); CA = CL × CR
traps: Don't include inventory or prepaid expenses in quick assets
ROI is composite, not a balance sheet ratio
Working capital ≠ current assets

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Debt-equity and debt to capital employed
topics.h: How much of the company is funded by lenders versus owners? Too much debt, and a bad year can sink it.
p: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Shareholders' funds (equity). Long-term debts = Long-term borrowings + Long-term provisions.
Shareholders' funds = Share capital + Reserves and surplus (+ money received against share warrants). Alternatively: Non-current assets + Working capital − Non-current liabilities.
A lower debt-equity ratio means more security for lenders; a common safe norm is 2 : 1.
Debt to capital employed ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Capital employed, where Capital employed = Long-term debts + Shareholders' funds (or Non-current assets + Working capital).

ex.q: Share capital ₹8,00,000; reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000; long-term borrowings (debentures) ₹5,00,000. Find debt-equity and debt to capital employed ratios.

topics.rl: RBI and banks watch the leverage of big Indian conglomerates closely; a high debt-equity ratio can trigger rating downgrades.

rv.summary: Debt-equity ratio = long-term debts ÷ shareholders' funds; debt to capital employed = long-term debts ÷ capital employed. Lower values mean more safety for long-term lenders.
focus: Finding long-term debts and shareholders' funds
Calculating debt-equity and debt to capital employed
remember: Debt-equity = (long-term borrowings + long-term provisions) ÷ shareholders' funds
Shareholders' funds = NCA + WC − NCL
Capital employed = long-term debts + shareholders' funds
traps: Don't include current liabilities in long-term debt
A lower debt-equity ratio means less, not more, risk for lenders
Capital employed is not working capital

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Proprietary, total assets to debt and interest coverage ratios
topics.h: Owners' share of the assets, assets backing each rupee of debt, and how many times profit covers interest – three more solvency checks.
p: Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets. A higher ratio means owners finance more of the assets.
Total assets to debt ratio = Total assets ÷ Long-term debts. A higher ratio means lenders are better protected.
Interest coverage ratio = Net profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt. It shows how many times interest is covered by profit.
Total assets here are taken as shown in the balance sheet (excluding fictitious items).

ex.q: Total assets ₹20,00,000; shareholders' funds ₹10,00,000; 10% debentures ₹5,00,000; profit before interest and tax ₹3,00,000. Compute the three ratios.

topics.rl: Credit analysts reviewing Indian infrastructure companies obsess over interest coverage – below 1.5 times rings alarm bells.

rv.summary: Proprietary ratio = shareholders' funds ÷ total assets; total assets to debt = total assets ÷ long-term debts; interest coverage = PBIT ÷ interest on long-term debt. Higher values mean more safety for lenders.
remember: Proprietary ratio = shareholders' funds ÷ total assets
Total assets to debt = total assets ÷ long-term debts
Interest coverage = PBIT ÷ interest on long-term debt (times)
traps: Interest coverage uses PBIT, not PAT
A proprietary ratio of 0.8 means 80% owner-financed, not debt-financed
Exclude fictitious items from total assets

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Inventory turnover ratio
topics.h: A sweet shop that sells its stock every few days is healthier than one whose laddoos sit for weeks. Inventory turnover measures that speed.
p: Inventory turnover ratio = Cost of revenue from operations ÷ Average inventory.
Average inventory = (Opening inventory + Closing inventory) ÷ 2.
Cost of revenue from operations = Revenue from operations − Gross profit, or = Opening inventory + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing inventory.
If gross profit is given on cost (e.g. 25% on cost), cost of revenue = Revenue × 100 ÷ (100 + 25). If given on revenue, cost = Revenue × (100 − GP%) ÷ 100.
A higher ratio generally means efficient inventory management; too high may mean stock-outs.

ex.q: Revenue ₹12,00,000; gross profit 25% on revenue; opening inventory ₹1,40,000; closing ₹1,60,000. Find inventory turnover.

topics.rl: Fast-moving consumer goods firms like those selling biscuits and soaps turn inventory many times a year; jewellers turn it far less often.

rv.summary: Inventory turnover ratio = cost of revenue from operations ÷ average inventory, where average inventory = (opening + closing) ÷ 2. Cost of revenue is found from revenue and gross profit (on cost or on revenue).
focus: Finding cost of revenue when GP is on cost or on revenue
remember: Inventory turnover = cost of revenue from operations ÷ average inventory
GP on cost: cost = revenue × 100 ÷ (100 + GP%)
GP on revenue: cost = revenue × (100 − GP%) ÷ 100
traps: Don't use revenue at selling price in the numerator
GP 25% on cost is not 25% on revenue
Very low turnover is a warning sign, not efficiency

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Trade receivables and trade payables turnover
topics.h: Customers pay you in 73 days but you pay suppliers in 60. That gap can squeeze your cash – turnover ratios reveal it.
p: Trade receivables turnover = Net credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables. Trade receivables = Debtors + Bills receivable (before deducting provision for doubtful debts).
Trade payables turnover = Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables. Trade payables = Creditors + Bills payable.
Average collection period = 365 days (or 12 months) ÷ Trade receivables turnover.
Average payment period = 365 days (or 12 months) ÷ Trade payables turnover.
Higher receivables turnover = faster collection; higher payables turnover = faster payment to suppliers.

ex.q: Credit revenue ₹7,50,000; trade receivables: opening ₹1,20,000, closing ₹1,80,000. Find turnover and average collection period.

topics.rl: Small suppliers to large companies in India often complain about long payment periods – which is why the MSME Act sets limits on delayed payments.

rv.summary: Trade receivables turnover = net credit revenue ÷ average trade receivables (gross); trade payables turnover = net credit purchases ÷ average trade payables. Collection and payment periods = 365 days (or 12 months) ÷ turnover.
remember: Trade receivables = debtors + bills receivable (before provision)
Average collection period = 365 ÷ receivables turnover
Average payment period = 365 (or 12 months) ÷ payables turnover
traps: Don't deduct the provision for doubtful debts
Use credit sales and credit purchases, not totals
Falling turnover means slower, not faster, collection

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Net assets, fixed assets and working capital turnover
topics.h: How many rupees of sales does each rupee of capital generate? Three turnover ratios measure how hard the company's money is working.
p: Net assets (capital employed) turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Capital employed.
Fixed assets turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Net fixed assets (after depreciation).
Working capital turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Working capital (current assets − current liabilities).
Higher ratios generally indicate better use of resources.

ex.q: Revenue ₹30,00,000; capital employed ₹15,00,000; net fixed assets ₹12,00,000; working capital ₹3,00,000. Compute the three ratios.

topics.rl: Asset-light Indian IT firms have very high fixed-asset turnover compared with steel plants that need huge factories.

rv.summary: Net assets (capital employed) turnover = revenue ÷ capital employed; fixed assets turnover = revenue ÷ net fixed assets; working capital turnover = revenue ÷ working capital. Higher ratios generally show better use of resources.
focus: Working back from turnover to capital employed
remember: Net assets turnover = revenue ÷ capital employed
Fixed assets turnover = revenue ÷ net fixed assets
Working capital turnover = revenue ÷ (CA − CL)
traps: Use net fixed assets, not original cost
Working capital is CA − CL, not CA alone
Net assets turnover is not the proprietary ratio

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Gross profit ratio, operating ratio and operating profit ratio
topics.h: Out of every ₹100 of sales, how much is left after the cost of goods – and after running the business? These three ratios tell you.
p: Gross profit ratio = Gross profit ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100. Net revenue = revenue − returns.

Operating ratio = (Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses) ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100. Operating expenses include office and administration, selling and distribution, employee benefits and depreciation.
Operating profit ratio = Operating profit ÷ Net revenue from operations × 100, where operating profit = revenue − operating cost.
Operating profit ratio = 100 − Operating ratio.
Non-operating items (interest on investments, loss by fire, profit on sale of assets) are excluded from operating ratios.

ex.q: Sales ₹10,50,000; returns ₹50,000; cost of revenue ₹7,00,000; operating expenses ₹1,00,000. Compute the three ratios.

topics.rl: Quick-service restaurant chains in India track operating ratio closely – rent and staff costs can eat margins fast.

rv.summary: Gross profit ratio = GP ÷ net revenue × 100; operating ratio = (cost of revenue + operating expenses) ÷ net revenue × 100; operating profit ratio = operating profit ÷ net revenue × 100 = 100 − operating ratio. Non-operating items are excluded.
focus: Calculating GP ratio, operating ratio and operating profit ratio
remember: GP ratio = GP ÷ net revenue × 100
Operating ratio = (cost of revenue + operating expenses) ÷ net revenue × 100
Operating profit ratio = 100 − operating ratio
traps: Exclude non-operating items like loss on sale of assets or interest received
Use net revenue (after returns)
Operating profit ratio is not the same as GP ratio

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Net profit ratio and return on investment
topics.h: The bottom line and the big question: for every ₹100 invested, how much does the business earn?
p: Net profit ratio = Net profit ÷ Revenue from operations × 100. It can be based on profit before tax or profit after tax.
Return on investment (ROI), or return on capital employed = Profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100.
PBIT = Profit before tax + interest on long-term debt (finance costs on long-term borrowings).
Capital employed = Shareholders' funds + Long-term debts (or Non-current assets + Working capital).
ROI judges overall efficiency; compare it with the cost of borrowing to decide whether more debt helps owners.

ex.q: Revenue ₹10,00,000; PBT ₹1,50,000; tax ₹50,000; interest on debentures ₹50,000; capital employed ₹10,00,000. Find NP ratios and ROI.

topics.rl: Investors comparing Indian banks and IT majors often look first at ROI/ROCE – it shows who uses capital best.

rv.summary: Net profit ratio = net profit ÷ revenue × 100 (before or after tax). ROI = PBIT ÷ capital employed × 100, where PBIT = PBT + interest on long-term debt. If ROI exceeds the cost of debt, more debt benefits equity holders.
focus: Comparing ROI with cost of debt
remember: ROI = PBIT ÷ capital employed × 100
PBIT = PBT + interest on long-term debt
Capital employed = shareholders' funds + long-term debts = NCA + working capital
traps: Use PBIT, not PAT, for ROI
Add back interest to PBT, don't subtract it
More debt helps owners only when ROI exceeds the cost of debt

topics.ch: Part II: Accounting Ratios
topics.t: Ratio applications: effects of transactions and missing figures
topics.h: Board-exam favourite: 'Will paying a creditor raise or lower the current ratio?' Master the logic, not just the formula.
p: When current ratio > 1: an equal decrease in CA and CL (e.g. paying a creditor) INCREASES the ratio; an equal increase (e.g. buying goods on credit) DECREASES it.
Transactions within current assets (e.g. collecting from debtors) do not change the current ratio; a current asset used for a non-current asset (buying machinery for cash) reduces it.
Debt-equity: issue of equity shares or conversion of debentures into shares reduces it; issue of debentures for cash increases it.
Missing figures: use the ratio definitions as equations, e.g. CR 2.5, QR 1.5, CL ₹80,000 → CA ₹2,00,000, quick assets ₹1,20,000, inventory ₹80,000 (if no prepaid expenses).
Comprehensive questions: compute several ratios from one set of statements – always identify CA, CL, equity, long-term debt and capital employed first.

ex.q: Current ratio is 2 : 1 (CA ₹2,00,000, CL ₹1,00,000). Creditors of ₹50,000 are paid. New ratio?

topics.rl: Finance managers sometimes time payments to suppliers before year-end to improve the reported current ratio – one reason analysts watch for window dressing.

rv.summary: Transactions change ratios: with CR above 1, an equal fall in CA and CL raises it and an equal rise lowers it; swaps within current assets leave it unchanged. Issuing shares or converting debentures lowers debt-equity. Missing figures are found by using ratio definitions as equations.
focus: Effect of transactions on the current ratio
remember: CR > 1: equal decrease in CA and CL → ratio rises; equal increase → ratio falls
Collecting debtors: no change
Issue of shares or conversion of debentures: debt-equity falls
traps: Paying creditors raises, not lowers, a current ratio above 1
Collecting debtors does not change the current ratio
Issuing debentures for cash raises, not lowers, debt-equity

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Cash flow statement: meaning, objectives and benefits
topics.h: A company can report a big profit and still run out of cash to pay salaries. The cash flow statement shows where the money actually came from and went.
p: A cash flow statement shows inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. It is prepared as per AS 3 (Revised).
Objective: to show the sources and uses of cash and cash equivalents, and to explain the change between the opening and closing balances.

Benefits: assess liquidity and the ability to generate cash; help short-term planning; allow comparison across firms (removes effects of different accounting treatments); evaluate changes in net assets and financial structure.
A cash inflow increases, and an outflow decreases, total cash and cash equivalents.
Movements WITHIN cash and cash equivalents (e.g. cash deposited into bank, or cash used to buy a 2-month treasury bill) are not cash flows.

ex.q: Which of these is a cash flow? (a) ₹50,000 cash deposited into the bank; (b) machinery bought for ₹2,00,000 cash.
st: (a) Cash moves to bank – both are cash and cash equivalents, so total is unchanged → not a cash flow.
(b) Cash leaves for a non-cash asset → a cash outflow (investing activity).

topics.rl: Many Indian start-ups reporting rising revenue still shut down because they burn cash faster than they raise it – the cash flow statement exposes that.

rv.summary: A cash flow statement (AS 3 Revised) shows inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period under operating, investing and financing activities, explaining the change in cash. Movements within cash and cash equivalents are not cash flows.
focus: Meaning and objectives of a cash flow statement
What is and is not a cash flow
remember: AS 3 (Revised)
Three activities: operating, investing, financing
Movements within cash and cash equivalents are not cash flows
traps: Depositing cash in the bank is not a cash flow
Profit is not the same as cash
A 2-month treasury bill is a cash equivalent, not an investment outflow

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Cash and cash equivalents
topics.h: Cash is obvious. But a 60-day treasury bill? An overdraft? Knowing what counts as 'cash' is half the battle.
p: Cash comprises cash in hand and demand deposits with banks.

Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value – generally with maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition (e.g. treasury bills, commercial paper).
In CBSE questions, current investments are treated as marketable securities and hence as cash equivalents.
Bank overdraft and cash credit are treated as short-term borrowings, and changes in them are shown under financing activities.
Equity shares are not cash equivalents because their value can change significantly.

ex.q: Cash in hand ₹20,000; bank balance (current account) ₹60,000; treasury bills maturing in 2 months ₹30,000; current investments (marketable securities) ₹10,000; bank overdraft ₹25,000. Find cash and cash equivalents.
st: Bank overdraft is a short-term borrowing (financing), not deducted here.

topics.rl: 91-day treasury bills of the Government of India, auctioned by the RBI, are the textbook example of cash equivalents held by Indian companies.

rv.summary: Cash is cash in hand and demand deposits; cash equivalents are short-term (generally ≤ 3 months), highly liquid investments with insignificant risk of value change. In CBSE problems current investments are cash equivalents, while overdraft and cash credit are financing items.
focus: Meaning of cash and cash equivalents
Treatment of current investments, bank overdraft and cash credit
remember: Cash equivalents: maturity ≤ 3 months, insignificant value risk
Current investments = marketable securities = cash equivalents (CBSE)
Bank overdraft and cash credit → financing activities
traps: Equity shares are not cash equivalents
Don't deduct bank overdraft from cash and cash equivalents in CBSE problems
A 3-year fixed deposit is not a cash equivalent

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Operating, investing and financing activities
topics.h: Every rupee in or out of a company falls into one of three buckets. Sort them right and the statement writes itself.
p: Operating activities: principal revenue-producing activities – cash from sale of goods and services, royalties, fees and commissions; cash paid to suppliers and employees; income tax paid (unless linked to investing/financing).

Investing activities: acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments – purchase/sale of fixed assets and intangibles, purchase/sale of shares or debentures of other companies (not held for trading), loans to others and their recovery.

Financing activities: changes in the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings – issue of shares and debentures, long-term and short-term borrowings and their repayment, redemption, buy-back.
Exam type: classify given items into the three activities (for a non-financial company unless stated).

ex.q: Classify for a manufacturing company: (a) cash received from customers ₹8,00,000; (b) purchase of machinery ₹2,00,000; (c) issue of shares ₹5,00,000; (d) repayment of bank loan ₹1,00,000.

topics.rl: When an Indian telecom company pays for spectrum, it's an investing outflow; when it issues bonds to fund it, a financing inflow.

rv.summary: Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities; investing activities are purchase and sale of long-term assets and investments and loans to others; financing activities change the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings.
focus: Classifying items into the three activities
Calculating net cash from given items
remember: Operating: sales receipts, supplier and employee payments, tax
Investing: buying or selling fixed assets, intangibles, long-term investments, loans given
Financing: shares, debentures, borrowings, repayments, buy-back
traps: Sale of a patent is investing, not operating
Loans given by a manufacturing company are investing, not financing
Buy-back is financing, not investing

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Interest, dividend and income tax in the cash flow statement
topics.h: Interest paid by a bank is part of its business; interest paid by a car-maker is a financing cost. Same item, different bucket.
p: Financial enterprise (e.g. a bank, NBFC): interest paid, interest received and dividends received are operating activities; dividends paid are financing.
