Non-financial enterprise: interest paid and dividends paid are financing activities; interest received and dividends received are investing activities.
Dividends paid are always a financing activity.
Income tax paid is classified as an operating activity, unless it can be specifically identified with investing or financing activities. A tax refund received is an operating inflow.

ex.q: Classify for (i) a bank and (ii) a cement company: interest received ₹50,000; dividend paid ₹30,000.
st: Bank: interest received → operating; dividend paid → financing.
Cement company: interest received → investing; dividend paid → financing.
ex.a: Interest received: operating for the bank, investing for the cement company. Dividend paid: financing for both.

topics.rl: SBI's interest income is its core business, so it sits in operating activities; for Maruti Suzuki, interest earned on surplus funds is investing.

rv.summary: For non-financial companies, interest and dividends received are investing, and interest and dividends paid are financing. For financial companies, interest paid and received and dividends received are operating. Dividends paid are always financing; income tax is operating.
focus: Treatment of interest and dividend for financial vs non-financial companies
Classifying income tax and tax refund
remember: Non-financial: interest/dividend received → investing; interest/dividend paid → financing
Financial: interest paid and received, dividends received → operating
Dividends paid → always financing
Income tax → operating
traps: For a bank, interest received is operating, not investing
Dividend paid is never operating
Don't put income tax under financing

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Indirect method: from net profit to operating profit before working capital changes
topics.h: Start with the profit figure, then undo everything that isn't cash or isn't operating. That's the indirect method – the only method in the CBSE syllabus.
p: Step 1 – Net profit before tax and extraordinary items: Change in surplus (closing − opening balance of Statement of P&L) + transfer to reserves + provision for tax made during the year + interim dividend + dividend of the previous year paid this year (under AS 4 revised, proposed dividend is not a liability).
Step 2 – Add non-cash and non-operating charges: depreciation, amortisation (goodwill, patents), loss on sale of fixed assets/investments, interest paid on borrowings/debentures (finance cost).
Step 3 – Deduct non-operating incomes: profit on sale of fixed assets/investments, interest received, dividends received.
The result is Operating Profit before Working Capital Changes.

ex.q: Surplus rose from ₹50,000 to ₹1,30,000. Transfer to general reserve ₹20,000; provision for tax made ₹40,000; interim dividend ₹10,000. Depreciation ₹30,000; goodwill written off ₹10,000; loss on sale of machinery ₹5,000; interest on debentures ₹15,000; profit on sale of investments ₹8,000; dividend received ₹2,000. Find operating profit before working capital changes.

topics.rl: When analysts discuss 'EBITDA' of Indian companies, they are doing something similar – adding back depreciation and interest to see operating cash power.

rv.summary: In the indirect method, start from net profit before tax (change in surplus + transfers + tax provision + dividends), add non-cash and non-operating charges (depreciation, amortisation, losses, interest paid) and deduct non-operating incomes (profits on sale, interest and dividends received).
focus: Finding net profit before tax from the change in surplus
remember: NPBT = change in surplus + transfer to reserves + provision for tax + interim dividend + previous year's dividend paid
Add: depreciation, amortisation, losses on sale, interest paid
Less: profit on sale, interest and dividends received
traps: Don't start from the change in surplus alone; add back appropriations and tax
Profit on sale of assets is deducted, not added
Interest paid is added back, not deducted, for a non-financial company

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Working capital changes and income tax paid
topics.h: Profit is ready – but cash got stuck in extra stock and slow debtors. Working capital adjustments reveal the real operating cash.
p: Increase in a current asset (inventories, trade receivables, prepaid expenses) → DEDUCT; decrease → ADD.
Increase in a current liability (trade payables, outstanding expenses, income received in advance) → ADD; decrease → DEDUCT.
Exclude cash and cash equivalents (including current investments), short-term borrowings (financing) and provision for tax/dividend items from these adjustments.
Cash generated from operations = Operating profit before WC changes ± WC changes.
Net cash from operating activities = Cash generated from operations − Income tax paid.

ex.q: Operating profit before WC changes ₹2,00,000. Inventories +₹20,000; trade receivables −₹15,000; trade payables +₹10,000; outstanding expenses −₹5,000; prepaid expenses +₹2,000. Tax paid ₹38,000. Find net cash from operating activities.

topics.rl: Indian FMCG companies often run with negative working capital – suppliers fund them – which boosts operating cash flow.

rv.summary: Working capital changes adjust operating profit: increases in current assets and decreases in current liabilities are deducted; decreases in current assets and increases in current liabilities are added. Cash generated from operations less income tax paid gives net cash from operating activities.
focus: Direction of each working capital adjustment
Items excluded from working capital changes
Computing cash generated and net cash from operating activities
remember: Current asset ↑ → deduct; ↓ → add
Current liability ↑ → add; ↓ → deduct
Net cash from operating activities = cash generated from operations − tax paid
traps: Don't treat bank overdraft as a working capital item
An increase in receivables is deducted, not added
Exclude cash, cash equivalents and provision for tax from WC changes

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Investing and financing cash flows with working accounts
topics.h: The balance sheet shows machinery up by ₹1 lakh. But how much was actually bought, and how much sold? Working accounts dig out hidden figures.
p: Machinery (fixed asset) account: Opening + Purchases = Depreciation (if charged to asset) + Book value of asset sold + Closing. Solve for the missing purchase.
Provision for depreciation account: Opening + Depreciation charged = Accumulated depreciation on asset sold + Closing.
Provision for tax account: Opening + Provision made = Tax paid + Closing. So tax paid = Opening + Provision made − Closing.
Investing: purchase (outflow) and sale proceeds (inflow) of fixed assets and investments; interest and dividend received (non-financial).
Financing: issue of shares/debentures (including premium) and borrowings (inflows); redemption, repayment, interest paid and dividends paid (outflows).

ex.q: Machinery: opening ₹5,00,000; closing ₹6,00,000; depreciation ₹50,000; machinery with book value ₹40,000 sold for ₹35,000. Find purchases and net cash from these investing items.
st: Loss on sale ₹5,000 is added back in operating activities.

topics.rl: Annual reports of Indian infrastructure companies show heavy investing outflows (capex) funded by financing inflows (loans and bonds).

rv.summary: Working accounts find hidden figures like purchases, depreciation and tax paid. Investing covers purchases and full sale proceeds of fixed assets and investments; financing covers issues (with premium), borrowings, repayments, interest and dividends paid.
focus: Preparing the machinery and provision for depreciation accounts
Net investing and financing cash flows
remember: Purchases = closing + depreciation + book value sold − opening
Tax paid = opening provision + provision made − closing
Share issue inflow includes premium
traps: Show full sale proceeds, not the profit, under investing
Include the premium in share issue proceeds
Interest paid by a non-financial company is financing, not operating

topics.ch: Part II: Cash Flow Statement
topics.t: Preparing the cash flow statement (AS 3 format)
topics.h: Put the three blocks together, add them up, and the result must match the change in cash. If it does – you've nailed it.
p: Format (AS 3, indirect method): A. Cash Flows from Operating Activities; B. Cash Flows from Investing Activities; C. Cash Flows from Financing Activities.
Net increase/(decrease) in cash and cash equivalents = A + B + C.
Reconciliation: Opening cash and cash equivalents + Net increase (or − net decrease) = Closing cash and cash equivalents.
For a full question: compare two balance sheets, read additional information, prepare working accounts, then build A, B and C.
The direct method of computing operating cash flow is outside the CBSE syllabus.

ex.q: Net cash from operating activities ₹1,60,000; investing ₹(1,55,000); financing ₹75,000. Opening cash and cash equivalents ₹40,000. Find the net change and closing balance.
st: Check: this must equal the closing cash and cash equivalents in the balance sheet.

topics.rl: Every listed Indian company's annual report has exactly this three-block statement right after the balance sheet and P&L.

rv.summary: The AS 3 cash flow statement shows A (operating), B (investing) and C (financing). Net change = A + B + C, and opening cash and cash equivalents plus the net change must equal the closing balance.
remember: Net increase/(decrease) = A + B + C
Opening + net change = closing cash and cash equivalents
Indirect method only (CBSE)
traps: Don't add a net decrease to the opening balance
The direct method is outside the syllabus
Net profit is not equal to net cash flow

qa.q: Which section of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines 'partnership'?
qa.a: Section 4
qa.e: Section 4 gives the definition. Section 13 covers rights such as interest on loans, and Section 48 deals with settlement on dissolution.

qa.q: What is the maximum number of partners a partnership firm can have under the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014?
qa.e: Rule 10 of the 2014 Rules prescribes a maximum of 50 partners.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an essential feature of a partnership?
qa.a: Compulsory registration of the firm
qa.e: Registration is optional under the Act. Agreement, business, profit sharing and mutual agency are essential.

qa.q: 'Mutual agency' in a partnership means that:
qa.a: each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners, and also a principal
qa.e: Every partner can bind the firm by acts done in the ordinary course of business and is, in turn, bound by the acts of others.

qa.q: A firm's assets are ₹6,00,000 and its outside liabilities are ₹9,00,000. What happens to the shortfall?
qa.a: Partners must pay it from their private assets, as their liability is unlimited
qa.e: Partners are jointly and severally liable without limit, so creditors can recover the ₹3,00,000 shortfall from partners' personal assets.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two people who jointly own a godown and share its rent are not partners.
Reason (R): A partnership arises only from an agreement to carry on a business and share its profits.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Co-owning property and sharing its rent is not carrying on a business by agreement, which is exactly what R states.

qa.q: Which pair of accounts is special to partnership firms and not needed by a sole proprietor?
qa.a: Partners' current accounts and the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
qa.e: A sole trader takes the whole profit, so there is no appropriation among owners. Partners need appropriation and separate capital/current accounts.

qa.q: Which minimum number of persons is needed to form a partnership?
qa.e: Partnership is a relation between persons, so at least two are needed. Seven is the minimum for a public company.

qa.q: In the absence of a partnership deed, partners share profits and losses:
qa.a: equally
qa.e: The Act lays down equal sharing whenever the deed is absent or silent.

qa.q: Rate of interest allowed on a partner's loan when there is no deed:
qa.e: Section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act provides 6% per annum on loans and advances by partners.

qa.q: Karan, a partner, lent ₹50,000 to the firm on 1 October 2025. The firm has no deed and closes books on 31 March 2026. Interest on his loan for the year is:
qa.e: The loan was used for 6 months: ₹50,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,500.

qa.q: Interest on a partner's loan is treated as:
qa.a: a charge against profit, debited to the Profit and Loss Account
qa.e: A loan makes the partner a lender too; interest on it is an expense of the firm, payable even if there is a loss.

qa.q: Riya works full-time in the firm while her partner Dev works only on weekends. There is no deed. Riya claims a salary of ₹20,000 per month. Is she entitled to it?
qa.a: No, a partner gets no salary unless the deed or partners' agreement provides it
qa.e: Without a deed, no partner is entitled to salary or commission, however much time is devoted.

qa.q: Rohan's capital is ₹4,00,000 and Simran's is ₹2,00,000. There is no deed. The firm's profit is ₹90,000 and there are no loans. Simran's share of profit is:
qa.e: With no deed, profit is shared equally regardless of capital: ₹90,000 ÷ 2 = ₹45,000.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Interest on a partner's loan is paid even if the firm suffers a loss.
Reason (R): Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because it is a charge (an expense), it must be paid whether there is profit or loss.

qa.q: Which of these does a partnership deed usually NOT contain?
qa.a: The personal income-tax return of each partner
qa.e: A deed records the terms of the partnership among partners, not their personal tax filings.

qa.q: Under the fixed capital method, which item is recorded in the partner's Capital Account?
qa.a: Additional capital introduced
qa.e: Only permanent changes in capital, such as introducing or withdrawing capital, touch the fixed capital account.

qa.q: Nisha's current account (fixed capital method) opens at ₹20,000 Cr. Interest on capital ₹50,000, salary ₹30,000, profit share ₹60,000, drawings ₹40,000 and interest on drawings ₹2,000. Closing current account balance:
qa.e: Credits total ₹1,60,000 and debits ₹42,000, so the balance is ₹1,18,000 Cr.

qa.q: Under the fluctuating method, Arjun's opening capital is ₹3,00,000. Interest on capital ₹18,000, salary ₹24,000, profit share ₹40,000, drawings ₹30,000, interest on drawings ₹1,500. Closing capital:
Under the fixed capital method, which account of a partner may show a debit balance?
qa.a: Current Account
qa.e: Heavy drawings or losses can make the current account debit, while the fixed capital account stays credit.

qa.q: A question gives partners' capitals but does not say whether they are fixed or fluctuating. You should prepare:
qa.a: fluctuating capital accounts
qa.e: When no method is given, the fluctuating capital method is followed.

qa.q: Where is a debit balance in a partner's current account shown in the firm's balance sheet?
qa.a: On the assets side
qa.e: A debit balance means the partner owes money to the firm, so it is an asset of the firm.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under the fixed capital method, a partner's drawings are debited to the current account.
Reason (R): Under this method, the capital account changes only when capital is introduced or withdrawn permanently.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since the capital account is kept fixed, regular drawings must go elsewhere – the current account.

qa.q: Fixed capital method: Meena's capital is ₹4,00,000; her current account opens at ₹10,000 Dr. During the year she gets interest on capital ₹32,000 and a profit share of ₹48,000; her drawings are ₹50,000. Her closing current account balance (credit) is:
qa.e: Start at −10,000, add 32,000 and 48,000, subtract 50,000: the result is +20,000, a credit balance.

qa.q: Which of these is debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?
qa.a: Salary to a partner
qa.e: Partners' salary is an appropriation. Loan interest and rent to a partner are charges in the Profit and Loss Account; interest on drawings is credited.

qa.q: Profit before commission is ₹2,10,000. The manager-partner gets 5% commission on net profit after charging such commission. Commission =
qa.e: After-charging commission = 2,10,000 × 5/105 = ₹10,000; then 2,00,000 × 5% = 10,000 checks out.

qa.q: Same firm: profit before commission ₹2,10,000, but now commission is 5% of net profit before charging it. Commission =
qa.e: Before-charging commission is simply 5% of ₹2,10,000 = ₹10,500.

qa.q: Net profit ₹4,00,000; interest on capital A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000; salary B ₹50,000; interest on drawings A ₹4,000, B ₹6,000; reserve ₹40,000. A and B share 3:2. B's share of profit:
How is interest on drawings recorded?
qa.a: Dr Partner's Capital/Current A/c / Cr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c
qa.e: Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm and a burden on the partner, so the partner is debited and the appropriation account credited.

qa.q: A, B and C share profits equally. C gets a salary of ₹2,000 per month. Net profit is ₹1,20,000. A's share of profit:
qa.e: Salary for the year = ₹24,000; divisible profit ₹96,000 ÷ 3 = ₹32,000.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Salary to a partner is credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
Reason (R): Salary to a partner is an appropriation of profit.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Salary is an appropriation (R true), so it is debited – not credited – to the appropriation account (A false).

qa.q: Net profit ₹1,50,000. 10% of net profit is transferred to general reserve and the rest is shared by X and Y in 2:1. X's share:
Opening capital ₹4,00,000; additional capital ₹1,00,000 on 1 October; interest 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Interest on capital:
qa.e: ₹40,000 on opening capital plus ₹5,000 on the addition for 6 months.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000; ₹50,000 withdrawn on 1 January; interest 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Interest on capital:
qa.e: Interest on ₹3,00,000 for 12 months is ₹30,000, minus interest on ₹50,000 for the 3 months after withdrawal (₹1,250).

qa.q: Interest on capital: A ₹30,000 and B ₹20,000. The deed allows interest only out of profits. Profit is ₹40,000. B will get interest of:
qa.e: Profit is short, so ₹40,000 is shared in the ratio of interest 3:2. B gets 2/5 × 40,000 = ₹16,000.

qa.q: The deed provides interest on capital at 10% as an appropriation. The firm makes a loss of ₹25,000. Interest on capital allowed:
qa.a: None
qa.e: As an appropriation, interest on capital needs profits; with a loss, nothing is allowed.

qa.q: Ravi's closing capital (before interest on capital) is ₹5,40,000. During the year his profit share was ₹80,000, drawings ₹60,000 and additional capital ₹40,000 (introduced on day 1 of the year). His opening capital was:
qa.e: Reverse the year: remove the profit share and the additional capital, and add back the drawings.

qa.q: X's capital is ₹6,00,000 and Y's ₹4,00,000. Interest on capital is 5% p.a. Profit is ₹75,000, shared equally after interest. X's total (interest + share):
qa.e: X's interest ₹30,000; Y's ₹20,000. Balance ₹25,000 shared equally, so X gets ₹12,500 more.

qa.q: When the profit is less than the total interest on capital (interest payable only out of profit), the profit is divided in the ratio of:
qa.a: interest on capital due to each partner
qa.e: The available profit is shared in proportion to the interest each partner would have received.

qa.q: Interest on capital is normally calculated on:
qa.a: opening capital, adjusted for capital added or withdrawn on a time basis
qa.e: Closing capital already includes the year's profit; interest is on capital actually used during the year.

qa.q: Drawings: ₹10,000 on 1 July, ₹20,000 on 1 October, ₹15,000 on 1 January. Year ends 31 March. Rate 6% p.a. Interest on drawings:
A partner draws ₹5,000 at the beginning of every month for the year. Interest is 10% p.a. Interest on drawings:
qa.e: Beginning of each month → average 6.5 months on ₹60,000: 60,000 × 10% × 6.5/12 = ₹3,250.

qa.q: For equal drawings at the END of every month for a full year, interest is charged for an average period (in months) of:
qa.e: The first drawing stays out for 11 months and the last for 0; the average is 5.5 months.

qa.q: A partner draws ₹30,000 at the beginning of each quarter. Interest is 8% p.a. Interest on drawings for the year:
qa.e: Total ₹1,20,000; beginning of quarter → average 7.5 months: 1,20,000 × 8% × 7.5/12 = ₹6,000.

qa.q: A partner draws ₹30,000 at the end of each quarter. Interest is 8% p.a. Interest on drawings:
qa.e: End of quarter → average 4.5 months: 1,20,000 × 8% × 4.5/12 = ₹3,600.

qa.q: Total drawings of a partner are ₹48,000; dates are not given. Interest is 10% p.a. Interest on drawings:
qa.e: When dates are unknown, assume drawings were spread evenly and charge for 6 months.

qa.q: The deed says interest on drawings is to be charged at a flat 5% (not per annum). A partner drew ₹40,000 at various times. Interest on drawings:
qa.e: A flat rate ignores time, so interest = 40,000 × 5% = ₹2,000.

qa.q: A partner draws ₹4,000 in the middle of every month for the year. Interest is 12% p.a. Interest on drawings:
qa.e: Middle of each month → average 6 months: 48,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹2,880.

qa.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C is guaranteed ₹60,000 by the firm. Profit is ₹3,00,000. A's final share:
qa.e: Deficiency ₹10,000 is borne by A and B in 3:2; A bears ₹6,000.

qa.q: Same firm (3:2:1, profit ₹3,00,000), but only A guarantees C's ₹60,000. A's final share:
qa.e: A alone bears the ₹10,000 deficiency: 1,50,000 − 10,000 = ₹1,40,000.

qa.q: Same firm, but A and B bear C's deficiency equally. B's final share:
Same firm (3:2:1), C guaranteed ₹60,000, but profit is ₹4,20,000. C receives:
qa.e: C's actual share 4,20,000 × 1/6 = ₹70,000 exceeds the guarantee, so he takes ₹70,000.

qa.q: P, Q and R share 2:2:1. R is guaranteed ₹50,000; P and Q bear any deficiency equally. Profit is ₹1,20,000. P's final share:
qa.e: R's share ₹24,000; deficiency ₹26,000 borne equally, so P bears ₹13,000: 48,000 − 13,000 = ₹35,000.

qa.q: A guarantee of profit to a partner means:
qa.a: the partner gets at least the guaranteed amount; any shortfall is met by the guarantor(s)
qa.e: It is a minimum. If the actual share is higher, the partner keeps the higher amount.

qa.q: The firm (not any one partner) has guaranteed a minimum profit to D. The deficiency is borne by:
qa.a: all other partners in their profit-sharing ratio
qa.e: A guarantee by the firm means the remaining partners share the deficiency in their own ratio.

qa.q: C's guaranteed profit is short by ₹8,000, and A alone has to make it good. The journal entry is:
qa.a: Dr A's Capital A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹8,000
qa.e: A gives up ₹8,000 of his share, which goes to C.

qa.q: A (capital ₹3,00,000) and B (capital ₹1,00,000) shared ₹80,000 profit equally, omitting 10% interest on capital. Net effect on A:
qa.e: A should get ₹30,000 interest but bears half of the ₹40,000 total, a net gain of ₹10,000.

qa.q: For the case above, the adjusting entry is:
qa.a: Dr B's Capital A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000
qa.e: B received ₹10,000 too much and A ₹10,000 too little, so B is debited and A credited.

qa.q: Profit of ₹1,20,000 was shared equally between X and Y instead of 3:1. The adjusting entry amount is:
qa.e: X should get ₹90,000 but got ₹60,000; Y should get ₹30,000 but got ₹60,000. The transfer is ₹30,000 from Y to X.

qa.q: A and B share equally. Interest on drawings was omitted: A ₹2,000 and B ₹1,000. In the adjusting entry, A's account will be debited by:
qa.e: Charge A ₹2,000 and B ₹1,000; credit the ₹3,000 back equally (₹1,500 each). Net: A −₹500, B +₹500.

qa.q: A and B share 2:1. Salary of ₹12,000 to B was omitted. The adjusting entry amount (Dr A, Cr B) is:
qa.e: B gets ₹12,000 but bears 1/3 of it (₹4,000) through reduced profit; A bears 2/3 = ₹8,000.

qa.q: Why are past errors in partners' accounts corrected by an adjusting entry rather than by redoing the accounts?
qa.a: The accounts are already closed; one entry changes only how profit was shared, which is all that went wrong
qa.e: Total profit is unaffected; only partners' shares need correction, so one entry is enough.

qa.q: In a past-adjustment statement, the sum of the net effects on all partners is:
qa.a: zero
qa.e: Every rupee credited to one partner is debited to another; the firm's profit is unchanged.

qa.q: Partners' capitals are fixed. A past adjustment must be recorded through:
qa.a: partners' current accounts
qa.e: With fixed capitals, all such adjustments go through current accounts.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a case of reconstitution of a partnership firm?
qa.a: An increase in the firm's sales
qa.e: Reconstitution means a change in the partnership agreement; higher sales change nothing in the agreement.

qa.q: A newly admitted partner acquires:
qa.a: a share in the assets and in the future profits of the firm
qa.e: He becomes a co-owner of assets and shares future profits; past profits belong to the old partners.

qa.q: Why does an incoming partner bring a premium for goodwill?
qa.a: To compensate the old partners for the share of future profits they sacrifice
qa.e: Old partners give up part of their profit share; the premium is their compensation.

qa.q: Which adjustment is NOT required on admission of a partner?
qa.a: Preparing a Realisation Account
qa.e: A Realisation Account is used when a firm is dissolved, not when a partner is admitted.

qa.q: Why are assets and liabilities revalued at the time of admission?
qa.a: So that gains or losses up to the date of admission are shared only by the old partners
qa.e: Changes in value arose while the old partners owned the firm, so they must get the benefit or bear the loss.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): On admission of a partner, the shares of some or all old partners decrease.
Reason (R): The new partner's share comes out of the shares of the old partners.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The new partner's share is given up by old partners, so their shares fall; R explains A.

qa.q: Which of the following is a mode of reconstitution of a firm?
qa.a: Amalgamation of two partnership firms
qa.e: When two firms amalgamate, a new agreement among partners arises – a reconstitution.

qa.q: Capital brought in by a new partner is mainly for:
qa.a: his share in the firm's assets (stake in the business)
qa.e: Capital gives him his stake; goodwill premium is a separate payment that compensates old partners.

qa.q: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, taken in the old ratio. The new ratio is:
qa.e: Old partners keep 4/5 in 3:2: A 12/25, B 8/25, C 5/25.

qa.q: A and B share 3:2. C is admitted for 1/5 share, which A and B give up equally. The new ratio is:
A and B share 3:2. C gets 1/5 share, all of it from A. The new ratio is:
A and B share 3:2. A surrenders 1/3 of his share and B 1/4 of his share in favour of C. The new ratio is:
In the case above (A surrenders 1/3 of his 3/5 share), A's sacrifice is:
qa.e: Sacrifice = 3/5 × 1/3 = 1/5.

qa.q: A and B shared 3:2. After C's admission the new ratio is 4:3:3. The sacrificing ratio of A and B is:
X and Y shared equally. Z is admitted and the new ratio is X:Y:Z = 3:2:1. Who sacrificed?
qa.a: Only Y; X's share is unchanged
qa.e: X: 1/2 − 3/6 = 0; Y: 1/2 − 2/6 = 1/6. Only Y gave up a share.

qa.q: When the question is silent about how the new partner's share is given up, the sacrificing ratio is:
qa.a: the old profit-sharing ratio
qa.e: Old partners are assumed to give up the share in their old ratio.

qa.q: Goodwill is best described as:
qa.a: an intangible asset reflecting the ability to earn above-normal profits
qa.e: Goodwill has value and helps earn excess profits, but it cannot be seen or touched.

qa.q: Which factor is most likely to INCREASE a firm's goodwill?
qa.a: Location near a busy metro station
qa.e: A favourable location brings more customers and above-normal profits.

qa.q: Goodwill need NOT be valued when:
qa.a: a partner's salary is increased
qa.e: Salary changes do not shift future profit rights among partners in a way that needs goodwill valuation.

qa.q: Which statement about goodwill is correct?
qa.a: It can be realised only when the business as a whole is sold
qa.e: Goodwill is attached to the business and cannot be sold on its own.

qa.q: A firm holds an exclusive licence to run the only canteen at a large AIIMS campus. This affects goodwill through:
qa.a: special advantages
qa.e: Exclusive licences and contracts are special advantages that boost goodwill.

qa.q: A business dealing in essential goods with steady demand usually has:
qa.a: higher goodwill, because of stable earnings
qa.e: The nature of business matters: stable demand gives steady profits and stronger goodwill.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Goodwill is valued when a new partner is admitted.
Reason (R): The new partner will share future profits that are partly due to the reputation built by the old partners.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Old partners built the goodwill; the new partner must compensate them for sharing its benefits.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a factor affecting goodwill?
qa.a: The colour of the firm's letterhead
qa.e: Goodwill depends on factors that affect profitability, not cosmetic details.

qa.q: Profits: ₹80,000, ₹1,00,000 and ₹1,20,000. Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of average profit is:
Profits for four years: ₹1,50,000; loss ₹30,000; ₹1,80,000; ₹2,00,000. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase of average profit:
qa.e: Total = 5,00,000 (loss subtracted); average 1,25,000; × 3 = ₹3,75,000.

qa.q: Profits ₹60,000, ₹90,000, ₹1,20,000 (latest) with weights 1, 2, 3. Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of weighted average profit:
Profits: ₹1,10,000; ₹1,40,000 (includes ₹20,000 profit on sale of land); ₹1,20,000 (after a ₹10,000 loss by fire). Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of normal average profit:
Average profit is ₹1,50,000, but a working partner's reasonable salary of ₹30,000 a year has not been charged. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase:
The weighted average profit method is preferred when:
qa.a: profits show a rising or falling trend
qa.e: Weights give more importance to recent years, which better reflect the trend.

qa.q: Goodwill valued at 2.5 years' purchase of average profit is ₹3,00,000. Average profit is:
qa.e: Average profit = Goodwill ÷ years' purchase = 3,00,000 ÷ 2.5.

qa.q: While normalising past profits, an insurance claim of ₹15,000 received for an earlier loss (an abnormal gain) should be:
qa.a: deducted from that year's profit
qa.e: Abnormal gains will not recur, so they are removed before averaging.

qa.q: Capital employed ₹5,00,000; normal rate 10%; average profit ₹80,000. Goodwill at 3 years' purchase of super profit:
qa.e: Normal profit ₹50,000; super profit ₹30,000; × 3 = ₹90,000.

qa.q: Average profit ₹80,000; normal rate 10%; capital employed ₹5,00,000. Goodwill by capitalisation of average profit:
qa.e: Capitalised value ₹8,00,000 less capital employed ₹5,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

qa.q: Super profit is ₹24,000 and the normal rate of return is 12%. Goodwill by capitalisation of super profit:
Total assets ₹7,00,000 (including goodwill ₹50,000); outside liabilities ₹1,50,000. Capital employed for valuing goodwill:
Capital employed ₹6,00,000; normal rate of return 15%. Normal profit:
'Super profit' means:
qa.a: the excess of average profit over normal profit
qa.e: It is the extra profit the firm earns above what similar firms normally earn on the same capital.

qa.q: Goodwill by the super profit method at 2 years' purchase is ₹1,20,000. Normal profit is ₹1,00,000. Average profit is:
Average profit ₹1,50,000; normal rate 12%; capital employed ₹10,00,000. Goodwill by capitalisation of average profit:
Under AS 26, when a new partner is admitted:
qa.a: no Goodwill Account is raised; premium is shared by sacrificing partners
qa.e: Only purchased goodwill can be recorded, so the premium mechanism is used.

qa.q: A and B share 3:2. C joins for 1/5; firm's goodwill ₹1,50,000; C brings his premium in cash. Amount credited to A:
qa.e: C's premium ₹30,000 shared 3:2 → A ₹18,000.

qa.q: A and B share 3:2. New ratio A:B:C = 4:3:3. Firm's goodwill ₹1,00,000. C's premium is credited to A at:
qa.e: C's premium = 30,000; sacrificing ratio 2:1; A gets 2/3 = ₹20,000.

qa.q: Entry to distribute premium for goodwill brought in cash:
qa.a: Dr Premium for Goodwill A/c / Cr sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs
qa.e: The premium account is cleared by crediting the partners who sacrificed.

qa.q: Old partners withdraw the premium credited to them. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr old partners' Capital A/cs / Cr Cash A/c
qa.e: Withdrawal reduces their capital and the firm's cash.

qa.q: C brings machinery worth ₹1,00,000: ₹70,000 as capital and ₹30,000 as premium for goodwill. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Machinery ₹1,00,000 / Cr C's Capital ₹70,000, Cr Premium for Goodwill ₹30,000
qa.e: The asset is debited; the amount is split between his capital and the premium.

qa.q: C should bring ₹30,000 as premium but brings only ₹18,000. Amount debited to C's Capital/Current A/c:
qa.e: The part not brought (30,000 − 18,000) is debited to his account and credited to sacrificing partners.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Premium for goodwill brought by a new partner is credited to old partners in their sacrificing ratio.
Reason (R): Old partners give up a part of their future profits to the new partner.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Compensation follows sacrifice, so R explains A.

qa.q: New partner D cannot bring his share of goodwill in cash. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr D's Capital A/c / Cr sacrificing partners' Capital A/cs
qa.e: D is charged for his share of goodwill and the sacrificing partners are compensated.

qa.q: Goodwill of ₹40,000 appears in the books when C is admitted. A and B share 3:2. Amount debited to A when it is written off:
qa.e: Existing goodwill is written off among old partners in the old ratio: 40,000 × 3/5.

qa.q: A and B have adjusted capitals of ₹1,00,000 and ₹80,000. C brings ₹80,000 for 1/4 share. Hidden goodwill:
qa.e: Implied total ₹3,20,000 less actual ₹2,60,000 (including C's capital) = ₹60,000.

qa.q: In the case above, C's share of the hidden goodwill is:
C's share of goodwill is ₹24,000, which he cannot bring. A and B sacrifice equally. Amount credited to B:
qa.e: Sacrificing ratio 1:1, so B gets half of ₹24,000.

qa.q: Why is existing goodwill written off when a new partner is admitted?
qa.a: Because goodwill is adjusted through the new partner's premium, and the old goodwill belongs to the old partners
qa.e: Writing it off in the old ratio clears the books so goodwill is adjusted only through premium, as AS 26 requires.

qa.q: Hidden goodwill arises when:
qa.a: the capital implied by the new partner's contribution exceeds the actual combined capital of all partners
qa.e: The gap between implied and actual capital is attributed to goodwill.

qa.q: Capitals are fixed. The new partner's unpaid share of goodwill is debited to his:
qa.a: Current Account
qa.e: Fixed capitals stay unchanged; adjustments go to the current account.

qa.q: General Reserve of ₹50,000 appears at the time of C's admission. A and B share 3:2. A's capital is credited with:
qa.e: Reserves belong to old partners in the old ratio: 50,000 × 3/5.

qa.q: Workmen Compensation Reserve ₹30,000; claim ₹20,000. Amount credited to old partners:
qa.e: The claim is provided for first; the excess ₹10,000 goes to old partners.

qa.q: Workmen Compensation Reserve ₹30,000; claim ₹40,000. The extra ₹10,000 of claim is:
qa.a: debited to the Revaluation Account
qa.e: The reserve covers ₹30,000; the extra liability is a revaluation loss shared by old partners.

qa.q: Advertisement Suspense of ₹12,000 appears in the balance sheet; A and B share 2:1. Amount debited to A:
qa.e: Deferred revenue expenditure is written off among old partners in the old ratio: 12,000 × 2/3.

qa.q: Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹20,000; investments: book value ₹1,00,000, market value ₹92,000. Amount of the reserve credited to old partners:
qa.e: The fall of ₹8,000 is met from the reserve; the balance ₹12,000 goes to old partners.

qa.q: Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹20,000; investments: book value ₹1,00,000, market value ₹75,000. Amount debited to Revaluation Account:
qa.e: Fall ₹25,000; reserve absorbs ₹20,000; extra ₹5,000 is a revaluation loss.

qa.q: Partners decide not to disturb a General Reserve of ₹60,000. C is admitted for 1/4 share. Amount debited to C's Capital in the adjusting entry:
qa.e: C would get 1/4 of the reserve in future, so he compensates sacrificing partners now: 60,000 × 1/4.

qa.q: Why are accumulated reserves distributed among old partners in the old ratio on admission?
qa.a: They were earned when the old partners shared profits in that ratio
qa.e: Past profits belong to those who shared them, in the ratio then in force.

qa.q: An increase in the value of an asset on revaluation is:
qa.a: credited to the Revaluation Account
qa.e: A rise in asset value is a gain, so the Revaluation Account is credited (and the asset debited).

qa.q: An unrecorded liability (e.g. outstanding salary) found on admission is:
qa.a: debited to the Revaluation Account
qa.e: Recording a new liability is a loss to old partners, so Revaluation is debited.

qa.q: Credits to Revaluation A/c total ₹49,000 and debits total ₹12,000. Result:
qa.e: Profit = credits − debits = ₹37,000.

qa.q: Revaluation profit of ₹37,000 is shared by A and B (3:2) before C's admission. A's share:
qa.e: Old partners share in the old ratio: 37,000 × 3/5.

qa.q: Debtors ₹50,000 carry a provision of ₹1,000. A 5% provision is now required. Amount debited to Revaluation Account:
qa.e: Required ₹2,500 less existing ₹1,000 = extra ₹1,500.

qa.q: Profit or loss on revaluation at the time of admission is shared by:
qa.a: old partners in their old ratio
qa.e: The change in values arose before admission, so only old partners share it.

qa.q: The entry to transfer a revaluation LOSS is:
qa.a: Dr Old Partners' Capital A/cs / Cr Revaluation A/c
qa.e: A loss reduces old partners' capitals, closing the Revaluation Account's debit balance.

qa.q: Machinery of ₹80,000 is depreciated by 10% and stock is appreciated by ₹5,000. Net result on revaluation (loss):
qa.e: Loss ₹8,000 on machinery, gain ₹5,000 on stock: net loss ₹3,000.

qa.q: Before C's admission, A's capital is ₹2,00,000. A is credited with ₹22,200 as his share of revaluation profit and ₹30,000 as his share of general reserve. A's capital shown in the new balance sheet (before any capital adjustment):
qa.e: All reconstitution gains are credited to A's capital account, and its closing balance goes to the new balance sheet: 2,00,000 + 22,200 + 30,000.

qa.q: A's and B's adjusted capitals total ₹2,00,000 for their combined 4/5 share. C gets 1/5. C's capital should be:
C brings ₹1,00,000 as capital for 1/5 share. Total capital of the new firm:
C brings ₹60,000 for 1/4 share. New ratio A:B:C = 2:1:1. A's required capital:
qa.e: Total capital ₹2,40,000; A's share 2/4 → ₹1,20,000.

qa.q: In the case above, A's adjusted capital is ₹1,30,000. A must:
qa.a: withdraw ₹10,000
qa.e: A has ₹10,000 more than required, so he withdraws the excess.

qa.q: B's adjusted capital is ₹50,000 but his required capital is ₹60,000. B brings the deficiency in cash. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Cash A/c / Cr B's Capital A/c ₹10,000
qa.e: Bringing cash increases both cash and B's capital.

qa.q: Capitals are to be kept fixed. A partner's surplus capital after adjustment is:
qa.a: transferred to his current account
qa.e: With fixed capitals, the surplus is credited to his current account.

qa.q: Old partners' adjusted capitals: A ₹1,80,000 and B ₹1,20,000. D is admitted for 1/4 share. D's capital should be:
'Adjusted capital' of an old partner means capital after adjusting:
qa.a: goodwill, reserves, revaluation and accumulated profits or losses
qa.e: Capitals are compared only after all reconstitution adjustments are made.

qa.q: A and B share 3:2 and change to 1:1. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: A sacrifices 1/10 and B gains 1/10

qa.q: A and B change their ratio from 3:2 to 1:1. Goodwill is ₹1,00,000. Compensation paid by B to A:
qa.e: Compensation = goodwill × gain = 1,00,000 × 1/10 = ₹10,000.

qa.q: For the case above, the journal entry is:
qa.a: Dr B's Capital A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹10,000
qa.e: Gainer B is debited; sacrificer A is credited.

qa.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1 and agree to share equally from now. Who neither gains nor sacrifices?
qa.a: B
qa.e: B: 2/6 old and 2/6 new. A sacrifices 1/6; C gains 1/6.

qa.q: In the case above, goodwill is ₹60,000. Amount C pays to A:
qa.e: C gains 1/6 = A's sacrifice; 60,000 × 1/6 = ₹10,000.

qa.q: A and B share 3:2 and change to 1:1. General Reserve of ₹30,000 is to be distributed. A gets:
qa.e: Reserves are distributed in the old ratio 3:2.

qa.q: A and B (3:2 → 1:1) prefer NOT to distribute a General Reserve of ₹50,000. In the single adjusting entry, B is debited by:
qa.e: B gains 1/10, so he compensates A for 1/10 of the reserve.

qa.q: Revaluation profit arising on a change in profit-sharing ratio is shared in:
qa.a: the old ratio
qa.e: The value change happened under the old arrangement.

qa.q: Capital ₹1,00,000; goodwill share ₹30,000; reserve share ₹12,000; revaluation profit share ₹6,000; profit till date ₹8,000; interest on capital ₹2,000; drawings ₹15,000; interest on drawings ₹500. Amount due to the retiring partner:
qa.e: Add all credits (₹1,58,000) and deduct drawings and interest on drawings (₹15,500).

qa.q: Which of these is DEDUCTED while computing the amount due to a retiring partner?
qa.a: His drawings
qa.e: Drawings were already taken out of the firm, so they reduce his dues.

qa.q: Which item is ADDED to the retiring partner's capital account?
qa.a: His share of revaluation profit
qa.e: Revaluation profit belongs to all old partners, including the retiring one.

qa.q: Capital ₹2,00,000; goodwill share ₹40,000; revaluation loss share ₹10,000; share of advertisement suspense ₹6,000; drawings ₹20,000. Amount due:
The retiring partner's share in the debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account is:
qa.a: debited to his capital account
qa.e: Accumulated losses are borne by all partners in the old ratio, including the retiring one.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Interest on drawings is deducted from the amount due to a retiring partner.
Reason (R): Interest on drawings is a charge on the partner in favour of the firm.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the partner owes this interest to the firm, it reduces his dues.

qa.q: The final amount payable to a retiring partner is:
qa.a: the balance of his capital account after all adjustments
qa.e: Every adjustment is posted to his capital account; its closing balance is what he is owed.

qa.q: A retiring partner's current account has a debit balance of ₹5,000 and his capital is ₹80,000 (fixed). Other adjustments add ₹20,000. Amount due:
qa.e: A debit balance in the current account reduces his dues: 80,000 + 20,000 − 5,000.

qa.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires. Nothing is said about the new ratio. The new ratio of A and B is:
qa.e: When silent, continuing partners keep their old mutual ratio, 3:2.

qa.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires and his share is taken equally by A and B. New ratio:
A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires; A and B take his share in 2:1. New ratio:
A, B and C share 5:3:2. B retires; A and C take his share in 2:1. New ratio of A and C:
A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires; new ratio of A and B is 3:2. Gaining ratio:
qa.a: Only A gains; B's share is unchanged

qa.q: In the case above (2:2:1 → A:B 3:2), A's gain is:
qa.e: A's gain = new 3/5 − old 2/5 = 1/5.

qa.q: Gaining ratio differs from sacrificing ratio because:
qa.a: gaining ratio is new share minus old share, used mainly on retirement/death; sacrificing ratio is old minus new, used mainly on admission
qa.e: They measure opposite movements and are used in different reconstitutions.

qa.q: X, Y and Z share equally. Z retires. X and Y share future profits 3:2. Y's gain is:
On retirement, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is recorded as:
qa.a: Dr continuing partners' Capital A/cs (gaining ratio) / Cr retiring partner's Capital A/c
qa.e: Continuing partners pay for the share they gain; no goodwill account is raised.

qa.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires; goodwill ₹1,20,000. A's capital is debited by:
qa.e: C's share ₹20,000 is borne by A and B in 3:2 → A ₹12,000.

qa.q: Goodwill of ₹60,000 already appears in the books when C (share 1/6) retires. C's capital is debited, when writing it off, by:
qa.e: Existing goodwill is written off by ALL partners in the old ratio: 60,000 × 1/6.

qa.q: C's dues before goodwill are ₹1,50,000. The partners agree to pay him ₹1,70,000 in full settlement. Hidden goodwill (C's share):
qa.e: The extra ₹20,000 paid is his share of goodwill.

qa.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires; A and B will share 3:2. Firm's goodwill ₹1,00,000. A's capital is debited by:
qa.e: Only A gains (1/5); C's share (1/5 × 1,00,000 = ₹20,000) is fully debited to A.

qa.q: Why is the retiring partner's share of goodwill debited in the gaining ratio?
qa.a: The continuing partners gain his share of future profits in that ratio
qa.e: Those who gain must compensate in proportion to their gain.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A Goodwill Account is not raised when a partner retires.
Reason (R): AS 26 allows goodwill to be recorded only when consideration in money or money's worth has been paid for it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Self-generated goodwill cannot be recognised, so it is adjusted through capital accounts.

qa.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. B retires; goodwill ₹90,000; A and C take B's share equally. Amount credited to B's capital:
qa.e: B's share = 90,000 × 2/6 = ₹30,000 (debited to A and C ₹15,000 each).

qa.q: Revaluation profit on retirement of a partner is shared by:
qa.a: all partners, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio
qa.e: The change in values happened while all were partners.

qa.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. On C's retirement, revaluation shows a profit of ₹15,000. C's share:
Building +₹25,000, stock −₹5,000, unrecorded liability ₹5,000. Revaluation result:
General Reserve of ₹50,000 exists when C (share 1/5) retires. C's capital is credited with:
qa.e: Reserves are shared by all partners in the old ratio: 50,000 × 1/5.

qa.q: A debit balance of ₹20,000 in Profit and Loss Account exists when C (share 1/5) retires. Effect on C's capital:
qa.a: Debited by ₹4,000
qa.e: Accumulated losses are debited to all partners in the old ratio: 20,000 × 1/5 = ₹4,000.

qa.q: An unrecorded investment of ₹8,000 is found on retirement. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Investment A/c / Cr Revaluation A/c ₹8,000
qa.e: Bringing an asset into the books is a gain, credited to Revaluation.

qa.q: Machinery ₹1,00,000 is depreciated by 10% and a provision of ₹2,000 is created for doubtful debts on C's retirement. Revaluation loss:
qa.e: Loss = 10,000 (machinery) + 2,000 (provision) = ₹12,000.

qa.q: Why must the retiring partner share revaluation profit and reserves?
qa.a: They arose while he was a partner, so he is entitled to his share
qa.e: Gains and losses up to the date of retirement belong to all old partners.

qa.q: The amount due to a retiring partner is not paid immediately. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
qa.e: His capital account is closed and the amount becomes a loan owed by the firm.

qa.q: Loan of ₹1,20,000 repayable in 3 equal annual instalments plus 10% p.a. interest on the outstanding balance. First year's total payment:
qa.e: Principal ₹40,000 plus interest on ₹1,20,000 (₹12,000).

qa.q: In the same loan, interest for the second year is:
qa.e: Balance after first instalment = ₹80,000; 10% = ₹8,000.

qa.q: Total interest paid over the three years on that loan:
Amount due to C is ₹1,50,000. He is paid ₹50,000 in cash and the rest is transferred to his loan account. Loan balance:
Amount due ₹2,00,000; 40% paid immediately in cash; the balance becomes a loan. Loan amount:
A retiring partner's loan appears in the firm's balance sheet:
qa.a: on the liabilities side
qa.e: The firm owes him the amount, so it is a liability.

qa.q: Interest on the retiring partner's loan for the year is recorded as:
qa.a: Dr Interest on Loan A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
qa.e: Interest increases the amount owed, so the loan account is credited; it is an expense.

qa.q: Total capital of the new firm is fixed at ₹3,00,000; A and B share 3:2. A's required capital:
A's adjusted capital is ₹1,50,000 and his required capital is ₹1,80,000. A must:
qa.a: bring in ₹30,000
qa.e: Required exceeds actual by ₹30,000, so he brings cash.

qa.q: B's adjusted capital is ₹1,40,000; required ₹1,20,000. Amount B withdraws:
Total capital is not specified. After paying C, A and B have adjusted capitals of ₹1,60,000 and ₹1,40,000 and will share 3:2. A's required capital:
In the case above, B will:
qa.a: withdraw ₹20,000
qa.e: B's required capital = 3,00,000 × 2/5 = ₹1,20,000; he has ₹1,40,000, so he withdraws ₹20,000.

qa.q: The entry when a continuing partner brings cash to make up a capital deficiency:
qa.a: Dr Cash/Bank A/c / Cr Partner's Capital A/c
qa.e: Cash increases and so does his capital.

qa.q: ₹1,20,000 is to be paid to retiring partner C. The firm has ₹50,000 cash and wants to keep a minimum balance of ₹20,000. A and B (new ratio 2:1) bring the shortfall in their new ratio. Amount A brings:
When capitals of continuing partners are to be in the new ratio and a partner's surplus is NOT to be withdrawn, it is:
qa.a: transferred to his current account
qa.e: The surplus is moved to his current account, keeping capitals in the new ratio.

qa.q: Year ends 31 March. D (share 1/4) dies on 30 June. Last year's profit ₹1,20,000. D's share of profit (time basis):
Average profit of the last three years is ₹1,20,000. E (share 1/5) dies 5 months into the year. His share of profit (time basis):
Last year: sales ₹10,00,000, profit ₹1,50,000. Sales up to F's death this year: ₹4,00,000. F's share 1/3. His share of profit (turnover basis):
qa.e: Profit rate 15%; profit till death = 60,000; F's share = 20,000.

qa.q: The entry for the deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death is:
qa.a: Dr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c / Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c
qa.e: Profit is not yet ascertained, so it is debited to a suspense account and credited to his capital.

qa.q: Why is a Profit and Loss Suspense Account used on the death of a partner?
qa.a: Because the year's actual profit is not yet known on the date of death
qa.e: The estimate is parked in a suspense account until the final accounts are prepared.

qa.q: Accounting on the death of a partner is similar to that on retirement, except that:
qa.a: the amount due is paid to the executors (legal representatives) of the deceased
qa.e: Goodwill, revaluation and reserves are treated as on retirement; only the payee changes.

qa.q: Profit of the previous year ₹2,40,000; G (share 1/3) dies on 30 September (year began 1 April). G's share (time basis):
Which basis estimates profit using the ratio of last year's profit to last year's sales?
qa.a: Turnover (sales) basis
qa.e: Profit is assumed to bear the same ratio to sales as last year.

qa.q: D's capital ₹1,50,000; reserve share ₹20,000; goodwill ₹30,000; profit till death ₹10,000; revaluation profit ₹5,000; interest on capital ₹3,000; drawings ₹18,000. Amount transferred to executors:
qa.e: Credits ₹2,18,000 less drawings ₹18,000.

qa.q: The entry to transfer the deceased partner's capital balance is:
qa.a: Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Deceased Partner's Executor's A/c
qa.e: The capital account is closed and the liability now sits in the executor's account.

qa.q: Executors are paid ₹80,000 immediately out of ₹2,00,000 due. Balance in the executor's account:
The unpaid ₹1,20,000 carries 10% p.a. interest for a full year before any further payment. Interest credited to the executor's account:
Payment to the executors is recorded as:
qa.a: Dr Executor's A/c / Cr Bank A/c
qa.e: The liability to executors decreases and cash goes out.

qa.q: D's capital ₹1,00,000; his share of revaluation loss ₹4,000; share of goodwill ₹24,000; share of P&L debit balance ₹6,000; profit till death ₹6,000. Amount due to executors:
An unpaid balance in the deceased partner's executor's account appears in the balance sheet:
qa.a: on the liabilities side
qa.e: It is money the firm owes to the estate.

qa.q: Which of these is credited to the deceased partner's capital account?
qa.a: His share of profit up to the date of death
qa.e: Profit earned until death is his entitlement.

qa.q: Dissolution of partnership means:
qa.a: a change in the existing relationship among partners while the business may continue
qa.e: The old agreement ends and a new one forms; the firm can carry on.

qa.q: Dissolution of a firm means:
qa.a: the partnership among all partners ends and the business is closed
qa.e: All partners part ways; assets are realised, debts paid and books closed.

qa.q: Which event is a dissolution of PARTNERSHIP but not of the firm?
qa.a: Retirement of a partner while the others continue the business
qa.e: On retirement, the agreement ends but the business carries on.

qa.q: On dissolution of a firm, which account is prepared to sell assets and pay liabilities?
qa.a: Realisation Account
qa.e: A Realisation Account records the sale of assets and payment of liabilities.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Dissolution of a firm necessarily involves dissolution of the partnership.
Reason (R): When the firm is dissolved, the relationship among all the partners comes to an end.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Once the firm ends, no partnership remains among any partners; R explains A.

qa.q: In which case are the books of account closed?
qa.a: Dissolution of firm
qa.e: Only when the firm itself ends are all accounts settled and closed.

qa.q: Court intervention is possible in:
qa.a: dissolution of a firm
qa.e: A court can order dissolution of a firm on certain grounds; reconstitution is by agreement.

qa.q: Assets and liabilities are revalued in dissolution of partnership, but in dissolution of a firm they are:
qa.a: realised (sold) and settled
qa.e: A dissolved firm sells its assets and pays off its liabilities.

qa.q: A firm is dissolved when its business becomes unlawful. This is:
qa.a: compulsory dissolution
qa.e: Section 41 dissolves a firm automatically if the business becomes illegal.

qa.q: A partnership at will can be dissolved by:
qa.a: any partner giving written notice to all other partners
qa.e: In a partnership at will, written notice by a partner is enough (Section 43).

qa.q: Which is a ground on which the COURT may dissolve a firm?
qa.a: A partner has become of unsound mind
qa.e: Unsound mind is a Section 44 ground; the others dissolve the firm without a court.

qa.q: A firm formed for 5 years reaches the end of its term. It is dissolved:
qa.a: on the happening of a contingency, subject to any contract between partners
qa.e: Expiry of a fixed term is a contingency under Section 42.

qa.q: Compulsory dissolution takes place when:
qa.a: all partners, or all but one, are declared insolvent
qa.e: Insolvency of all (or all but one) partners leaves no one able to contract, so the firm is dissolved under Section 41.

qa.q: A partner transfers his whole interest in the firm to an outsider. The other partners may:
qa.a: apply to the court for dissolution
qa.e: Transfer of whole interest to a third party is a ground for dissolution by the court.

qa.q: Dissolution by agreement can happen:
qa.a: with the consent of all the partners or under a contract among them
qa.e: Section 40 allows dissolution by mutual consent or contract.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a ground for dissolution by court?
qa.a: A partner takes a two-week holiday
qa.e: A short holiday is not misconduct or incapacity.

qa.q: Under Section 48, which is paid FIRST out of the firm's assets?
qa.a: Debts of the firm to third parties
qa.e: Outside creditors rank first.

qa.q: After paying outside creditors, the next payment is:
qa.a: partners' loans and advances
qa.e: Loans by partners rank after outside debts but before capitals.

qa.q: Cash available ₹3,00,000; creditors ₹1,80,000; A's loan ₹40,000; capitals total ₹1,00,000. Loss to be borne by partners:
qa.e: After creditors and A's loan, ₹80,000 remains for ₹1,00,000 of capitals – a shortfall of ₹20,000.

qa.q: Losses on dissolution, including deficiency of capital, are borne by partners:
qa.a: in their profit-sharing ratio
qa.e: Section 48 says losses are made good by partners in the ratio in which they share profits.

qa.q: Under Section 49, a partner's private property is applied:
qa.a: first to his private debts; any surplus can go towards the firm's debts
qa.e: Private assets serve private creditors first.

qa.q: A partner's private creditors claim against the firm's property. Under Section 49, the firm's property is applied:
qa.a: first to pay the firm's debts
qa.e: The firm's property is first used for the firm's own debts.

qa.q: Which topic is NOT part of the CBSE dissolution syllabus for this course?
qa.a: Piecemeal distribution of cash
qa.e: Piecemeal distribution, sale to a company and insolvency of partners are excluded.

qa.q: After paying creditors, partners' loans and capitals, ₹12,000 is left. A and B share 2:1. A gets:
qa.e: Surplus is shared in the profit-sharing ratio: 12,000 × 2/3.

qa.q: Which asset is NOT transferred to the Realisation Account?
qa.a: Cash in hand
qa.e: Cash is the medium of settlement and stays in the Cash Account.

qa.q: A partner's loan to the firm on dissolution is:
qa.a: not transferred to Realisation Account; it is paid separately after outside liabilities
qa.e: Partners' loans are settled directly through cash, after outsiders.

qa.q: Provision for doubtful debts on dissolution is:
qa.a: credited to the Realisation Account
qa.e: Debtors go to Realisation at gross value, so the provision is credited to offset it.

qa.q: A and B dissolve their firm. Building ₹2,00,000; Machinery ₹1,00,000; Stock ₹50,000; Debtors ₹40,000 (provision ₹2,000); Cash ₹20,000; Creditors ₹60,000; Bills payable ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; General reserve ₹28,000. Total of assets debited to Realisation Account (book value):
qa.e: Building + Machinery + Stock + Debtors = 2,00,000 + 1,00,000 + 50,000 + 40,000.

qa.q: Using the same data, the total credited to Realisation Account on transfer of liabilities and provision:
qa.e: Creditors 60,000 + Bills payable 20,000 + Provision 2,000. A's loan and reserve are excluded.

qa.q: Stock with a book value of ₹50,000 is sold for ₹45,000. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Cash A/c / Cr Realisation A/c ₹45,000
qa.e: Stock is already in the Realisation Account; cash received is credited to it.

qa.q: No realisable value is given for furniture (book value ₹30,000) and goodwill (book value ₹20,000). Assume they realise:
qa.a: furniture ₹30,000; goodwill nil
qa.e: Tangible assets are assumed to realise book value; intangibles realise nothing.

qa.q: Advertisement suspense on dissolution is:
qa.a: written off to partners' capitals in profit-sharing ratio, not taken to Realisation Account
qa.e: It is a fictitious asset with no realisable value.

qa.q: Partner A takes over stock at ₹45,000. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr A's Capital A/c / Cr Realisation A/c ₹45,000
qa.e: A receives an asset, reducing what the firm owes him.

qa.q: Partner B agrees to take over bills payable of ₹20,000. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Realisation A/c / Cr B's Capital A/c ₹20,000
qa.e: B pays the firm's debt, so the firm owes B more.

qa.q: Creditors of ₹50,000 accept machinery of book value ₹40,000 in full settlement. The entry is:
qa.a: No entry
qa.e: Both are already in the Realisation Account; no cash moves.

qa.q: Creditors of ₹50,000 accept machinery and ₹8,000 cash in full settlement. Amount recorded (Dr Realisation, Cr Cash):
qa.e: Only the cash paid is recorded.

qa.q: Creditors of ₹70,000 accept stock valued at ₹30,000 in part settlement; the rest is paid in cash. Cash paid:
qa.e: Cash = 70,000 − 30,000 = ₹40,000; only this is recorded.

qa.q: An unrecorded computer is sold for ₹6,000 on dissolution. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Cash A/c / Cr Realisation A/c ₹6,000
qa.e: Any realisation from assets is credited to the Realisation Account.

qa.q: An unrecorded liability of ₹5,000 for a pending repair bill is paid. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Realisation A/c / Cr Cash A/c ₹5,000
qa.e: Paying any liability on dissolution is debited to the Realisation Account.

qa.q: Partner C takes over an unrecorded typewriter at ₹2,000. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr C's Capital A/c / Cr Realisation A/c ₹2,000
qa.e: C receives an asset of the firm, so his capital is debited.

qa.q: Realisation expenses of ₹3,000 are paid by the firm. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Realisation A/c / Cr Cash A/c ₹3,000
qa.e: The firm bears and pays the expense, reducing realisation profit.

qa.q: Partner A pays realisation expenses of ₹4,000 on behalf of the firm. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Realisation A/c / Cr A's Capital A/c ₹4,000
qa.e: The firm bears the expense but owes A for paying it.

qa.q: Realisation expenses are to be borne by partner B, and the firm pays them ₹2,500. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr B's Capital A/c / Cr Cash A/c ₹2,500
qa.e: The firm paid on B's behalf; B must bear it, so his capital is debited.

qa.q: C is given ₹10,000 to complete the dissolution and bears all expenses; actual expenses are ₹7,000. Entries needed:
qa.a: Dr Realisation A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹10,000 only
qa.e: Only the agreed remuneration is recorded; C's actual expenses are his own.

qa.q: On dissolution, assets of book value ₹3,90,000 (other than cash) and a provision for doubtful debts of ₹2,000 are transferred, along with creditors and bills payable of ₹80,000. Assets realise ₹4,01,000; the liabilities are paid ₹80,000; expenses are ₹3,000. Profit on realisation:
A loss on realisation is transferred by:
qa.a: Dr Partners' Capital A/cs / Cr Realisation A/c (profit-sharing ratio)
qa.e: A loss reduces partners' capitals in their profit-sharing ratio.

qa.q: Realisation shows a loss of ₹18,000. A and B share 2:1. A's capital is debited by:
Realisation expenses ₹5,000 are to be borne by partner D, who pays them himself. The entry is:
qa.a: No entry
qa.e: The firm neither bears nor pays the expense.

qa.q: A and B (1:1) dissolve their firm. Cash ₹20,000; A's loan ₹30,000; general reserve ₹28,000; capitals A ₹1,50,000, B ₹1,20,000. Other assets realise ₹4,01,000; creditors and bills payable (₹80,000) and expenses (₹3,000) are paid. Cash available before paying A's loan:
In the same case (profit on realisation ₹10,000, shared 1:1), the final amount paid to A is:
qa.e: A: capital 1,50,000 + half of reserve 14,000 + half of profit 5,000. His loan of ₹30,000 is paid separately.

qa.q: In the same case, the final amount paid to B is:
The entry to pay a partner's loan on dissolution is:
qa.a: Dr Partner's Loan A/c / Cr Cash A/c
qa.e: Partners' loans are not routed through Realisation; they are paid directly.

qa.q: General reserve of ₹28,000 on dissolution is shared by A and B (1:1). The entry is:
qa.a: Dr General Reserve A/c ₹28,000 / Cr A's Capital ₹14,000, Cr B's Capital ₹14,000
qa.e: Reserves are partners' accumulated profits, credited to their capitals.

qa.q: After all adjustments, C's capital account shows a debit balance of ₹6,000. The entry is:
qa.a: Dr Cash A/c / Cr C's Capital A/c ₹6,000
qa.e: C owes the firm and brings in cash to close his account.

qa.q: Total cash available for partners is ₹3,08,000. A's final capital balance is ₹1,69,000. B's must be:
qa.e: Cash and capitals must match exactly: 3,08,000 − 1,69,000.

qa.q: Why does the cash account close without any balance after dissolution?
qa.a: All receipts are used to pay liabilities, loans and partners' final balances
qa.e: Every rupee realised is paid out; total receipts equal total payments.

qa.q: 'Perpetual succession' means that a company:
qa.a: continues to exist even when its members change or die
qa.e: Change of membership does not affect the company's existence; it ends only by legal process.

qa.q: Priya holds 100 shares of ₹10 each, ₹7 paid. Her maximum further liability is:
qa.e: Only the unpaid ₹3 per share can be called: 100 × 3.

qa.q: A company is called an artificial person because:
qa.a: it is created by law and has a legal existence separate from its members
qa.e: It can own property and enter contracts like a person but exists only in law.

qa.q: Who manages a company on behalf of its shareholders?
qa.a: The Board of Directors elected by shareholders
qa.e: Ownership and management are separate; directors manage.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A company can own property in its own name.
Reason (R): A company has a separate legal entity distinct from its members.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the law treats it as a separate person, it can hold property.

qa.q: Which feature lets an investor sell shares of a listed public company on the stock exchange?
qa.a: Transferability of shares
qa.e: Shares of a public company are freely transferable.

qa.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the common seal of a company is:
qa.a: optional
qa.e: After the 2015 amendment, a company may choose whether to have a common seal.

qa.q: Separation of ownership and management in a company means:
qa.a: owners (shareholders) need not take part in management, which is done by directors
qa.e: Shareholders elect directors who manage; most shareholders take no part in daily decisions.

qa.q: Minimum number of members required to form a public company:
qa.e: A public company needs at least seven members.

qa.q: Maximum number of members of a private company (excluding employee members):
qa.e: The Companies Act, 2013 caps private company membership at 200.

qa.q: A company in which members' liability is limited to the amount they undertake to contribute on winding up is:
qa.a: a company limited by guarantee
qa.e: Members guarantee a fixed contribution only when the company is wound up.

qa.q: Which company is formed with only one person as its member?
qa.a: One Person Company
qa.e: A One Person Company has a single member.

qa.q: A company where the Central Government holds 55% of the paid-up share capital is a:
qa.a: Government company
qa.e: At least 51% held by government makes it a government company.

qa.q: Company H controls the composition of the Board of Directors of Company S. S is H's:
qa.a: subsidiary company
qa.e: Control of the board composition makes S a subsidiary of H.

qa.q: Company A holds 25% of the voting power of Company B but does not control it. B is A's:
qa.a: associate company
qa.e: Significant influence (≥ 20% of voting power) without control makes B an associate.

qa.q: Which of these is a feature of a private company?
qa.a: It restricts the right to transfer its shares
qa.e: A private company restricts transfer and cannot invite public subscription.

qa.q: Preference shares carry preferential rights regarding:
qa.a: dividend and repayment of capital
qa.e: Their two preferences are a fixed dividend and capital repayment ahead of equity.

qa.q: 10,000 8% cumulative preference shares of ₹100 each; no dividend paid last year. Dividend payable this year:
qa.e: Cumulative: both years' dividend (₹80,000 each) must be paid.

qa.q: Shares that receive a share in surplus profits in addition to their fixed dividend are:
qa.a: participating preference shares
qa.e: Participating shares take part in surplus profits after equity dividend.

qa.q: Under the Companies Act, 2013, which preference shares CANNOT be issued?
qa.a: Irredeemable preference shares
qa.e: Section 55 bars a company from issuing irredeemable preference shares.

qa.q: Equity shares carry:
qa.a: residual rights, voting rights and a dividend that varies with profits
qa.e: Equity holders get what remains after preference claims and control the company by voting.

qa.q: The nature of a share in law is:
qa.a: movable property
qa.e: A share is movable property, transferable in the manner the articles provide.

qa.q: Unpaid dividend on non-cumulative preference shares for a year:
qa.a: lapses and is not carried forward
qa.e: Non-cumulative shares lose the dividend for a year in which none is declared.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Equity shareholders are called the real owners of a company.
Reason (R): They have residual rights to profits and capital and exercise voting control.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Bearing the residual risk and controlling by vote makes them the real owners.

qa.q: The maximum capital a company can raise, as stated in its Memorandum, is:
qa.a: authorised capital
qa.e: Authorised (nominal/registered) capital is the ceiling.

qa.q: 36,000 shares of ₹10 are subscribed and ₹8 per share is called. Called-up capital:
Called-up capital ₹2,88,000; calls in arrears ₹2,000. Paid-up capital:
qa.e: Paid-up = called-up − calls in arrears.

qa.q: Reserve capital is:
qa.a: the part of uncalled capital to be called only on winding up, decided by special resolution
qa.e: Reserve capital is uncalled capital set aside for winding up; capital reserve is a different item.

qa.q: Authorised 50,000 shares; issued 40,000; subscribed 36,000 (₹10 each). Unissued capital:
qa.e: Unissued = authorised − issued = 5,00,000 − 4,00,000.

qa.q: When the full face value of subscribed shares has been called and received, the capital is:
qa.a: subscribed and fully paid up
qa.e: Fully called and fully received means fully paid up.

qa.q: 36,000 subscribed shares of ₹10 with ₹8 called. Uncalled capital:
qa.e: ₹2 per share is uncalled: 36,000 × 2.

qa.q: Shares issued to vendors for assets purchased form part of:
qa.a: issued capital
qa.e: Issued capital includes shares allotted for consideration other than cash.

qa.q: In the company balance sheet, share capital appears under:
qa.a: Shareholders' Funds
qa.e: Share capital and reserves together form Shareholders' Funds.

qa.q: 40,000 shares of ₹10 fully called and subscribed; calls in arrears ₹5,000. Share capital shown in the balance sheet:
qa.e: Called-up ₹4,00,000 less arrears ₹5,000.

qa.q: Calls received in advance are shown under:
qa.a: Other Current Liabilities
qa.e: They are owed back to shareholders until the call is made.

qa.q: Subscribed capital ₹6,00,000 fully called; calls in arrears ₹10,000; share forfeiture balance ₹4,000. Total share capital in the balance sheet:
Securities premium appears in the balance sheet under:
qa.a: Reserves and Surplus
qa.e: Premium is a capital profit, kept in Reserves and Surplus.

qa.q: Authorised capital in the notes to accounts is:
qa.a: shown for information but not added to the balance sheet total
qa.e: Only the subscribed (paid-up) amount is carried to the balance sheet.

qa.q: 50,000 shares of ₹10 subscribed; ₹8 called; calls in arrears ₹3,000. Amount under 'Subscribed but not fully paid up':
qa.e: Called-up 50,000 × 8 = ₹4,00,000 less arrears ₹3,000.

qa.q: In which part of the annual report are the details of authorised, issued and subscribed capital given?
qa.a: Notes to Accounts
qa.e: The balance sheet shows one line; the Note gives the breakdown.

qa.q: Minimum subscription (as a percentage of the issue) required before a company can allot shares in a public issue:
qa.e: If at least 90% is not subscribed, the application money must be refunded.

qa.q: Entry when application money is received:
qa.a: Bank A/c Dr / Share Application A/c Cr
qa.e: Money is first held in the Share Application Account until allotment.

qa.q: Entry when allotment money becomes due:
qa.a: Share Allotment A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr
qa.e: The amount due is debited to allotment and credited to capital.

qa.q: 10,000 shares of ₹10 at par: ₹3 application, ₹4 allotment, ₹3 call. Amount due on allotment:
Issue of shares 'at par' means issue:
qa.a: at face value
qa.e: Par = nominal or face value.

qa.q: A company issues 20,000 shares of ₹10 at par, fully payable on application, and all are subscribed. Share capital credited:
qa.e: Lump-sum issue: 20,000 × 10.

qa.q: Without separate call accounts, cash received on the first call is recorded as:
qa.a: Bank A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr
qa.e: The amount received is credited straight to Share Capital.

qa.q: If minimum subscription is not received, the company must:
qa.a: refund the application money
qa.e: Allotment cannot be made below minimum subscription; money is refunded.

qa.q: 10,000 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12; allotment ₹5 including premium. Securities premium credited on allotment:
qa.e: Premium ₹2 × 10,000 shares.

qa.q: In the same case, share capital credited on allotment:
qa.e: Capital part = ₹5 − ₹2 = ₹3 per share.

qa.q: Which is NOT a permitted use of securities premium under Section 52?
qa.a: Payment of dividend
qa.e: Premium is a capital receipt and cannot be distributed as dividend.

qa.q: Under Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013, issue of shares at a discount is:
qa.a: not allowed, except sweat equity shares
qa.e: Any issue at discount is void except sweat equity under Section 54.

qa.q: Securities premium is shown in the balance sheet under:
qa.a: Reserves and Surplus
qa.e: It is a reserve of capital nature.

qa.q: Shares of ₹100 each are issued at a premium of 10%. Issue price per share:
qa.e: Issue price = face value + premium = 100 + 10.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Securities premium can be used to write off preliminary expenses.
Reason (R): Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 lists the purposes for which securities premium may be applied.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Writing off preliminary expenses is one of the Section 52 purposes, so R explains A.

qa.q: Entry for allotment money due on shares issued at a premium (premium with allotment):
qa.a: Share Allotment A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr, Securities Premium A/c Cr
qa.e: The allotment amount is split between capital and premium.

qa.q: First call of ₹3 on 10,000 shares; holders of 1,000 shares fail to pay. Amount debited to Calls in Arrears:
qa.e: 1,000 × 3 = ₹3,000 remains unpaid.

qa.q: In the same case, cash received on the first call:
Entry when a shareholder pays the final call along with allotment (before the call is made):
qa.a: Bank A/c Dr / Share Allotment A/c Cr, Calls in Advance A/c Cr
qa.e: The extra amount is held in Calls in Advance until the call is made.

qa.q: When the final call is made later, the calls in advance are adjusted by:
qa.a: Calls in Advance A/c Dr / Share Final Call A/c Cr
qa.e: The advance is applied against the call money due.

qa.q: Calls in advance appear in the balance sheet under:
qa.a: Other Current Liabilities
qa.e: They are owed to shareholders until set off.

qa.q: Called-up capital ₹5,00,000; calls in arrears ₹8,000; calls in advance ₹4,000. Paid-up capital shown in the share capital note:
qa.e: Paid-up = 5,00,000 − 8,000. Calls in advance are not part of share capital.

qa.q: A shareholder holding 200 shares pays the final call of ₹2 per share along with allotment. Calls in advance:
Calls in arrears are shown in the share capital note as:
qa.a: a deduction from called-up capital
qa.e: Paid-up capital = called-up capital − calls in arrears.

qa.q: A company offers 10,000 shares and receives applications for 9,500. Minimum subscription is 90%. The company:
qa.a: can allot 9,500 shares
qa.e: 9,500 is 95% of the issue, above the 90% minimum, so all applicants get shares.

qa.q: 10,000 shares offered (₹3 application, ₹4 allotment); applications for 15,000; pro-rata allotment. Cash due on allotment:
qa.e: Excess application money ₹15,000 is adjusted against allotment due ₹40,000.

qa.q: Applications for 18,000 shares are received for 10,000 offered (₹3 application). Applications for 3,000 shares are rejected; the rest get pro-rata allotment. Refund:
qa.e: Only rejected applicants get a refund: 3,000 × 3.

qa.q: In the same case, excess application money adjusted towards allotment:
qa.e: Pro-rata applicants applied for 15,000 shares and got 10,000; excess 5,000 × 3.

qa.q: Applications for 25,000 shares for 10,000 offered, all allotted pro-rata (₹3 application, ₹4 allotment). The articles do not allow adjustment against calls. Amount refunded:
qa.e: Excess = 15,000 × 3 = 45,000; ₹40,000 adjusted against allotment; ₹5,000 refunded.

qa.q: Pro-rata allotment means:
qa.a: allotting shares in proportion to the shares applied for
qa.e: Each pro-rata applicant gets a fixed fraction of what he applied for.

qa.q: The entry for transferring excess application money to allotment is:
qa.a: Share Application A/c Dr / Share Allotment A/c Cr
qa.e: Excess application money is moved from application to allotment.

qa.q: X applied for 600 shares and was allotted 400 (₹3 application, ₹4 allotment). Amount X must pay on allotment:
qa.e: Excess on application = 200 × 3 = ₹600; allotment due 400 × 4 = ₹1,600; payable ₹1,000.

qa.q: Machinery of ₹4,40,000 is bought; shares of ₹10 are issued at 10% premium. Number of shares issued:
In the same case, securities premium credited:
qa.e: 40,000 shares × ₹1 premium.

qa.q: First entry on purchasing assets from a vendor (before issuing shares):
qa.a: Assets A/c Dr / Vendor A/c Cr
qa.e: First the liability to the vendor is recorded; then shares discharge it.

qa.q: Assets ₹6,00,000 and liabilities ₹1,00,000 of a business are taken over for a purchase consideration of ₹5,50,000. Goodwill:
qa.e: Net assets = ₹5,00,000; consideration exceeds it by ₹50,000.

qa.q: Net assets of ₹5,00,000 are taken over for ₹4,80,000. The difference is credited to:
qa.a: Capital Reserve
qa.e: Paying less than net assets gives a capital profit, credited to capital reserve.

qa.q: A business is bought for ₹6,00,000, paid by issuing ₹100 shares at a 20% premium. Number of shares:
Shares issued to promoters for their services in forming the company are credited to:
qa.a: Share Capital A/c
qa.e: Promoters receive shares, so Share Capital is credited; the services are treated as a formation cost.

qa.q: Entry for issuing shares at par to a vendor for ₹3,00,000:
qa.a: Vendor A/c Dr / Share Capital A/c Cr ₹3,00,000
qa.e: The vendor's claim is discharged by allotting shares.

qa.q: Issue of shares to a select group of persons, not to the public, is called:
qa.a: private placement
qa.e: Section 42 governs offers to a selected group through a private placement offer letter.

qa.q: Under the private placement rules, an offer in a financial year can be made to at most how many persons (excluding QIBs and ESOP employees)?
qa.e: The limit is 200 persons in a financial year.

qa.q: ESOP stands for:
qa.a: Employee Stock Option Plan
qa.e: It gives employees an option to buy shares at a fixed future price.

qa.q: An ESOP gives an employee:
qa.a: the right, but not the obligation, to buy shares at a predetermined price in future
qa.e: It is an option the employee may or may not exercise.

qa.q: Sweat equity shares are issued:
qa.a: to directors or employees at a discount or for non-cash consideration for know-how or value additions
qa.e: They reward intellectual contribution, not cash.
