qa.q: The only case in which a company may issue shares at a discount under the Companies Act, 2013 is:
qa.a: sweat equity shares
qa.e: Section 53 bars discount issues except sweat equity under Section 54.

qa.q: An employee exercises options for 1,000 shares at ₹50 each. Cash received by the company:

Assertion (A): Shares issued under private placement are not offered to the general public.
Reason (R): Private placement is made through a private placement offer letter to identified persons.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The offer letter goes only to identified persons, which is why the public is not invited.

qa.q: 100 shares of ₹10 at par; ₹7 received; ₹3 final call unpaid; shares forfeited. Amount credited to Share Forfeiture:
qa.e: Forfeiture is credited with the money actually received: 100 × 7.

qa.q: In the same case, Share Capital is debited with:
qa.e: Share Capital is debited with the called-up amount: 100 × 10.

qa.q: 200 shares of ₹10 issued at ₹12 (₹2 premium in allotment). The holder paid application ₹3 and allotment ₹5 but not the final call ₹4. Forfeiture credit:
qa.e: Received towards capital = 3 + (5 − 2) = ₹6 per share; premium was received and stays.

qa.q: 100 shares of ₹10 at ₹12 (premium ₹2 in allotment). Holder paid only application ₹3; failed allotment ₹5 and call ₹4. On forfeiture, Securities Premium is:
qa.a: debited with ₹200
qa.e: Premium was credited on allotment but never received, so it is reversed: 100 × 2.

qa.q: In the same case, amount credited to Share Forfeiture:
qa.e: Only the application money of ₹3 per share was received.

qa.q: X applied for 600 shares and was allotted 400 (₹10 shares: ₹3 application, ₹4 allotment, ₹3 call). Excess application money was adjusted against allotment. X paid nothing more, and his shares were forfeited after the call. Amount credited to Share Forfeiture:
qa.e: All money X paid (600 × 3 = ₹1,800) is forfeited, including the excess already adjusted.

qa.q: In the same case, unpaid allotment money credited to Share Allotment A/c on forfeiture:
qa.e: Allotment due 400 × 4 = 1,600 less excess 200 × 3 = 600.

qa.q: Balance of Share Forfeiture Account (not yet reissued) is shown in the balance sheet:
qa.a: added to paid-up capital in the Share Capital note
qa.e: It represents money received on capital, so it is added.

qa.q: 100 shares (₹10) forfeited after ₹7 was received are re-issued at ₹8 fully paid. Amount debited to Share Forfeiture for discount:
qa.e: Discount ₹2 per share × 100.

qa.q: In the same case, amount transferred to Capital Reserve:
qa.e: Forfeited ₹700 less discount ₹200.

qa.q: Shares of ₹10 were forfeited after ₹7 per share was received. The maximum discount per share allowed on their re-issue is:
qa.e: Discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount forfeited on each share.

qa.q: Forfeited shares (₹10 each) are re-issued at ₹11 fully paid. The extra ₹1 per share is credited to:
qa.a: Securities Premium A/c
qa.e: Any amount above face value on re-issue is premium.

qa.q: 200 shares (₹6 per share forfeited, total ₹1,200) were forfeited. 150 are re-issued at ₹9 fully paid. Capital reserve:
qa.e: Forfeiture on 150 shares = 900; discount 150; capital reserve = 750. The ₹300 on 50 unissued shares stays.

qa.q: In the same case, the balance left in Share Forfeiture after transfer:
qa.e: Relates to the 50 shares not yet re-issued: 50 × 6.

qa.q: Capital reserve arising on re-issue of forfeited shares is shown under:
qa.a: Reserves and Surplus
qa.e: It is a capital profit and part of reserves.

qa.q: Entry to transfer the gain on re-issued forfeited shares:
qa.a: Share Forfeiture A/c Dr / Capital Reserve A/c Cr
qa.e: The surplus is a capital profit, so it goes to Capital Reserve.

qa.q: A debenture is:
qa.a: an acknowledgement of debt by a company carrying a fixed rate of interest
qa.e: It certifies that the company has borrowed money.

qa.q: Debenture-holders are:
qa.a: creditors of the company
qa.e: They lend money; they do not own the company.

qa.q: Which is TRUE of debentures but NOT of shares?
qa.a: The return is a fixed interest payable even if there is a loss
qa.e: Debenture interest is a charge; dividend is an appropriation of profit.

qa.q: Interest on 50 9% debentures of ₹100 each for a year:
On winding up, debenture-holders are repaid:
qa.a: before shareholders
qa.e: As creditors, they rank ahead of owners.

qa.q: The document that records the terms of a debenture issue and appoints trustees is the:
qa.a: debenture trust deed
qa.e: The trust deed protects debenture-holders through trustees.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Debenture-holders do not have voting rights.
Reason (R): Debenture-holders are creditors and not owners of the company.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Voting is an ownership right; creditors do not get it.

qa.q: Bonds and debentures together are best described as:
qa.a: borrowed (debt) capital
qa.e: They represent money lent to the company.

qa.q: Debentures that carry a charge on the company's assets are:
qa.a: secured debentures
qa.e: A charge on assets gives security to holders.

qa.q: Unsecured debentures are also called:
qa.a: naked debentures
qa.e: 'Naked' means without any security.

qa.q: Debentures that are not repayable during the life of the company are:
qa.a: perpetual (irredeemable) debentures
qa.e: They are repaid only on winding up.

qa.q: A zero coupon debenture of face value ₹1,000 is issued at ₹750 and redeemed at ₹1,000. The investor's return per debenture:
qa.e: No interest is paid; the gain is the difference between redemption and issue price.

qa.q: Debentures transferable by mere delivery are:
qa.a: bearer debentures
qa.e: No transfer deed is needed for bearer debentures.

qa.q: Debentures that will be converted into equity shares only partly are:
qa.a: partly convertible debentures
qa.e: Only a portion converts; the rest is redeemed.

qa.q: NCDs commonly offered by NBFCs in India are:
qa.a: non-convertible debentures
qa.e: NCD = non-convertible debenture; they cannot become shares.

qa.q: Registered debentures differ from bearer debentures because:
qa.a: holders' names are recorded in the company's register and transfer needs a transfer deed
qa.e: Registration is about how ownership is recorded and transferred.

qa.q: 5,000 9% debentures of ₹100 issued at a 10% discount, fully payable on application. Amount credited to 9% Debentures A/c:
qa.e: Debentures are always credited at face value.

qa.q: In the same case, Discount on Issue of Debentures:
5,000 debentures of ₹100 issued at ₹105. Securities premium:
qa.e: Premium ₹5 × 5,000.

qa.q: Entry on allotment of debentures issued at a premium:
qa.a: Debenture Application & Allotment A/c Dr / Debentures A/c Cr, Securities Premium A/c Cr
qa.e: The issue price is split into face value and premium.

qa.q: A company offers 5,000 debentures of ₹100 at par, payable in full on application, and receives applications for 7,000. Excess applications are rejected. Refund:
Which statement is correct about issue price?
qa.a: Debentures may be issued at a discount, but shares (except sweat equity) cannot
qa.e: Section 53 bars discount on shares, not debentures.

qa.q: Securities premium received on debentures can be used to:
qa.a: write off discount or loss on issue of debentures
qa.e: Section 52 permits this use.

qa.q: Debentures of ₹100 issued at 8% discount, payable ₹40 on application and the rest on allotment. Amount due on allotment per debenture:
qa.e: Issue price ₹92 less ₹40 on application.

qa.q: Assets ₹5,50,000 and liabilities ₹50,000 are bought for ₹4,80,000. Capital reserve:
qa.e: Net assets ₹5,00,000 exceed the consideration by ₹20,000.

qa.q: Purchase consideration ₹4,80,000 is paid by 10% debentures of ₹100 at a 20% premium. Number of debentures:
In the same case, amount credited to Securities Premium on issuing the debentures:
Purchase consideration ₹2,70,000 is paid by issuing ₹100 debentures at a 10% discount. Number of debentures:
Net assets ₹5,00,000 are acquired for ₹5,40,000. The difference is:
qa.a: goodwill, debited
qa.e: Paying more than net assets means goodwill is purchased.

qa.q: Entry to issue debentures to a vendor at par:
qa.a: Vendor A/c Dr / Debentures A/c Cr
qa.e: Issuing debentures discharges the amount owed to the vendor.

qa.q: Net assets ₹4,00,000 are acquired for ₹4,40,000, paid in 9% debentures of ₹100 at a 10% premium. Goodwill and number of debentures:
qa.a: Goodwill ₹40,000; 4,000 debentures

qa.q: Purchase of a business: assets taken over are recorded as:
qa.a: Sundry Assets A/c Dr / Sundry Liabilities A/c Cr, Vendor A/c Cr
qa.e: Purchase is recorded first; payment through debentures follows.

qa.q: Debentures issued as collateral security means debentures:
qa.a: given as additional security for a loan, enforceable only on default
qa.e: They back a loan; the lender realises them only if the company defaults.

qa.q: Interest on debentures issued as collateral security is:
qa.a: not payable
qa.e: Interest is paid on the loan itself, not on the collateral debentures.

qa.q: Under the first method of recording collateral debentures:
qa.a: no entry is made; a note is given under the loan
qa.e: The loan account carries a note about the collateral.

qa.q: Under the second method, the entry for issuing ₹12,00,000 debentures as collateral is:
qa.a: Debenture Suspense A/c Dr / Debentures A/c Cr ₹12,00,000
qa.e: Suspense is debited and Debentures credited at face value.

qa.q: 12,000 9% debentures of ₹100 are issued as collateral. Amount debited to Debenture Suspense:
qa.e: Face value 12,000 × 100.

qa.q: In the balance sheet (second method), Debenture Suspense is:
qa.a: deducted from the debentures under Long-term Borrowings
qa.e: Deducting it shows that no real liability arises from collateral debentures.

qa.q: When the loan secured by collateral debentures is repaid (second method), the entry is:
qa.a: Debentures A/c Dr / Debenture Suspense A/c Cr
qa.e: The collateral debentures are cancelled by reversing the original entry.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Debentures issued as collateral are not a real liability of the company.
Reason (R): They become a claim only if the company fails to repay the loan.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Their liability is contingent on default, so they are offset or noted.

qa.q: 1,000 debentures of ₹100 issued at 5% discount, redeemable at 10% premium. Loss on Issue of Debentures:
qa.e: Discount ₹5,000 + premium on redemption ₹10,000.

qa.q: Debentures issued at par, redeemable at a 10% premium. The issue entry is:
qa.a: Bank Dr, Loss on Issue Dr / Debentures Cr, Premium on Redemption Cr
qa.e: The redemption premium is a future liability recorded now, with a matching loss.

qa.q: Premium on Redemption of Debentures account is:
qa.a: a liability, payable at redemption
qa.e: The company owes this extra amount to holders at redemption.

qa.q: 2,000 debentures of ₹100 issued at ₹105, redeemable at ₹110. Loss on issue:
qa.e: Loss on issue equals premium on redemption ₹10 × 2,000; the ₹5 issue premium goes to securities premium.

qa.q: In the same case (₹105 issue, ₹110 redemption), securities premium credited:
qa.e: Issue premium ₹5 × 2,000.

qa.q: Debentures issued at a 5% discount, redeemable at par. Per ₹100 debenture, the amount debited to Discount on Issue:
qa.e: Only the issue discount arises.

qa.q: Which case gives NO loss or discount on issue?
qa.a: Issued at par, redeemable at par
qa.e: With par on both ends, no extra cost arises.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT in the CBSE syllabus for this chapter?
qa.a: Creating a Debenture Redemption Reserve and sinking fund
qa.e: Actual redemption and DRR are excluded.

qa.q: ₹5,00,000 10% debentures; interest payable half-yearly. Interest for each half-year:
Interest on debentures is calculated on:
qa.a: face value of debentures
qa.e: The coupon rate applies to nominal value.

qa.q: 1,000 9% debentures of ₹100 were issued at ₹95. Annual interest:
qa.e: Interest on face value: 1,00,000 × 9%.

qa.q: Entry when debenture interest becomes due:
qa.a: Debenture Interest A/c Dr / Debentureholders' A/c Cr
qa.e: Interest due is an expense and a liability to holders until paid.

qa.q: ₹2,00,000 9% debentures were issued on 1 July; the year ends 31 March. Interest for the year:
qa.e: Outstanding for 9 months: 2,00,000 × 9% × 9/12.

qa.q: At the year-end, debenture interest is transferred by:
qa.a: Statement of Profit and Loss Dr / Debenture Interest A/c Cr
qa.e: Interest is an expense charged to profit.

qa.q: In the Statement of Profit and Loss, debenture interest is shown under:
qa.a: Finance Costs
qa.e: Interest on borrowings is a finance cost.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Debenture interest must be paid even when the company suffers a loss.
Reason (R): Debenture interest is a charge against profits, not an appropriation.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A charge must be met regardless of profit.

qa.q: Loss on issue ₹60,000; Securities Premium balance ₹40,000. Amount written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss:
qa.e: Premium absorbs ₹40,000 first; the remaining ₹20,000 goes to P&L.

qa.q: Discount or loss on issue of debentures is written off:
qa.a: in the year of allotment of debentures
qa.e: The current approach is to write it off in the year of allotment.

qa.q: The first source used to write off discount on issue of debentures is:
qa.a: Securities Premium
qa.e: Section 52 allows premium to absorb it; the rest goes to P&L.

qa.q: Discount on issue ₹30,000; Securities Premium ₹50,000. Securities Premium remaining after write-off:
qa.e: ₹30,000 is used from premium, leaving ₹20,000.

qa.q: Entry to write off ₹60,000 loss using ₹40,000 premium and the rest from profit:
qa.a: Securities Premium Dr 40,000; Statement of P&L Dr 20,000 / Loss on Issue of Debentures Cr 60,000
qa.e: Both sources are debited and the loss account is closed.

qa.q: When charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss, the discount on issue of debentures is shown as:
qa.a: finance cost
qa.e: It is a cost of borrowing.

qa.q: 1,000 debentures of ₹100 issued at ₹96, redeemable at par; no securities premium exists. Amount charged to profit in the year of allotment:
qa.e: Discount ₹4 × 1,000, fully charged as there is no premium.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Securities premium can be used to write off loss on issue of debentures.
Reason (R): Securities premium can be distributed as cash dividend.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true under Section 52, but premium can never be used for dividend, so R is false.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT part of a company's financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013?
qa.a: Directors' personal income-tax returns
qa.e: Financial statements cover the company's balance sheet, profit and loss statement, cash flow statement and notes.

qa.q: Financial statements are called 'end products' of accounting because:
qa.a: they are prepared at the end of the accounting process from recorded data
qa.e: Journal → ledger → trial balance → financial statements.

qa.q: Valuing inventory at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, reflects:
qa.a: the convention of conservatism
qa.e: Anticipating losses but not gains is conservatism.

qa.q: The choice between written-down value and straight-line depreciation is an example of:
qa.a: personal judgement
qa.e: Management decides the method, so judgement is involved.

qa.q: Which is an objective of financial statements?
qa.a: To give information about the company's earning capacity
qa.e: They help users judge profitability and financial position.

qa.q: The going concern assumption means:
qa.a: the business is expected to continue for the foreseeable future
qa.e: It is a basic postulate behind historical-cost accounting.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Financial statements are affected by personal judgements.
Reason (R): Accountants have to choose methods, such as for depreciation and inventory valuation, and make estimates.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Choices and estimates are personal judgements, so R explains A.

qa.q: Information about the 'stewardship' of management in financial statements helps owners to:
qa.a: judge how well managers have used the company's resources
qa.e: Owners entrust resources to managers; statements report on their use.

qa.q: The form of a company's balance sheet is laid down in:
qa.a: Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013
qa.e: Section 129 read with Schedule III prescribes the format.

qa.q: Which of these is a sub-head of Shareholders' Funds?
qa.a: Money received against share warrants
qa.e: Shareholders' Funds = share capital + reserves and surplus + money against share warrants.

qa.q: Share capital ₹10,00,000; securities premium ₹1,00,000; general reserve ₹2,00,000; debit balance of P&L ₹50,000. Shareholders' funds:
qa.e: Reserves and surplus = 2,50,000 after deducting the P&L debit balance.

qa.q: A debit balance of the Statement of Profit and Loss is shown:
qa.a: as a negative figure under Reserves and Surplus
qa.e: Schedule III requires a debit balance to be shown as a negative under Reserves and Surplus.

qa.q: Share application money pending allotment is shown:
qa.a: as a separate head between Shareholders' Funds and Non-current Liabilities
qa.e: It is not yet capital, so it gets its own head.

qa.q: Securities premium is shown under:
qa.a: Reserves and Surplus
qa.e: It is a capital reserve-type item in Reserves and Surplus.

qa.q: Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires financial statements to:
qa.a: give a true and fair view and comply with accounting standards
qa.e: True and fair view, accounting standards and Schedule III format.

qa.q: The two main parts of a Schedule III balance sheet are:
qa.a: Equity and Liabilities; Assets
qa.e: The balance sheet is in vertical form with these two parts.

qa.q: Debentures appear in the balance sheet under:
qa.a: Long-term Borrowings
qa.e: Debentures are long-term debt.

qa.q: Bank overdraft is shown under:
qa.a: Short-term Borrowings
qa.e: Overdraft is repayable on demand – a short-term borrowing.

qa.q: Bills payable are shown under:
qa.a: Trade Payables
qa.e: Bills payable arise from trade purchases.

qa.q: Provision for tax is shown under:
qa.a: Short-term Provisions
qa.e: Tax is payable within a year.

qa.q: Unpaid dividend is shown under:
qa.a: Other Current Liabilities
qa.e: Declared but unpaid dividend is owed to shareholders.

qa.q: Provision for employee benefits such as gratuity (payable after more than a year) is shown under:
qa.a: Long-term Provisions
qa.e: Employee benefit provisions not due within 12 months are long-term provisions.

qa.q: Interest accrued but not due on debentures is shown under:
qa.a: Other Current Liabilities
qa.e: Accrued interest is a current obligation, separate from the borrowing itself.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a current liability?
qa.a: Term loan repayable after 5 years
qa.e: A term loan due after more than 12 months is a long-term borrowing.

qa.q: Patents and trademarks are shown under:
qa.a: Intangible Assets
qa.e: They have no physical form but provide long-term benefits.

qa.q: Loose tools are shown under:
qa.a: Inventories
qa.e: Schedule III lists loose tools among inventories.

qa.q: Bills receivable are shown under:
qa.a: Trade Receivables
qa.e: Bills receivable arise from credit sales.

qa.q: A building under construction is shown under:
qa.a: Capital Work-in-Progress
qa.e: It becomes PPE only when ready for use.

qa.q: Cheques in hand are shown under:
qa.a: Cash and Cash Equivalents
qa.e: Cheques and drafts on hand are part of cash and cash equivalents.

qa.q: Shares of another company held for a long time (not for trading) are shown under:
qa.a: Non-current Investments
qa.e: Investments held for long-term are non-current.

qa.q: Provision for doubtful debts is presented:
qa.a: as a deduction from trade receivables
qa.e: It reduces the expected collectible amount of debtors.

qa.q: Which of these is a current asset?
qa.a: Stores and spares
qa.e: Stores and spares are inventories, a current asset.

qa.q: When the normal operating cycle cannot be identified, it is assumed to be how many months?
qa.e: Schedule III takes 12 months as the default.

qa.q: Operating cycle means the time between:
qa.a: acquisition of assets for processing and their realisation in cash or cash equivalents
qa.e: It covers buying, processing, selling and collecting cash.

qa.q: A shipbuilder's work-in-progress will be realised in 30 months, within its normal operating cycle. It is classified as:
qa.a: a current asset (inventory)
qa.e: Items realised within the normal operating cycle are current.

qa.q: Under which major head and sub-head is 'calls in advance' shown?
qa.a: Current Liabilities – Other Current Liabilities
qa.e: It is owed to shareholders until the call is made.

qa.q: Under which major head and sub-head is 'goodwill' shown?
qa.a: Non-current Assets – Intangible Assets
qa.e: Goodwill is an intangible non-current asset.

qa.q: The main purpose of Notes to Accounts is to:
qa.a: give details and explanations of items in the financial statements
qa.e: Notes give breakups, policies and contingent liabilities.

qa.q: Under which head and sub-head is 'provision for tax' shown?
qa.a: Current Liabilities – Short-term Provisions
qa.e: Tax provision is payable within the year.

qa.q: Under which head and sub-head is 'interest accrued on investments' (receivable) shown?
qa.a: Current Assets – Other Current Assets
qa.e: It is income earned but not yet received, a current asset.

qa.q: Revenue from operations ₹10,00,000 and other income ₹50,000. Total income:
qa.e: Total income = revenue from operations + other income.

qa.q: Opening inventory of stock-in-trade ₹1,00,000; closing ₹1,50,000. 'Changes in inventories' shown in expenses:
qa.e: Opening − closing = −₹50,000 (inventory increased, reducing expenses).

qa.q: Using the worked example data, total expenses:
PBT ₹2,50,000; tax rate 30%. Profit for the period:
Interest received on investments by a manufacturing company is shown as:
qa.a: Other income
qa.e: It is not from the company's main operations.

qa.q: Interest on debentures is shown under:
qa.a: Finance costs
qa.e: Interest on borrowings is a finance cost.

qa.q: Sale of scrap by a manufacturing company is shown as:
qa.a: Revenue from operations (other operating revenue)
qa.e: Scrap arises from normal operations, so it is other operating revenue.

qa.q: Which item is outside the scope of this course's Statement of Profit and Loss?
qa.a: Extraordinary items
qa.e: Exceptional, extraordinary items and discontinued operations are excluded.

qa.q: A bank studies a company's financial statements before granting a loan. This is the use of:
qa.a: credit decisions
qa.e: Lenders judge repayment ability from the statements.

qa.q: Land bought in 1995 for ₹10 lakh is still shown at ₹10 lakh though now worth ₹5 crore. This shows that financial statements:
qa.a: ignore price-level changes
qa.e: Historical cost ignores inflation.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of financial statements?
qa.a: They ignore qualitative aspects such as employee morale
qa.e: Non-monetary factors are not captured.

qa.q: A company pays off a large part of its creditors just before the year-end only to show a better current ratio, then borrows again in the new year. This is an example of:
qa.a: window dressing
qa.e: Window dressing makes the position look better than it really is.

qa.q: Financial statements are 'not exact' mainly because:
qa.a: they include estimates such as depreciation and provisions
qa.e: Estimates and judgements make figures approximate.

qa.q: The government using company accounts to frame tax and economic policies is the use as a:
qa.a: basis for fiscal policy
qa.e: Fiscal policy relies on information about business earnings.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Financial statements are historical documents.
Reason (R): They record transactions that have already taken place.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: They summarise the past, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which is NOT a limitation of financial statements?
qa.a: They provide a report on management's stewardship
qa.e: Stewardship reporting is a use.

qa.q: Analysis of financial statements means:
qa.a: studying relationships among items in financial statements to judge profitability and financial position
qa.e: It works on finished statements to draw meaning.

qa.q: Analysis differs from interpretation because:
qa.a: analysis arranges and relates data; interpretation explains the meaning of the results
qa.e: Interpretation builds on analysis.

qa.q: Which user is most interested in long-term solvency?
qa.a: Debenture-holders and long-term lenders
qa.e: Long-term lenders want assurance of interest and principal over years.

qa.q: Which user is most interested in short-term solvency?
qa.a: Trade payables (suppliers)
qa.e: Suppliers want to be paid within the credit period.

qa.q: Comparing this year's performance of Company X with its own previous years is:
qa.a: intra-firm comparison
qa.e: Intra = within the same firm.

qa.q: Labour unions use financial analysis mainly to judge:
qa.a: the company's capacity to pay wages and bonus
qa.e: Profitability and liquidity show the room for wage demands.

qa.q: Which is an objective of financial analysis?
qa.a: Assessing the earning capacity of the business
qa.e: Objectives include judging earning capacity, efficiency and solvency.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Analysis of financial statements helps in forecasting.
Reason (R): Trends found from past data give a basis for estimating future performance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Past trends help predict future figures.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a tool of analysis of financial statements?
qa.a: Trial balance
qa.e: A trial balance checks arithmetical accuracy of ledger balances; it is not an analysis tool.

qa.q: Horizontal analysis compares:
qa.a: figures of two or more periods
qa.e: It looks across time.

qa.q: Vertical analysis is also called:
qa.a: static analysis
qa.e: It relates items of a single period.

qa.q: A common-size balance sheet is an example of:
qa.a: vertical analysis
qa.e: It expresses items of one period as % of total assets.

qa.q: A comparative statement of profit and loss for 2024-25 and 2025-26 is an example of:
qa.a: horizontal analysis
qa.e: It compares two periods.

qa.q: Two firms use different depreciation methods, so their profits are not comparable. This limitation is:
qa.a: differences in accounting policies
qa.e: Policy differences distort comparisons.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of financial analysis?
qa.a: It ignores qualitative factors such as management quality
qa.e: Non-monetary factors are left out.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Financial analysis may give misleading results in times of high inflation.
Reason (R): Financial statements ignore price-level changes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Historical-cost figures do not reflect inflation, so analysis can mislead.

qa.q: Revenue ₹10,00,000 in 2024-25 and ₹12,50,000 in 2025-26. Percentage change:
Expenses ₹6,00,000 → ₹7,20,000. Absolute change:
PBT ₹4,00,000 → ₹5,30,000. Percentage change:
Trade receivables fell from ₹2,00,000 to ₹1,80,000. Percentage change:
Revenue rose 25% and expenses rose 20%. This suggests that:
qa.a: profit margin has improved
qa.e: When revenue grows faster than expenses, profit grows faster than revenue.

qa.q: Current assets rose 5% while current liabilities rose 30%. The likely interpretation:
qa.a: short-term liquidity has weakened
qa.e: Liabilities growing much faster than assets reduce liquidity.

qa.q: Total assets ₹20,00,000 → ₹25,00,000. Percentage change:
In a comparative balance sheet, the base for computing % change of each item is:
qa.a: the previous year's figure of that item
qa.e: Comparative % change uses the earlier year as base; common-size uses totals.

qa.q: In a common-size statement of profit and loss, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
qa.a: revenue from operations
qa.e: Revenue from operations is the base (100).

qa.q: In a common-size balance sheet, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
qa.a: total assets (or total equity and liabilities)
qa.e: The balance sheet total is the base.

qa.q: Cost of materials consumed ₹6,00,000; revenue from operations ₹10,00,000. Common-size %:
Inventories ₹5,00,000; total assets ₹50,00,000. Common-size %:
Revenue ₹10,00,000 and total expenses ₹8,00,000. PBT as a common-size %:
Trade payables ₹7,50,000; total equity and liabilities ₹50,00,000. Common-size %:
Employee benefits were 10% of revenue last year and 14% this year. This indicates:
qa.a: employee costs have risen faster than revenue
qa.e: A higher share of revenue means costs grew faster than revenue.

qa.q: The main advantage of common-size statements is that they:
qa.a: make comparison of firms of different sizes easy
qa.e: Percentages remove differences in scale.

qa.q: An accounting ratio is:
qa.a: an arithmetical relationship between two related accounting figures
qa.e: Ratios relate two meaningful figures.

qa.q: Current assets ₹3,00,000; current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Expressed as a percentage, current assets are what % of current liabilities?
Which is an objective of ratio analysis?
qa.a: Judging the liquidity and solvency of the business
qa.e: Ratios help assess liquidity, solvency, efficiency and profitability.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of ratio analysis?
qa.a: It simplifies complex accounting figures
qa.e: Ratios condense data into simple, comparable numbers.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of ratio analysis?
qa.a: Different firms may follow different accounting policies
qa.e: Different policies make ratios less comparable.

qa.q: A ratio computed from window-dressed figures is:
qa.a: misleading
qa.e: Ratios are only as good as the data behind them.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors.
Reason (R): Ratios are calculated only from monetary figures in financial statements.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Ratios use money figures, so factors like morale are left out.

qa.q: Comparing a firm's ratios with those of another firm in the same industry is:
qa.a: inter-firm comparison
qa.e: Inter = between firms.

qa.q: Current assets ₹3,00,000; current liabilities ₹1,50,000. Current ratio is ___ : 1.
Same data: inventories ₹1,00,000 and prepaid expenses ₹20,000 are included in current assets. Quick ratio is ___ : 1.
Quick assets are current assets minus:
qa.a: inventories and prepaid expenses
qa.e: Inventory and prepaid expenses cannot be quickly turned into cash.

qa.q: Current ratio is 2.5 : 1 and working capital is ₹3,00,000. Current liabilities:
In the same case, current assets:
The traditionally accepted ideal quick ratio is:
qa.e: Quick assets should at least equal current liabilities.

qa.q: Return on investment uses figures from both the Statement of Profit and Loss and the Balance Sheet. In the traditional classification it is a:
qa.a: composite ratio
qa.e: It combines PBIT (P&L) with capital employed (balance sheet).

qa.q: Functionally, the current ratio is a:
qa.a: liquidity ratio
qa.e: It measures short-term ability to pay.

qa.q: Share capital ₹8,00,000; reserves ₹2,00,000; debentures ₹5,00,000. Debt-equity ratio is ___ : 1.
Same data. Debt to capital employed ratio is ___ : 1.
Long-term debts for the debt-equity ratio include:
qa.a: long-term borrowings and long-term provisions
qa.e: Only long-term obligations count.

qa.q: Non-current assets ₹12,00,000; working capital ₹3,00,000; non-current liabilities ₹5,00,000. Shareholders' funds:
qa.e: Equity = NCA + WC − NCL.

qa.q: Long-term borrowings ₹6,00,000; long-term provisions ₹1,00,000; shareholders' funds ₹14,00,000. Debt-equity ratio is ___ : 1.
A lower debt-equity ratio indicates:
qa.a: greater long-term security for lenders
qa.e: Owners fund more of the business, cushioning lenders.

qa.q: Capital employed equals:
qa.a: long-term debts + shareholders' funds
qa.e: Capital employed is the long-term funds in the business.

qa.q: Debentures ₹4,00,000; share capital ₹5,00,000; general reserve ₹1,00,000; debit balance of P&L ₹1,00,000. Debt-equity ratio is ___ : 1.
Shareholders' funds ₹10,00,000; total assets ₹20,00,000. Proprietary ratio is ___ : 1.
Total assets ₹20,00,000; long-term debts ₹5,00,000. Total assets to debt ratio is ___ : 1.
PBIT ₹3,00,000; 10% debentures ₹5,00,000. Interest coverage ratio (times):
Profit after tax ₹1,40,000; tax ₹60,000; interest on long-term loan ₹50,000. Interest coverage ratio (times):
A higher interest coverage ratio indicates:
qa.a: the company can meet its interest obligations more comfortably
qa.e: More profit per rupee of interest means safety for lenders.

qa.q: A proprietary ratio of 0.8 : 1 means:
qa.a: 80% of total assets are financed by shareholders' funds
qa.e: Proprietary ratio shows owners' share of asset financing.

qa.q: Which ratio shows how many times the long-term debt is covered by total assets?
qa.a: Total assets to debt ratio
qa.e: It is total assets ÷ long-term debts.

qa.q: Interest coverage ratio uses:
qa.a: net profit before interest and tax
qa.e: Interest is paid out of profit before interest and tax.

qa.q: Revenue ₹12,00,000; GP 25% on revenue; opening inventory ₹1,40,000; closing ₹1,60,000. Inventory turnover (times):
Revenue ₹10,00,000; gross profit 25% on cost. Cost of revenue from operations:
Opening inventory ₹1,40,000; purchases ₹8,80,000; direct expenses ₹40,000; closing inventory ₹1,60,000. Cost of revenue from operations:
Inventory turnover is 5 times; cost of revenue ₹6,00,000; closing inventory is ₹20,000 more than opening. Opening inventory:
Inventory turnover ratio is calculated using:
qa.a: cost of revenue from operations and average inventory
qa.e: Both numerator and denominator are at cost.

qa.q: A very low inventory turnover ratio may indicate:
qa.a: slow-moving or obsolete stock
qa.e: Stock is not selling fast enough.

qa.q: Revenue ₹8,00,000; GP 20% on revenue; average inventory ₹1,60,000. Inventory turnover (times):
Inventory turnover ratio is classified as:
qa.a: an activity (turnover) ratio
qa.e: It measures how efficiently inventory is used.

qa.q: Credit revenue ₹7,50,000; trade receivables opening ₹1,20,000, closing ₹1,80,000. Trade receivables turnover (times):
Trade receivables turnover is 5 times. Average collection period:
qa.a: 73 days

qa.q: Net credit purchases ₹6,00,000; average trade payables ₹1,00,000. Trade payables turnover (times):
Trade payables turnover is 6 times. Average payment period in months:
qa.e: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 months.

qa.q: Total revenue ₹10,00,000, of which cash revenue is ₹2,00,000. Debtors ₹70,000 and bills receivable ₹10,000 (both average). Trade receivables turnover (times):
qa.e: Credit revenue ₹8,00,000 ÷ average receivables ₹80,000.

qa.q: Trade receivables for this ratio are taken:
qa.a: before deducting provision for doubtful debts
qa.e: Gross receivables are used, as provision is only an estimate.

qa.q: A falling trade receivables turnover over three years suggests:
qa.a: customers are taking longer to pay
qa.e: Lower turnover = more days outstanding.

qa.q: Average collection period is 73 days and credit revenue is ₹7,30,000. Average trade receivables:
qa.e: Turnover = 365 ÷ 73 = 5; receivables = 7,30,000 ÷ 5.

qa.q: Revenue ₹30,00,000; capital employed ₹15,00,000. Net assets turnover (times):
Revenue ₹30,00,000; net fixed assets ₹12,00,000. Fixed assets turnover (times):
Revenue ₹30,00,000; current assets ₹5,00,000; current liabilities ₹2,00,000. Working capital turnover (times):
Fixed assets turnover uses fixed assets:
qa.a: net of depreciation
qa.e: Net fixed assets (after depreciation) are used.

qa.q: Net assets turnover is 2 times and revenue is ₹40,00,000. Capital employed:
qa.e: Capital employed = 40,00,000 ÷ 2.

qa.q: A higher working capital turnover ratio generally indicates:
qa.a: efficient use of working capital
qa.e: More sales per rupee of working capital.

qa.q: Net assets turnover ratio is also called:
qa.a: capital employed turnover ratio
qa.e: Net assets = capital employed.

qa.q: Revenue ₹18,00,000; net fixed assets ₹6,00,000; working capital ₹3,00,000. Capital employed turnover (times):
Sales ₹10,50,000; sales returns ₹50,000; cost of revenue ₹7,00,000. Gross profit ratio:
Cost of revenue ₹7,00,000; operating expenses ₹1,00,000; net revenue ₹10,00,000. Operating ratio:
Operating ratio is 80%. Operating profit ratio:
qa.e: Operating profit ratio = 100 − operating ratio.

qa.q: Which is excluded while calculating operating ratio?
qa.a: Loss on sale of a fixed asset
qa.e: It is a non-operating item.

qa.q: Revenue ₹8,00,000; gross profit 25% on cost. Gross profit ratio (on revenue):
Operating profit ₹2,40,000; net revenue from operations ₹12,00,000. Operating profit ratio:
Gross profit ratio is a:
qa.a: profitability ratio
qa.e: It shows profit margin on revenue.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Operating ratio + Operating profit ratio = 100%.
Reason (R): Operating cost and operating profit together make up net revenue from operations.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Revenue = operating cost + operating profit, so their percentages total 100.

qa.q: PBT ₹1,50,000; revenue from operations ₹10,00,000. Net profit ratio (before tax):
PBT ₹1,50,000; tax ₹50,000; revenue ₹10,00,000. Net profit ratio (after tax):
PBT ₹1,50,000; interest on debentures ₹50,000; capital employed ₹10,00,000. ROI:
Share capital ₹5,00,000; reserves ₹1,00,000; 10% debentures ₹4,00,000; PBT ₹1,60,000. ROI:
qa.e: Interest ₹40,000 → PBIT ₹2,00,000; capital employed ₹10,00,000.

qa.q: Return on investment is computed as:
qa.a: PBIT ÷ Capital employed × 100
qa.e: ROI relates operating earnings to all long-term funds used.

qa.q: ROI is 20% while debentures cost 10%. Raising more debt (other things equal) is likely to:
qa.a: increase the return to equity shareholders
qa.e: Earning 20% on funds costing 10% benefits owners (trading on equity).

qa.q: PAT ₹90,000; tax ₹30,000; revenue ₹8,00,000. Net profit ratio based on PBT:
Capital employed for ROI can also be found as:
qa.a: non-current assets + working capital
qa.e: Assets-side view of capital employed.

qa.q: Current ratio 2 : 1 (CA ₹2,00,000; CL ₹1,00,000). Creditors of ₹50,000 are paid. New current ratio is ___ : 1.
Same firm (CA ₹2,00,000; CL ₹1,00,000) buys goods on credit for ₹50,000. New current ratio is ___ : 1.
Cash collected from debtors (current ratio 2 : 1). Effect on current ratio:
qa.a: No change
qa.e: One current asset replaces another; totals are unchanged.

qa.q: Issue of equity shares for cash. Effect on debt-equity ratio:
qa.a: Decrease
qa.e: Equity rises while debt is unchanged.

qa.q: Conversion of debentures into equity shares. Effect on debt-equity ratio:
qa.a: Decrease
qa.e: Debt falls and equity rises.

qa.q: Current ratio 2.5 : 1; quick ratio 1.5 : 1; current liabilities ₹80,000; no prepaid expenses. Inventory:
qa.e: CA = ₹2,00,000; quick assets = ₹1,20,000; inventory = difference.

qa.q: Revenue ₹6,00,000; gross profit ratio 25%; inventory turnover 6 times. Average inventory:
qa.e: Cost of revenue ₹4,50,000 ÷ 6.

qa.q: A company: current assets ₹4,00,000 (inventory ₹1,00,000); current liabilities ₹2,00,000; shareholders' funds ₹6,00,000; debentures ₹3,00,000. Which pair is correct?
qa.a: Quick ratio 1.5 : 1; debt-equity 0.5 : 1

qa.q: A cash flow statement shows:
qa.a: inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period
qa.e: It is a period statement of cash movements.

qa.q: Cash flow statements are prepared as per:
qa.a: AS 3 (Revised)
qa.e: AS 3 deals with cash flow statements.

qa.q: Which is NOT a cash flow?
qa.a: Cash deposited into the bank
qa.e: Both cash and bank are cash; the total does not change.

qa.q: A main benefit of a cash flow statement is that it helps to:
qa.a: assess the firm's ability to generate cash and meet obligations
qa.e: It reveals liquidity and cash-generating ability.

qa.q: Buying a treasury bill maturing in 2 months with cash is:
qa.a: not a cash flow, as both are cash and cash equivalents
qa.e: A treasury bill of ≤ 3 months is a cash equivalent.

qa.q: Why can a profitable company have a cash shortage?
qa.a: Profit includes non-cash items and credit sales, and cash may be tied up in inventories, receivables or new assets
qa.e: Accrual profit and cash flow differ.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A cash flow statement helps in short-term financial planning.
Reason (R): It shows the sources and uses of cash during a period.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Knowing where cash comes from and goes helps plan future needs.

qa.q: The three activities in a cash flow statement are:
qa.a: operating, investing and financing
qa.e: AS 3 uses these three heads.

qa.q: Cash in hand ₹20,000; bank ₹60,000; 2-month treasury bills ₹30,000; current investments ₹10,000; bank overdraft ₹25,000. Cash and cash equivalents:
qa.e: Cash ₹80,000 + equivalents ₹40,000; overdraft is a short-term borrowing.

qa.q: Cash equivalents generally have a maturity, from the date of acquisition, of:
qa.a: three months or less
qa.e: AS 3 uses the three-month test.

qa.q: Bank overdraft, in CBSE cash flow questions, is treated as:
qa.a: a short-term borrowing under financing activities
qa.e: Changes in overdraft are financing flows.

qa.q: Which is a cash equivalent?
qa.a: Commercial paper maturing in 60 days
qa.e: Short-term, highly liquid, with insignificant risk of value change.

qa.q: Why are equity shares not treated as cash equivalents?
qa.a: Their value can change significantly
qa.e: Cash equivalents must carry insignificant risk of change in value.

qa.q: Current investments in CBSE problems are treated as:
qa.a: marketable securities, i.e. cash equivalents
qa.e: This convention avoids treating their changes as cash flows.

qa.q: Cash includes:
qa.a: cash in hand and demand deposits with banks
qa.e: Demand deposits can be withdrawn at any time.

qa.q: Cash credit from a bank increased by ₹40,000 during the year. In the cash flow statement it is:
qa.a: a financing inflow of ₹40,000
qa.e: Cash credit is a short-term borrowing.

qa.q: Cash received from sale of goods is:
qa.a: an operating activity
qa.e: It arises from the principal revenue-producing activity.

qa.q: Purchase of machinery for cash is:
qa.a: an investing activity
qa.e: Acquisition of a long-term asset.

qa.q: Issue of debentures for cash is:
qa.a: a financing activity
qa.e: It changes the borrowings of the company.

qa.q: Sale of a patent for ₹50,000 is:
qa.a: an investing inflow
qa.e: Disposal of an intangible long-term asset.

qa.q: Payment of wages and salaries is:
qa.a: an operating outflow
qa.e: Employee costs are part of operations.

qa.q: Buy-back of equity shares is:
qa.a: a financing outflow
qa.e: It changes owners' capital.

qa.q: A manufacturing company receives ₹1,00,000 back from a loan it had given to another company. This is:
qa.a: an investing inflow
qa.e: Loans given and recovered by non-financial companies are investing activities.

qa.q: Cash received from customers ₹8,00,000; paid to suppliers ₹5,00,000; machinery bought ₹2,00,000; shares issued ₹3,00,000. Net cash from operating activities (ignoring other items):
qa.e: Only customer receipts and supplier payments are operating: 8,00,000 − 5,00,000.

qa.q: For a manufacturing company, interest paid on debentures is:
qa.a: a financing activity
qa.e: For non-financial enterprises it is a cost of borrowing – financing.

qa.q: For a manufacturing company, dividend received on investments is:
qa.a: an investing activity
qa.e: It is a return on investments.

qa.q: For a bank, interest received on loans given is:
qa.a: an operating activity
qa.e: Lending is the bank's principal business.

qa.q: Dividend paid by a bank is:
qa.a: a financing activity
qa.e: Dividends paid are always financing.

qa.q: Income tax paid is generally classified as:
qa.a: an operating activity
qa.e: Tax arises mainly from operations.

qa.q: A manufacturing company: interest received ₹20,000, dividend received ₹10,000, interest paid ₹15,000, dividend paid ₹40,000. Net cash flow from these items under investing activities:
qa.e: Only interest and dividend received go to investing: 20,000 + 10,000.

qa.q: In the same case, outflow under financing activities from these items:
qa.e: Interest paid ₹15,000 + dividend paid ₹40,000.

qa.q: An income tax refund received by a trading company is:
qa.a: an operating inflow
qa.e: Tax is operating, so its refund is an operating inflow.

qa.q: Surplus rose from ₹50,000 to ₹1,30,000; transfer to reserve ₹20,000; provision for tax made ₹40,000; interim dividend ₹10,000. Net profit before tax:
qa.e: Change ₹80,000 plus the three appropriations/charges.

qa.q: Using NPBT ₹1,50,000: depreciation ₹30,000; goodwill written off ₹10,000; loss on sale of machinery ₹5,000; interest on debentures ₹15,000; profit on sale of investments ₹8,000; dividend received ₹2,000. Operating profit before working capital changes:
Depreciation is added back to net profit in the indirect method because:
qa.a: it is a non-cash expense
qa.e: No cash goes out when depreciation is charged.

qa.q: Profit on sale of machinery is deducted from net profit because:
qa.a: the full sale proceeds are shown under investing activities
qa.e: Leaving it in would double count the gain.

qa.q: Interest paid on debentures is added back to net profit (for a non-financial company) because:
qa.a: it is shown as a financing outflow
qa.e: It is moved from operating to financing activities.

qa.q: Under AS 4 (revised), dividend of the previous year paid during the current year is:
qa.a: added back to find net profit before tax, and shown as a financing outflow
qa.e: It is an appropriation of current year's profit, not an expense.

qa.q: Which item is DEDUCTED while computing operating profit before working capital changes?
qa.a: Interest received on investments
qa.e: Interest received is a non-operating (investing) income for a non-financial company.

qa.q: Net profit before tax ₹1,00,000; depreciation ₹25,000; profit on sale of land ₹5,000. Operating profit before working capital changes:
An increase in trade receivables during the year is, in the indirect method:
qa.a: deducted from operating profit
qa.e: More credit sales uncollected means less cash.

qa.q: An increase in trade payables during the year is:
qa.a: added to operating profit
qa.e: Buying on credit conserves cash.

qa.q: Operating profit before WC changes ₹2,00,000; inventories +₹20,000; receivables −₹15,000; payables +₹10,000; outstanding expenses −₹5,000; prepaid expenses +₹2,000. Cash generated from operations:
qa.e: Net WC change = −₹2,000.

qa.q: Cash generated from operations ₹1,98,000; income tax paid ₹38,000. Net cash from operating activities:
A decrease in inventories is:
qa.a: added, because cash tied up in stock is released
qa.e: Selling stock without replacing it frees cash.

qa.q: Which item is NOT adjusted as a working capital change in operating activities?
qa.a: Increase in bank overdraft
qa.e: Bank overdraft is a short-term borrowing – financing activity.

qa.q: Profit before WC changes ₹1,00,000; trade receivables increased ₹30,000; trade payables decreased ₹10,000. Cash generated from operations:
qa.e: Both changes reduce cash: 1,00,000 − 30,000 − 10,000.

qa.q: Income tax paid during the year is shown:
qa.a: as a deduction to arrive at net cash from operating activities
qa.e: Tax paid is an operating outflow.

qa.q: Machinery: opening ₹5,00,000; closing ₹6,00,000; depreciation ₹50,000; book value of machinery sold ₹40,000. Machinery purchased:
In the same case, machinery is sold for ₹35,000. Net cash flow from these investing items:
Provision for tax: opening ₹30,000; closing ₹40,000; provision made during the year ₹50,000. Tax paid:
Provision for depreciation: opening ₹1,00,000; closing ₹1,30,000; accumulated depreciation on machinery sold ₹20,000. Depreciation charged for the year:
